On two benchmarks the method led standard accuracy and lost only about eleven percent under severe dual-modality dropout, beating supervised fusion baselines.
arxiv-2511-04451:
Patrik Valábek and three colleagues model nonlinear systems whose inputs arrive late. Delays make prediction and control hard, since the present state depends on the past. Their approach lifts the system into a space where its motion looks linear, using the Koopman operator.

A deep network with memory layers learns that lifted form on its own. The memory layers store past inputs, so no fixed dictionary of basis functions is needed. Older dictionary methods must guess those functions in advance, which often limits accuracy. A learned, delay-aware linear model could make control design for such systems far simpler.
arxiv-2511-04551:
Mohsen Hafez-Torbati and his co-author propose a route to a high-temperature quantum anomalous Hall effect. Their setting is a Néel antiferromagnetic Mott insulator on a buckled honeycomb lattice. Buckling lets a perpendicular electric field create a staggered potential across the layers.

Using a generalized Kondo lattice model, they show that potential can drive a phase change. The insulator becomes an antiferromagnetic Chern insulator with chiral edge states. The temperature where Hall conductance stays quantized depends mainly on spin-orbit strength and hopping. Above it, the conductance drifts as the spectrum broadens, which the authors track in detail.
arxiv-2511-04751:
Matteo Cercola and three colleagues add sensor guidance to human-in-the-loop optimization. Preference methods learn from pairwise choices when no direct cost can be measured. Tools like GLISp treat the system as a black box and ignore sensor readings.

Their regularized extension feeds measured descriptors into the preference loop. A physics-informed hypothesis function carries the sensor structure into the model. A least-squares penalty keeps that structure honest against user feedback. The grey-box mix keeps the freedom of preference learning while grounding it in numbers the system already measures during calibration. Calibration tasks stand to gain most from that added guidance.
arxiv-2511-04951:
Hexu Zhao and co-authors present CLM, a system that lets 3D Gaussian Splatting render huge scenes on one home-grade graphics card. Splatting gives fast, sharp new views, but large scenes need more memory than most cards hold.

CLM stores most Gaussians in main memory and loads each one only when the view needs it. Its plan uses known access patterns to overlap data moves with work and to shrink traffic. Tests show a scene with one hundred million Gaussians rendered on a single RTX 4090 card, with top-level image quality kept.
arxiv-2511-05151:
Marco Ornigotti links paraxial vector beams, light beams whose polarization varies across the beam, to topological field theory. Past work used a high-order sphere picture for such beams, which leaves their deep structure partly hidden.

Ornigotti shows the natural home for these beams is a bundle with SU(2) symmetry over space-time. In that frame, the linked spin and orbit parts of the beam match a non-Abelian Chern-Simons gauge theory. He ties the theory's charge to spin-orbit coupling and gives a simple test, via Wilson lines, to spot non-Abelian phases in the lab.
arxiv-2511-05351:
Sam Patrick and co-authors ask when a sloshing vortex in a tank acts like a black hole bomb. In the gravity tale, waves bounce between a spinning black hole and a mirror, grow each round, and destabilize the system.

A draining vortex in a finite tank does the same trick at its walls, seen as sloshing of the surface. The authors study a non-draining Rankine vortex with a smooth core, a more real case. They trace when the analogy holds and when the core's smooth swirl breaks it, a guide for lab tests of black hole traits.
arxiv-2511-05451:
Liz Blum and co-authors define the Sign Game, a two-player game on a graph where players take turns to mark each vertex plus one or minus one. Edges then take the product of their end marks, and the final score is the sum over all edges.

One player wants a positive score, the other a negative one. The authors play the game on many graph types and work out who wins and how. A simple rule set hides rich structure, since early marks set up late edge signs. The results add a fresh game to the study of graphs.
arxiv-2511-05651:
Hooman Davoudiasl, Jaime Hoefken Zink, and Sebastian Trojanowski argue that neutron stars could expose a dark matter candidate that Earth-based searches cannot touch. Their candidate is made in the early universe's heat and couples to electrons and muons through a flavor-changing particle. Earth has no muon targets, and its annihilation signal is weak, so normal searches fail.

Inside a neutron star, infalling dark matter speeds up and can scatter off both electrons and muons. A kinematic effect blocks it from cooling and settling, which keeps annihilation brisk. The star's surface would then glow warmer than expected. Future infrared telescopes could spot that heat, probing candidates beyond the reach of labs and accelerators.
arxiv-2511-05851:
Wen-Zhe Xi leads a team reporting a 2023 campaign to weigh the black hole in the galaxy NGC 5548. Their method, reverberation mapping, clocks how long light from near the black hole takes to echo off surrounding gas. Spectra came from a telescope in Lijiang, China, with visits roughly every two days.

Different emission lines lagged the continuum by different amounts, from about a day to about two weeks, mapping the gas region's layered structure. Combined with older seasons, the structure looks stable, while the gas motion shifts over time between orderly orbits and flows in or out. The black hole's average mass lands in line with a known relation tying mass to stellar motion.
arxiv-2511-06051:
Mahmoud El-Bahnasawi detects hate speech with a model a hundred times smaller than leading large models, at a fraction of the cost. Real-time moderation needs speed and low compute, which giant models cannot offer. His framework stacks three layers: rule-based pre-filtering, a tuned compact model, and continuous learning.

The core is BERTweet, a model built for social media text, tuned with a low-rank method that trains under two percent of its weights. Unified data sets and careful fine-tuning lift its quality. The system reached a macro F1 of zero point eight five, about ninety-four percent of a much larger safety model's score. Training took about two hours on one modest GPU. The author pitches it for settings where resources are tight.
arxiv-2511-06151:
Kristen Mazur and five co-authors classify the model structures that can live on a finite lattice. Model structures are the organizing frameworks of abstract homotopy theory, and transfer systems on finite posets have recently become central tools in equivariant homotopy theory. The two topics meet because transfer systems also appear naturally inside model structure data.

Using transfer systems as their main tool, the authors give a complete characterization of all model category structures on a finite lattice. Every such structure is accounted for, with no cases left open. The result builds new bridges between abstract homotopy theory and equivariant methods, two areas that often develop separately.
arxiv-2511-06251:
Mingde Xu and colleagues introduce WebVIA, a framework that turns interface designs into working web code. Turning a mockup into code is repetitive manual labor, and current vision-language tools produce only static pages with no working buttons or interactions. WebVIA is presented as the first agent-based system for interactive generation with built-in checking.

Three parts share the work: an exploration agent captures screenshots of an interface in many states, a generation model writes executable interactive code, and a validation module verifies that the interactions work. The exploration agent proved steadier than general-purpose rivals, and the fine-tuned generator beat its base models on both interactive and static benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-06451:
Jian'an Zhang builds a neural operator that prices options surfaces for the S&P 500 and the VIX together without allowing arbitrage. A term structure maps strikes and maturities to implied volatility, and any free lunch hidden in its shape breaks market logic. Prior learning methods often ignore those no-arbitrage rules entirely.

The system, ARBITER, learns under risk-neutral pricing while its decoders enforce calendar, vertical, and butterfly arbitrage bans plus smoothness and monotonicity limits. Training uses extragradient-style updates with projection steps. New scoring metrics for term structures accompany the model, and tests on historical data beat Fourier operators, DeepONet, and state-space rivals, with joined index and volatility legs helping most.
arxiv-2511-06751:
Tao Lv and five co-authors work on computational spectral imaging, a tool that captures a full spectrum of color at every pixel. Their target is spectral deconvolution imaging, a compact design that uses built optics but yields equations whose coefficients depend on the scene itself. That dependence makes fast, accurate reconstruction hard.

Their system, HSFAUT, unfolds an iterative solver into a neural network and moves subproblems into the frequency domain, turning tangled nonlinear steps into simpler linear ones. A transformer module gathers information across both space and frequency at each step. In simulated and real tests the method beat leading alternatives while using less memory and computation, and it worked across different imaging systems.
arxiv-2511-07051:
Yuxuan Zhou and five co-authors improve deepfake detectors by teaching them with a staged curriculum of synthetic fakes. Detectors generalize poorly when trained with one fixed augmentation strategy, while real forgeries keep evolving, from facial warping to expression tricks. Their system, CRDA, generates extra fakes from a tunable pool of forgery operations and raises difficulty as the detector learns.

A reinforcement learning agent picks augmentation actions based on how the detector is doing, searching the huge space of possible forgeries and shaping fake samples to its weaknesses. Causal inference guides the variation, cutting spurious correlations so the detector focuses on cues that truly mark a fake. Across multiple cross-domain data sets the method greatly beat leading methods at detecting unseen forgery types.
arxiv-2511-07251:
Valentina Bais and ten co-authors test whether a knot's trace remembers the knot in high dimensions. For a knot in a sphere, its trace is a manifold built from a surgery construction, and whether non-isotopic knots can share a diffeomorphic trace is a basic detection question. The team works with smooth knots of codimension two in spheres of dimension at least four.

They prove non-detection in general: for every such dimension there exist non-isotopic knots whose traces are diffeomorphic, shown twice, once by generalizing the RBG link construction and once through Plotnick's work. But the unknot is special. In every dimension at least four, the unknot is detected by the diffeomorphism type of its surgery, and hence of its trace, so no nontrivial knot can masquerade as nothing.
arxiv-2511-07551:
Charlie Hoy and Konstantin Leyde check whether fancier gravitational wave models change cosmology answers. Merging black holes give distances and masses that together can measure the universe expansion rate without any light. That trick depends on wave models matching Einstein theory closely.

Precession and higher-order ripples add realism but also heavy computing cost. Comparing inferences with and without those effects shows no significant gain for expansion measurements in the cases tested. Simpler models may suffice for this task, saving scarce analysis time. The finding helps survey teams spend effort where it truly sharpens cosmic measurements.
arxiv-2511-07651:
Yicheng Zhan, Fahim Ahmed, and Amy Burrell link crimes that one offender likely committed. Linking helps catch serial offenders, but crime records are high-dimensional, sparse, and mixed in type, which dilutes behavioral signals. Their Siamese autoencoder learns compact representations that expose hidden correlations.

Data come from the United Kingdom Violent Crime Linkage Analysis System run by the National Crime Agency. Geographic and time features enter at the decoder stage, strengthening behavioral patterns instead of washing them out. Paired network training then scores how alike two crimes are. Better linkage focuses detective work and can surface serial patterns earlier.
arxiv-2511-08351:
Bhawna Mukhija and co-authors examine how gravity darkening and stellar oblateness change winds from rapidly rotating massive stars. Fast rotation makes a star bulge and darkens its equator, altering the radiation driven wind. Within modified CAK theory, a fast wind answer can switch to a dense, slow Omega slow answer once rotation passes about three quarters of the critical speed.

Using the stationary Hydwind code for B type star models, the team separates the individual effects of darkening and oblateness before combining them. For some rotation ranges both wind answers coexist, and that interval depends strongly on starting settings. Gravity darkening alone shifts the coexistence range toward higher rotation values.
arxiv-2511-08551:
Bernhard Haeupler, Yonggang Jiang, and Thatchaphol Saranurak give the first deterministic algorithm that finds shortest paths in nearly linear time even when edge weights can be negative. Given a directed graph and a starting point, their method either computes every distance or reports a negative cycle.

Every earlier fast method for this problem used randomness, leaning on decompositions that split graphs into small-diameter pieces. The new work replaces that tool with path covers, a structure for directed graphs that plays the role neighborhood covers play for undirected ones. Beyond this result, the authors expect path covers to become a basic tool for removing randomness from other directed-graph algorithms.
arxiv-2511-09051:
Parsa Hedayatnia and four co-authors rebuild the catalog of smart contract bugs around how attacks actually work. Smart contracts lock large value into small locked programs, yet existing schemes sort flaws by symptoms like reentrancy rather than by the deep causes that let exploits happen.

The new scheme unifies Solidity flaws into eight root-cause families: control flow, external calls, state integrity, arithmetic safety, environmental dependencies, access control, input validation, and cross-domain protocol assumptions. Each family comes with compact code examples, the mechanics of the exploit, the fixes, and the signals that static, dynamic, and learning-based tools can observe. Legacy sets such as SmartBugs and SolidiFI are cross-mapped onto the families, showing label drift and coverage gaps. The authors intend the scheme as a shared language and audit checklist.
arxiv-2511-09251:
Lan Ma and three co-authors design storage codes that repair failed nodes while reading little data. Their codes aim for the smallest possible repair traffic. Their setting is binary MDS array codes, where any k of the stored columns can rebuild the whole file. Each column lives on a separate node in a distributed system.

Starting from any existing binary MDS array code, they give two generic constructions with optimal access for single-node failures. The first offers smaller sub-packetization and flexible choices of helper nodes and coefficients. The second, for suitable parameters, achieves the smallest sub-packetization known among optimal-bandwidth binary MDS array codes, the authors say. Both constructions generalize earlier hand-built families.
arxiv-2511-09651:
Yang Peng introduces a quantum energy pump whose workings are governed by geometry rather than brute force. The device uses a geometric quantum drive. It pairs a time-dependent Hamiltonian with a counterdiabatic term following a prescribed path on a control manifold. States are transported coherently within a degenerate subspace, without transitions out of it.

When the path's coordinates are driven independently, the net energy exchanged between drives is set by the non-abelian Berry-curvature tensor. Average pumping power is separately fixed by the initial state and by the Hamiltonian's topology through its Euler class. Peng outlines implementations with artificial atoms on trapped-ion, superconducting, and quantum-dot platforms. The pump could serve as a quantum transducer, a charger, or a probe of phase coherence.
arxiv-2511-09851:
Brendon Madison, writing alone, quantifies how precisely beam polarization must be known at future electron-positron Higgs factories. Polarized beams sharpen Higgs and electroweak measurements, but the benefit depends on how well the polarization itself is known. The study separates measurements that scale with the effective polarization from those that scale with the product of the two beam polarizations.

One finding cuts against intuition: better positron polarization relaxes precision demands for the first class of measurements but tightens them for the second. Checking three target measurements, Madison finds goals away from the Z pole are plausible with polarization known better than a tenth of a percent. The left-right asymmetry target is stricter, needing about two hundredths of a percent unless polarization values rise toward unity.
arxiv-2511-10151:
Alfio M. Bonanno, Samuele Silveravalle, and Andrea Spina study naked singularities in Einstein-Weyl gravity, a higher-derivative extension of general relativity. In Einstein's theory, such points without horizons are expected to be unstable and are excluded by the cosmic censorship idea. The authors focus on a class of horizonless solutions called attractive naked ones of a specific type, and test them against tensor perturbations.

Evolving the perturbation equations numerically in time, they find every mode decays with oscillatory tails, like massive field ripples in quadratic gravity. The configurations are therefore linearly stable and can persist as stationary objects. Because they mimic black holes observationally while having no horizon, the authors call them veiled ones and propose them as viable alternatives in higher-derivative gravity.
arxiv-2511-10351:
Matis Marcadier, Nicolas Forget, Yoann Pertot, and Aurelie Jullien measure the phase noise of supercontinuum light made in all-normal dispersion fibers that preserve polarization. Supercontinuum sources broaden a laser pulse into a rainbow of frequencies, and their coherence decides their value for precision work. The team quantifies stochastic phase noise driven by energy fluctuations, along with coefficients describing how intensity noise transfers into phase noise across the spectrum.

Their analysis confirms the supercontinuum they produce is highly coherent. The nonlinear broadening process is fundamentally deterministic, with ultra-low spectral phase noise, yet it shows large coupling from intensity to phase. Both facts matter for uses such as frequency metrology, where a quiet phase is the product being sold.
arxiv-2511-10551:
Suzanne Schlich studies Bowditch representations, a class of representations of the free group on two generators into the isometry groups of Gromov-hyperbolic spaces. These representations generalize conditions introduced by Bowditch and developed by Tan, Wong, and Zhang. They matter for understanding group actions on negatively curved spaces.

Schlich proves that one explicit constant, depending only on the space's hyperbolicity, controls the situation. Hyperbolicity of the images of primitive elements, plus finiteness of the short ones, forces a linear growth of lengths with word length. She characterizes Bowditch representations in several ways and shows they form an open domain of discontinuity in the character variety. As a result, she obtains a new characterization of Minsky's primitive-stable representations and a finite way to certify Bowditch representations.
arxiv-2511-10751:
Gabriel-Dominique Marleau and five co-authors forecast what the Extremely Large Telescope will see when it watches gas giants still in the act of forming. Few accreting planets have been caught so far, but the telescope's METIS spectrograph, with far higher sensitivity and a smaller inner working angle than current tools, should change that.

Focusing on hydrogen recombination lines such as Brackett alpha, the team combines a semianalytical model of the flow onto a planet and its circumplanetary disc with shock-emission physics. Their test case is the planet PDS 70 b. Both the planetary and disc surface shocks feed the line, which keeps a nearly constant width at low densities. For their fiducial case, the line's peak should be detectable in about ten minutes of observing.
arxiv-2511-10851:
Chris Umans and Siki Wang propose a new route past a long-standing barrier in factoring polynomials over finite fields. The fastest known algorithm runs with an exponent of three halves in the degree, and that exponent is widely believed to be a genuine barrier for the standard baby-steps giant-steps strategy.

Their alternative strategy leads them to a number-theoretic conjecture. It concerns covering the integers up to n by differences drawn from two surprisingly small sets of bounded size. They show that if the conjecture holds with both set-size and magnitude exponents below one half, the polynomial factoring exponent improves. The sets must also carry suitable structure. The strongest plausible case would give an exponent of four thirds, and a second consequence would speed up the best deterministic algorithms for factoring integers as well.
arxiv-2511-11351:
Jason Beh, Jerome Morio, and Florian Simatos study when covariance matrices estimated by importance sampling stay accurate in high dimensions, a question driven by the cross-entropy algorithm for rare-event problems. Their random matrix model has two twists: the data matrix and its weight matrix are dependent, and the weights are heavy-tailed. Sample size grows as a power of dimension in the regime they study.

They prove a sharp phase transition: the estimate converges exactly when the power passes a threshold set by the largest likelihood ratios. In common cases the threshold equals the inverse of the auxiliary spread's smallest eigenvalue. Simulations confirm that schemes with a larger smallest eigenvalue perform better.
arxiv-2511-11551:
Dena Mujtaba and three co-authors propose a way to steer already trained AI agents toward safer behavior without retraining them. Agents trained only to maximize reward can adopt harmful strategies, and retraining is slow and costly, so alignment has to happen while the agent acts.

Their method shapes policy at test time under model guidance, giving precise control over separate behavioral attributes rather than one blunt score. It is tested across varied reinforcement learning settings, where it manages the trade-off between reward and ethical limits in a principled way. For teams deploying agents in messy real settings, test-time steering offers a practical middle path.
arxiv-2511-11751:
Sanchit Sinha and three co-authors build Concept-RuleNet, a multi-agent system that makes vision-language model decisions explainable without giving up visual grounding. Such models predict well but hallucinate reasons, and existing neurosymbolic fixes extract their symbols from task labels alone, leaving symbols loosely tied to the actual image.

A concept generator first mines discriminative visual concepts straight from training images. Those concepts then condition a rule-based reasoning stage, so explanations cite features the system actually saw. Multiple agents divide the perception and reasoning labor. The design targets out-of-distribution cases, where fluent but ungrounded explanations are most dangerous and transparent reasoning matters most.
arxiv-2511-12051:
Scott Staniewicz and fourteen co-authors present a way to track ground movement with radar satellite data within hours of a new image arriving. The method uses interferometric synthetic aperture radar, which compares radar phases to spot surface shifts. Older workflows often reprocess the full archive each time, which slows real monitoring.

Their chain links phases in sequence, keeps consistency across batches without redoing past steps, and updates how it finds stable pixels as surfaces change. It helps make a continental-scale displacement product for North America from Sentinel-1 data. Checks against GPS show agreement at the millimetre level for ground speed estimates.
arxiv-2511-12351:
Bahareh Golchin and Banafsheh Rekabdar present a deep reinforcement learning system for finding anomalies in multivariate time series, such as data from many industrial sensors at once. High dimension, scarce labels and subtle links between sensors make the task hard. Their framework joins several tools in one learning loop.

A variational autoencoder compresses the data and cuts noise, while a recurrent Q-network classifies anomalies step by step. Dynamic reward scaling adjusts how much reconstruction and classification signals count during training, balancing exploration and exploitation. An active learning part picks the most uncertain samples for labeling, reducing hand work. Tests on two benchmarks are used to show what each part adds.
arxiv-2511-12551:
Md Fahad Equbal, S R Hassan and M. A. H. Ahsan use principal component analysis, an unsupervised learning tool, to reveal how competing correlations organize in quarter-filled Hubbard models of interacting electrons. Exact diagonalization on small cylindrical clusters gives correlation data, but charge, spin and pairing signals cross over in ways that are hard to read directly.

As the on-site repulsion grows, the analysis shows localization and a reordering of the low-energy spectrum without any assumed order parameter. The leading components separate cleanly into charge-dominated, spin-dominated and pairing-dominated regimes for both the simple and extended models. The authors present the approach as a transparent bridge between exact calculations and machine learning diagnostics for strongly correlated matter.
arxiv-2511-12751:
Timur Anvar, Jeffrey Chen, Yuyan Wang, and Rohan Chandra run a case study on using small language models to help self-driving cars on highways. Reinforcement learning drivers struggle because reward functions miss the social and semantic richness of merging and dense traffic. Language models reason well about such context, but they can be unstable, inconsistent, slow, and costly when used for direct control. The authors test a middle path: the model only shapes rewards in training, while a learned policy drives.

They compare three setups. Plain reinforcement learning reached moderate success rates. Language-model-only drivers succeeded more often, up to ninety-four percent, but drove far too slowly. Hybrids landed between the two. Even when told to value efficiency, the language-model-guided agents showed a systematic conservative bias that varied by model. The authors conclude today's small models have real limits in control loops.
arxiv-2511-12851:
Kang Yin and Hye-Bin Shin introduce NeuroLex, a small language model trained only on EEG report text. Electroencephalogram reports follow tight linguistic and diagnostic conventions that general models handle poorly. NeuroLex learns from the Harvard Electroencephalography Database, using span-corruption pretraining plus fine-tuning on report polishing, paragraph summarization, and terminology questions. The aim is a model that speaks the dialect of EEG interpretation, usable alone or as the language backbone of systems that pair brain signals with text.

In tests it reached lower perplexity, better extraction and summary scores, and stronger robustness to negation and factual hallucination than general models of the same size, while needing fewer labels. The authors position it as a bridge between biomedical text modeling and brain-computer interface work. A small model that knows one clinical genre deeply may serve hospitals better than a giant generalist.
arxiv-2511-13451:
Alice P. G. Hall, Carlos H. S. Vieira, and Jonas F. G. Santos study how to sharpen estimates of unknown values in Gaussian quantum states. Gaussian states are central to quantum optics and can be read through their first and second moments, which makes them practical in the lab. Their twist is to prepare the probe with two non-commuting Gaussian measurements.

Adjustable uncertainty settings in that preparation can raise the quantum Fisher information, the measure that caps how precise any estimate can be. Starting from a thermal probe can also create coherence, and both its amount and its rate of change affect the gain. Tests on attenuator and amplifier channels show the idea works with current optical tools.
arxiv-2511-13751:
Shinnung Jeong and 5 co-authors describe VOLT, an open-source compiler toolchain for the Vortex graphics processor. Open GPU hardware now defines its own instruction sets, but running and tuning existing GPU programs on them needs a compiler whose cost is often undercounted. VOLT was built to fill that gap for the Vortex architecture.

Its layered design generates and optimizes single-instruction multiple-thread code across several abstraction levels, so many front-end languages and hardware variants can share one core. Core analyses and optimizations live in the middle end, where they can be reused and adapted as architectures evolve. Two case studies, on instruction extensions and host runtime support, show how the toolchain absorbs new hardware features.
arxiv-2511-14451:
Zhijun Tu and four co-authors test PyEMILI, a program that names spectral lines in gas clouds in space. They run it on deep spectra from glowing nebulae, young star regions, and jets from young stars. Clear line names are needed before anyone can infer heat, density, or chemical makeup from the light.

The program finds more lines, and names them more correctly, than past manual lists. The team also add new data for faint lines from heavy elements and a fitting tool based on random sampling. Their results form a benchmark set for future studies. The paper shows how automated naming can support careful plasma analysis.
arxiv-2511-14551:
Gabriel Mastrilli studies how to estimate the structure factor of spatial point processes with best possible accuracy. The structure factor summarizes second order clustering in a random pattern of points. Mastrilli first proves a minimax lower bound tailored to those second order traits. No estimator can beat that bound in the worst case.

He then builds a multitaper estimator that reaches the optimal rate. Under a mixing condition he proves a sharp concentration bound. A data driven rule chooses the number of tapers with an oracle guarantee. Numerical tests show the method works well in practice. The paper gives both limits and a matching practical estimator.
arxiv-2511-14651:
Jan Naumann explains how to compute derivatives of truncated matrix decompositions, a need that shows up across machine learning and physics codes. Modern software learns and simulates by automatic differentiation, which requires stable gradient formulas for linear algebra steps. Truncation keeps only the largest parts of a decomposition, yet the derivative must be written using only those kept parts.

The note gathers prior results and works through the missing terms in full detail. It covers both the singular value and eigenvalue versions of the problem. Readers get a careful reference for building gradient code that stays correct even when most of the decomposition has been thrown away.
arxiv-2511-14851:
Shengyi Liu, Kun-Feng Lyu, and four co-authors propose hunting axion dark matter with an unusually sharp nuclear transition in silver. The silver-109 line used in Mössbauer spectroscopy is extremely narrow, which makes it a fine sensor for tiny energy shifts. A passing axion field would make a key angle of the strong force wobble in time, and that wobble would shift nuclear binding energies.

From existing line-width measures, the team already draws limits that beat other laboratory bounds in part of the range. They then design a dedicated setup to watch for the time-varying signal directly. The method could reach axion masses that atomic-clock searches cannot, opening fresh ground in the dark matter hunt.
arxiv-2511-14951:
Sam Fisher, Dmitry Lesnik, and Tobias Schäfer build sound frequentist methods for measuring racial gaps in loan approvals when race itself is not recorded. Fair lending checks often must guess each applicant's race from name and address, using a standard geocoding method. Popular shortcut estimators built on those guesses are known to be biased, even under generous assumptions.

The authors recast the problem as an instrumental variables design, where the race predictors must be unrelated to the approval decision itself. On that footing they deliver ordinary least squares and maximum likelihood estimators with valid frequentist behavior. A recent Bayesian solution showed the way; this work gives regulators and banks a matching classical toolkit.
arxiv-2511-15951:
Alexander Galarraga and Alexander Wang characterize degree sets of certain curves over Henselian fields. Such fields are valued fields with a strong lifting property, and they include the p-adic numbers. The degree set of a curve collects the degrees of its points over field extensions. Past work showed it can miss infinitely many multiples of the curve index over p-adic fields. That cannot occur over finitely generated fields.

They focus on curves with a cyclic cover of the projective line of prime degree. Under mild assumptions, they fully characterize how and when that missing-multiples behavior can occur. They also give a method to compute degree sets for curves of this special type.
arxiv-2511-16351:
Abhishek Mandal, Joy Ghosh, Maruthi Manoj Brundavanam, and Shailendra K Varshney study how genuine three-way entanglement can be created in a small hybrid device. The device has two coupled light resonators, one of them also coupled to a single two-level atom. Entanglement shared by all three parts at once is a valuable resource for quantum networks.

Working in a weak driving regime, the authors build an analytic description of a shared excitation spread across both photonic modes and the atom. Using a tripartite concurrence measure, they map where the three-way correlation is strongest. Loss rates and detuning mismatches control a switch from ordinary atom-photon entanglement to a delocalized three-party state, giving designers a clear route to steady multipartite resources in coupled cavity systems.
arxiv-2511-16451:
L. J. Milligan reports the status of the SABRE South dark matter test at an underground laboratory in Australia. SABRE tests a long standing claimed seasonal signal from an Italian sensor using ultra pure sodium iodide crystals. A southern hemisphere twin can split seasonal site effects from a true dark matter modulation. Crystals sit inside a liquid scintillator veto with passive shielding and a muon veto.

The underground facility lies more than a kilometer deep in a former mine. Background from sensor solids has been assessed and mitigated in detail. Crystal and veto performance are characterized before full science running. Assembly was nearing completion with first subsystems installed. The proceedings update the community on expected sensitivity and readiness.
arxiv-2511-16551:
Perrine Chassat and four co-authors test whether generative AI can supply synthetic control arms for clinical trials, where slow enrollment and high cost bite hardest in oncology and rare diseases. The hard part is the time-to-event endpoint, the primary outcome in such trials, which censoring and small samples make difficult to model.

Their variational autoencoder generates mixed-type patient covariates and survival outcomes together in one latent framework, without assuming censoring is independent. On synthetic and real trial data it beat GAN baselines on fidelity, utility, and privacy, in both data-sharing and control-arm uses. The study also exposes miscalibration of error rates and power, and proposes a later selection step that improves calibration, marking both progress and open problems.
arxiv-2511-16651:
Yang Tian and fifteen co-authors release InternData-A1, a large synthetic dataset for training generalist robot policies, and the first evidence that synthetic data alone can match top real-robot data at pre-training scale. The set holds over 630,000 trajectories and about 7,400 hours across four robot bodies, 18 skills, 70 tasks, and 227 scenes.

A highly autonomous simulation pipeline composes long-horizon skills with little manual tuning, covering rigid, articulated, deformable, and fluid objects. A model with the same architecture as a leading real-data policy, pre-trained only on InternData-A1, matched that policy across 49 simulation tasks, five real-world tasks, and four long-horizon dexterous tasks. It even transferred from simulation to reality without fine-tuning on several hard tasks. The dataset is public.
arxiv-2511-17051:
Chek Beng Chua studies homogeneous convex cones, geometric objects that appear in optimization and in the theory of symmetric spaces. A basic question about a cone is its Carathéodory number, roughly the smallest number of extreme pieces needed to build any point inside it. Chua approaches the question through spectrahedral representations, which describe cones using matrix inequalities.

He characterizes exactly which homogeneous cones have ranks matching their Carathéodory numbers. That result then settles a second question: a homogeneous cone is self-dual precisely when its rank matches the numbers of both the cone's closure and its dual. A third result pins down which sparse matrix-described cones can be homogeneous, tying them to special graphs. The paper gives cone theory a sharper set of classification tools.
arxiv-2511-17151:
Naira Petrosyan and five co-authors model a solar cell design that tries to beat the usual limits by adding an intermediate energy band. In their device, a superlattice of quantum dots sits inside gallium arsenide based material. The dots are tiny semiconductor islands in a regular cubic pattern. Together they create that extra band, letting the cell harvest photons that would otherwise pass through unused. Modeling such a device realistically requires linking quantum physics to device-scale transport.

Their multiscale framework computes the superlattice band structure and its absorption accurately, mixes in measured absorption data, and feeds the result into a drift-diffusion device simulation that includes thermal and radiative losses. The best design used a superlattice period of about 14 nanometers and reached an efficiency near 13 percent. Wider spacing absorbed more in the miniband but generated less current elsewhere, so efficiency fell.
arxiv-2511-17251:
Lucas Darius Konrad asks a familiar question with a sharper model: do free markets underinvest in basic research? Basic discoveries spill over to everyone, so no single firm captures their full value, while applied research pays its sponsor more directly. Konrad builds a general equilibrium growth model with firms entering and exiting freely, and distinguishes basic research from high-type and low-type applied research in a heterogeneous firm population. A new, flexible formulation captures how basic research spillovers spread.

His findings are stark: no market outcome gives basic research a noteworthy share, because private returns cannot support it. A sizable subsidy is needed just to crowd basic research in, and the welfare gains then become substantial. Approaching the social planner's solution in a feasible way, he argues, requires purely state-financed basic research alongside the market.
arxiv-2511-17351:
Massimiliano Manenti and Andrea Iannelli supply missing theory for hierarchical reinforcement learning, where an agent learns at several levels of abstraction at once. Their focus is feudal Q-learning, a scheme in which managers set goals and workers learn to achieve them, with all levels updating together. Coupled updates like these can oscillate or diverge, and guarantees have lagged behind the method's practical appeal.

Using stochastic approximation theory and its associated ordinary differential equation method, the authors prove conditions under which feudal Q-learning converges and remains stable. A pleasing interpretation follows: the limit point is an equilibrium of a suitably defined game between the levels. Experiments with the algorithm support the theory's predictions. The result opens hierarchical reinforcement learning to game theory analysis, and gives practitioners sound conditions to design against.
arxiv-2511-17651:
Tommaso Milanese, Baris Can Efe, Claudio Bruschini, Nobukazu Teranishi, and Edoardo Charbon propose putting the programmable logic chip inside a single-photon camera rather than beside it. Their sensors count individual photons and time their arrival, and they are usually paired with a separate programmable board for flexible processing. Moving that logic on-chip, in direct contact with the sensing pixels or clusters, is the core idea.

The team shows an architecture that handles time stamps and photon counts through programmable weighted sums built from look-up tables, processed in layers to save power and simplify connections. They also show how small neural networks can be built and reprogrammed the same way. The design aims at cameras that adapt to a scene on the fly.
arxiv-2511-17751:
Jason DeVito and Joan West construct new curved spaces in geometry, working in dimensions that follow a specific pattern starting from eleven. They focus on generalized Eschenburg spaces and on metrics whose sectional curvature is positive almost everywhere, a strong and rare kind of bending.

In each such dimension they build infinitely many examples. For higher dimensions, many of these spaces differ in shape type from every uniform, homogeneous space. That gives the first endless family of its kind, expanding what geometers know about spaces that can carry almost positive curvature.
arxiv-2511-17851:
Hiroyoshi Nakano and Yuki Minami show that a strange feature of turbulence, energy dissipation that stays finite even as viscosity vanishes, also appears in a much simpler flow. In their setup a fluid sits still at large scale while a steady gradient is imposed, yet tiny thermal fluctuations grow very large.

Simulations and a self consistent theory show that those long range fluctuations create the anomaly. Simple linear theory predicts a runaway, but nonlinear coupling tames it into a finite value. The finding gives a non turbulent setting for studying singular behavior in fluids and links it to noise plus driving.
arxiv-2511-18151:
Rajat Bhattacharjya, Sing-Yao Wu, Hyunwoo Oh, and five co-authors present AVERY, a system that lets drones in disaster zones use large vision language models for queryable intelligence. Such models are too heavy to run on board, and disaster networks are slow and unstable, so naive cloud offloading fails.

AVERY treats the operator's intent as a first class goal and splits computation by function. A fast, low resolution stream gives live awareness, and a slower, high fidelity stream gives deep analysis, partitioned between edge and cloud as needed. A small onboard controller watches network and intent and picks compression settings. Tests show large energy savings and accuracy near the best static setup.
arxiv-2511-18351:
Voalaza Mahavily Romuald Aubert and Benjamin Randrianirina give closed forms for a wide class of number triangles. Such triangles grow row by row, with each entry built from two in the row above, scaled by weights that may shift with place. Path counting on a grid yields a master formula for the whole class.

In the case where the weights are straight line forms in the row and column, the formula takes a neat closed shape. Simpler forms drop out in key sub cases, and a known formula style handles the fully general case. A much used sub case, with one weight fixed at one, gets a matrix form too. Uses include closed forms for the r-Eulerian numbers and checks on known sequences.
arxiv-2511-18451:
Susanne Pumpluen sorts a family of nonstandard division algebras by when they count as the same under a loose match. The algebras, named for Petit, are built from skew polynomials over a field with a cyclic twist. In such a ring the order of factors matters, guided by a field symmetry.

She shows two seed polynomials give like algebras just when they share a bound value, a key invariant. A finer result links seeds whose core plain polynomials share degree and sit in one orbit of a group action. For finite fields she counts the exact number of match classes when the twist degree tops two. The count settles the sort for this family.
arxiv-2511-18751:
Daiqing Wu, Dongbao Yang, Yu Zhou, and Can Ma read the sentiment of image text posts when one part is poor or missing. Social posts pair a photo with a caption, and joint reads beat single part reads. In the wild, though, a photo may be blurred or a caption lost, and most models assume both parts arrive clean.

Their DRF method keeps a queue of past features for each part, which sketches that part's feature distribution. A weak part can then be rebuilt from its queue, and its weight in the joint call can be cut. Missing and low grade parts are handled in one frame. Tests target robust calls under real post flaws. Sentiment tools that bend, not break, are the goal.
arxiv-2511-18951:
Pablo Tuero and five co-authors join superconductivity with spintronics through a filtered tunnel barrier. The field aims at spin polarized supercurrents for energy thrifty cryogenic devices. A key prize is pairs of electrons with matched spins, which carry spin over long range in superconductor ferromagnet hybrids.

Most devices join the two materials in direct contact, since an insulating layer was thought to cut spin from charge flow. The team show that view fails when a thin barrier filters by electron symmetry and spin orbit traits. Such a barrier can in fact boost the giant tunneling magnetoresistance that symmetry filtering drives. Epitaxial stacks with a tuned barrier may thus carry spin supercurrents across a gap once thought dead.
arxiv-2511-19051:
Xiaogang Li and Changchang Xi study a special family of algebras built from a single matrix, called centralizer matrix algebras. Every finite algebra over a field can be viewed through two matrices, so the one-matrix case is a basic building block. Their work asks when two such algebras are linked by a stable equivalence, a loose form of sameness used in representation theory.

The authors give a complete answer using a new equivalence relation on matrices, valid over any field. They show that these stable links are also equivalences of Morita type, so they preserve three key size measures: dominant, finitistic, and global dimension. Their methods also settle a named conjecture for pairs involving a centralizer algebra.
arxiv-2511-19351:
Abdurahman Ali Mohammed and six co-authors release CellFMCount, a large data set for teaching computers to count cells in microscope images. Counting by hand is slow and error-prone, yet training data have stayed scarce, often under five hundred images. Their collection changes that scale.

The set holds over three thousand fluorescence images from cell differentiation experiments, with more than four hundred thirty thousand hand-marked cell locations. Dense packing, overlapping and varied cell shapes, and uneven staining make it a hard test. The authors benchmark regression, crowd-counting, and cell-counting methods on the data, giving the field a shared and demanding yardstick.
arxiv-2511-19551:
Mikhail Zubarev presents SPARTA, a scheduler for variational quantum algorithms that are plagued by barren plateaus, flat regions where training stalls. As quantum systems grow, those plateaus make optimization exponentially hard, and no practical method offered finite-sample safety for crossing them. SPARTA aims to explore risky regions while controlling that risk.

Three parts work together. A chi-square calibrated test tells plateaus from informative ground. A trust-region step rejects false gains caused by shot noise. An exploitation phase then converges at an optimal rate. The author proves bounds on plateau exit times and linear convergence inside good basins, using Lie-algebraic proxies to sharpen the tests.
arxiv-2511-19651:
Lishuo Pan and four co-authors keep small flying robots safe when the world refuses to match their models. Control barrier functions can certify safety, but wind gusts or extra payload change a drone's dynamics and void the certificate. Their controller learns the mismatch while flying.

A neural ordinary differential equation model updates online inside a high-order adaptive barrier function, which handles safety limits that depend on several derivatives. The hybrid controller is flown on a thirty-eight gram nano quadrotor. It holds a safe distance from an obstacle against wind near eighteen kilometers per hour, showing the guarantee can adapt in real time.
arxiv-2511-19751:
Abdul Rahman Diab and four co-authors release a software toolkit for putting pathology foundation models to clinical work. Whole-slide images are huge, model features are opaque, and adaptation choices are many, so testing these models on a real task is slow. PathFMTools is a light Python package for running, analyzing, and visualizing such models.

The test task is grading cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, a skin cancer grade that guides staging and care. Two leading vision-language models, CONCH and MUSK, are benchmarked on four hundred forty stained slides. Several adaptation strategies are compared, and small specialist models trained on foundation features show real promise.
arxiv-2511-20251:
Ruan, Hsiao, Lo, Wu, and Shuai restore variety to images made from long prompts. Their 2025 paper studies text-to-image models under detailed instructions. Long prompts add content, layout, and style detail. Fidelity rises, but outputs grow repetitive and dull. The team measures that trade-off systematically.

A new benchmark, LPD-Bench, scores fidelity and diversity together. Four leading models were tested on it. SD3.5-Large, Flux, CogView4, and Qwen-Image all showed the slump. Diversity fell clearly as prompts grew longer. Their fix, PromptMoG, needs no retraining at all. It jitters the prompt embedding before generation. Samples come from a mixture of Gaussians around it. Sampling entropy rises while meaning stays anchored. Diversity improved across all four models consistently. Semantic drift stayed in check throughout tests. Theory links prompt rewriting to higher entropy. Creative tools regain range without losing obedience. Other media may adopt the trick later.
arxiv-2511-20451:
Fang, Wei, and Zheng construct heat flows that explode at chosen spots. Their 2025 mathematics paper studies a nonlinear heat equation on a half-space. Heat spreads inside a four-dimensional region above a flat boundary. Along that boundary, outward flow feeds back as the square of temperature. Such feedback can drive temperatures to infinity in finite time.

The authors prove blow-up solutions exist for any small time horizon. Pick any number of distinct boundary points in advance. Suitable starting data makes the solution blow up exactly there. Near the blow-up moment the profile decomposes into bubbles. Each bubble is a rescaled copy of one universal shape. That shape comes from a fractional Yamabe problem. A smooth background term stays negative at the blow-up points. Bubble scales shrink to zero at a rate with logarithmic corrections. Centers drift toward the prescribed points as time runs out.
arxiv-2511-20751:
Minju Lee and a large team unveil in 2025 ECOGAL, a project mining the ALMA radio telescope's public archive for galaxy data. Instead of new observations, they reprocessed archived data wherever the Webb and Hubble telescopes had already mapped the sky. From those overlaps they built two catalogues, one anchored to known optical galaxies and one blind, from ALMA detections alone.

This first release covers the CANDELS fields COSMOS, GOODS-S, and UDS, taking in about 130,000 optically selected galaxies. Together the methods found 1,288 detections, 622 of them unique sources. Of those, 307 have spectroscopic redshifts, placing them across most of cosmic history. Adding the UDS field and public Webb data pushes past the earlier A3COSMOS and A3GOODS-S projects. The team releases the catalogues as science-ready products for studying cosmic gas, dust, and hidden star formation.
arxiv-2511-20851:
Mousam Sinha, Tirtha Sarathi Ghosh, and Ridam Pal put in 2025 a feature-selection folk trick on firm statistical footing. Faced with thousands of candidate predictors, analysts often add random noise features and keep every real feature ranked more important than the strongest noise one. The trick works but has no theory and no principled stopping rule. Their method, NABFS, keeps the noise calibration and adds a non-parametric bootstrap hypothesis test for each feature.

Every candidate is tested against the maximum importance among the noise features, with resampling supplying the significance judgement that heuristics lack. In controlled simulations the method recovered signal more consistently than Boruta, the random-forest wrapper it most resembles, and than Knockoff-based methods. On real-world datasets it surpassed Boruta, Recursive Feature Elimination, and Extra Trees. The authors argue principled stopping matters as datasets grow: a selector should certify which rankings mean something.
arxiv-2511-21151:
Marco Alecci and colleagues document in 2025 how the same Android app quietly becomes a different app depending on where it is downloaded. They name one phenomenon GeoTwins: look-alike apps with shared branding released under different package names in different countries, like the game Unison League's Japanese and English editions. Despite the identical storefront face, twins diverge in privacy disclosures, requested permissions, and third-party libraries. A second finding cuts deeper: even the base.apk inside Android App Bundles, assumed identical everywhere, varies by region.

The consequences are practical. A malware study can call an app benign while another calls it malicious, purely because of download geography, silently biasing years of research. Users, meanwhile, consent to one product and receive another. The team built a multi-region collection pipeline, analysed thousands of apps, and released a curated dataset of 81,963 GeoTwins. Their advice targets researchers, developers, platforms, and regulators alike.
arxiv-2511-21751:
Single author Mohsen Soltanifar classifies every real-valued sequence by its long-run behavior, in 2025. The space of all such sequences is usually studied as an infinite-dimensional vector space. Soltanifar instead sorts each sequence by a pair of numbers: its limit inferior and limit superior, the floor and ceiling its values approach.

That simple profile partitions the whole space into seven mutually disjoint blocks, running from finite convergence through bounded and unbounded oscillation. Each block gets explicit closed-form examples. Every class holds as many sequences as there are real numbers. The paper maps how blocks connect at two scales: an idealized graph from injective mappings, and a finer relation from pointwise multiplication. The finite-convergence block emerges as the only true subspace and a global attractor with no outgoing links. The product structure realizes about two-thirds of all possible connections between blocks.
arxiv-2511-21851:
Rodriguez and colleagues revisit ADE minimal string theories, simplified two-dimensional string models. The A-series is understood through solvable two-matrix models. The D- and E-series are conjectured to correspond to unsolvable four-matrix integrals nobody can solve directly. The team instead computes observable amplitudes, scattering-like quantities, by direct numerical integration over the moduli space, the space of possible surfaces.

They calculated sphere four-point and torus one-point amplitudes for the A, D, and E minimal strings, confirming some results, disproving others, and supplying new data where matrix models make no prediction. From amplitudes with conformal boundaries they found evidence for multi-matrix structure in the D-series, including a ramp behaviour in cylinder diagrams and departures from the instanton pattern expected of two-matrix models. They also ran a preliminary positivity bootstrap fencing in the D-series critical points.
arxiv-2511-21951:
Wang and colleagues demonstrate a quantum machine learning advantage that grows as the system gets bigger, using light. Photons are robust, work at room temperature, and keep their quantum states for a long time, but how their large state space helps learning was unclear until now. The combined team proves that the learning capacity of linear optical circuits grows polynomially with the number of photons, so more photons mean learning from less data.

They then ran real experiments on a fully programmable integrated photonic chip, training it online, on the device, for unitary learning and metric learning tasks. The experiments confirmed the theory: higher photon numbers reached lower test loss and needed smaller training datasets to generalize, exactly the scaling their proofs predict for this platform. Adding photons becomes a reliable dial for better performance, not fragility.
arxiv-2511-22251:
Hojny and Roy, optimization researchers, bring symmetry handling to Benders decomposition. A workhorse method that solves large mixed-integer programs by projecting out some variables and reintroducing their effect through cuts generated on demand by a separation oracle. Symmetry techniques turbocharge ordinary solvers, but they never transferred systematically to Benders setups because the cuts are not written down anywhere; they exist only inside the oracle. So the symmetry of the whole problem was invisible.

The authors build a tailored family of graphs capturing the symmetry information of both the master problem and the oracles. Once graph symmetries are computed by established tools, classical symmetry handling becomes available inside the decomposition. They add separation and aggregation techniques for symmetric cuts that substantially cut the number of oracle calls. Numerical tests on bin packing and scheduling problems show the combined effect, .
arxiv-2511-22351:
Bagaria, a machine learning researcher, builds a deepfake detector that also explains itself, even on heavily degraded images. Detectors usually emit a bare verdict and collapse under compression, downsampling, and domain shift, which undermines trust exactly where verification matters. INSIGHT super-resolves the image to amplify forensic traces, localizes suspicious regions with Grad-CAM heat maps. Aligns them with CLIP semantics, then has a vision-language model reason step by step over what it found.

A dual-stage check screens explanations for hallucination. Across test scenes, down to 16 by 16 pixel resolutions in their evaluation, the system improves detection robustness and explanation quality over prior baselines. The framework aims at forensic workflows where an unexplained flag is not enough. Each explanation names the artifact it relies on, so a human reviewer can verify the claim against the image instead of trusting the model.
arxiv-2511-22751:
Papazov, D'Angelo, and Flammarion ask whether gradient learning can master an algorithm exactly. Neural networks fail at length generalisation in arithmetic, memorising patterns that break on longer inputs. Their framework uses Differentiable Finite-State Transducers, a Turing-complete model family avoiding earlier architectures' traps: constant precision, constant time per step, and end-to-end log-parallel differentiable training. Training data are policy-trajectory observations, an expert's intermediate steps, not just inputs and outputs.

Trained on tiny datasets, the transducers learn binary and decimal addition and multiplication, then generalise without error to inputs thousands of times longer than any seen in training. That is exact learning in the strict sense: the correct rule applied to every input, achieved by ordinary gradient descent. They present it as evidence that differentiable agents given structured intermediate supervision can acquire precise algorithmic skills, toward systems whose arithmetic can be trusted rather than checked.
arxiv-2512-00051: Amelia Fernández Seguel, an undergraduate engineering student at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, studies how magnetic forces act between tiny robots. Her project covers modeling those forces and using them to control the robots' motion. Microrobots are small machines that can be steered without direct contact, and magnetic fields are a common way to move them. The surviving record gives the topic, the author, and the program setting, but no abstract text. Her methods and results therefore cannot be described in more detail here.
arxiv-2512-00251:
Internet-of-things networks are easy targets for denial-of-service attacks, because their devices are many and often weak. Henry Onyeka and co-authors propose SD-CGAN in 2025, a framework for spotting such attacks at the network edge. Traffic there is dynamic and heavily imbalanced.

SD-CGAN is a conditional generative adversarial network enhanced with Sinkhorn divergence, tailored for anomaly detection in edge environments. It is designed to catch sophisticated attacks and zero-day exploits that known signatures miss. Reliable detection protects everyday connected devices, from cameras to sensors, that owners rarely monitor themselves. Edge deployment keeps detection close to the devices under attack, cutting response time. Generative models help because attack traffic is too varied for fixed signatures alone.
arxiv-2512-00451:
Voice calls over satellite, maritime, and tactical links are expensive because bandwidth is scarce. Siyu Wang, Haitao Li, and Donglai Zhu present STCTS in 2025, a generative semantic compression framework for speech at ultra-low bitrates. Traditional codecs struggle below one kilobit per second.

Earlier semantic approaches convert speech to text and back, sacrificing prosody and speaker identity. STCTS decomposes speech explicitly into text, prosody, and timbre, then regenerates natural voice from that compact description. Keeping the speaker's tone and identity at very low rates could change communication wherever bandwidth is precious. The target rate, around eighty bits per second, is far below ordinary telephony. Prosody carries emotion and emphasis, which text-only schemes throw away.
arxiv-2512-00551:
Equal sums of like powers form a classical Diophantine puzzle: two pairs of numbers whose powers match. Valery Asiryan studies the equation under an extra linear constraint in 2025, calling the approach the linear slicing method. The variables are nonnegative integers and the exponent is real and greater than one.

Modular and geometric constraints narrow where solutions can hide. Linear slicing cuts the search space with a condition linking the pair sums, turning a wild problem into a structured one. Such equations connect to taxicab numbers and Euler's sum of powers, small questions that have driven number theory for centuries. The linear constraint is the slicing move that gives the method its name.
arxiv-2512-00651:
Mohammed Latif Siddiq, Arvin Islam-Gomes, Natalie Sekerak, and Joanna Santos examine how repeatable recent software research really is. Their 2025 study covers papers that use large language models to help with software engineering tasks. Repeatable work lets other teams check results and build on them with trust.

The team mined and reviewed hundreds of papers from top venues in software, machine learning, and language work, spanning 2020 to 2025. They pulled structured details from the papers, code stores, and project notes. Their large survey gives the field a clear baseline on what authors share, and what they leave out.
arxiv-2512-00851:
Du Wenzhang wrote a 2025 paper on forecasting traffic across many cities at once. Traffic patterns differ sharply by city: road networks vary in size and shape, and data volume can differ by orders of magnitude. New cities may join with only a few weeks of logs.

Most deep traffic models are trained for one city and one backbone model at a time. Keeping a separate predictor for every city is costly. The author's city-conditioned memory gives one model a store of city-specific patterns it can draw on. That design aims to help forecasts transfer to new cities with little data.
arxiv-2512-01151:
Dong Liu proposes Fiber Bundle Networks in a 2025 machine learning paper. Most deep networks fit functions as black boxes, powerful but hard to interpret. Liu instead combines differential geometry with machine learning, recasting classification as a geometric optimization problem on fiber bundles.

In a fiber bundle, points of a base space each carry a fiber, a small space attached above them. Here, categories form the base space, and wavelet-transformed features lie in the fibers above each category. Classification then becomes a structured geometric choice rather than a blind fit. Interpretable geometry could help users see why a model sorted an item as it did.
arxiv-2512-01551:
Yunfeng Jiang and co-authors extend the rational Q-system to spin chains without U(1) symmetry. The Q-system solves Bethe ansatz equations in full. It has been a fast, complete tool. Its use was stuck to systems with that symmetry, though.

Their extension covers closed XXZ-type chains that lack it. Removing the symmetry cap widens the tool a lot. Many real integrable models lack U(1) symmetry. A complete solver for them helps in condensed matter work on magnets and cold atoms. The closed XXZ case is a proving ground, chosen since its spectrum is known well enough to expose any gap in the new frame.
arxiv-2512-01751:
Christian Bonatti and Theo Marty build foliations from pre-laminations on a circle. A singular foliation on the plane has a circular boundary at infinity. That boundary carries a pre-lamination structure. The forward link was known. The converse was open.

The pair solve the converse in full. They state which pre-laminations arise from a foliation. They then build the unique matching foliation. Both regular and prong-singular cases are covered. The result completes a dictionary between plane dynamics and circle data. Uniqueness matters as much as existence, since a boundary that matched two foliations would leave the dictionary ambiguous at its core.
arxiv-2512-01851:
Nishil Savla rebuilds the PMNS matrix with a classical pendulum system. Neutrino oscillations come from interference between mass states. The PMNS matrix governs that mixing. The effect is quantum at its core. Its math mirrors coupled classical oscillators, though.

Savla builds three pendulums linked by springs as an analog. The pendulum modes mimic three-flavor oscillation traits. A tabletop analog makes abstract mixing tangible for students. It also offers an intuitive check on how mixing angles shape oscillation patterns. Spring constants map to mixing angles, so turning a lab knob sweeps the analog through the same space neutrino fits explore.
arxiv-2512-01951:
The Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 has an infrared detector whose response bends slightly as signals grow, and astronomers correct that bend pixel by pixel. Sachindev Shenoy and co-authors revisit the correction in 2025, which rests on ground test data gathered during a thermal vacuum campaign before launch.

In the current reference file, each pixel's correction coefficients are averaged across the detector's four quadrants, smoothing away pixel-level detail. A per-pixel correction promises cleaner measurements of faint infrared sources. Work of this kind quietly underpins the accuracy of every infrared image the camera delivers, long after its ground tests ended.
arxiv-2512-02051:
If two whole-plane functions share enough values, must they be one and the same? Jeet Sarkar and Debabrata Pramanik chase this question in 2025. They compare a function with a shifted form built from its own rate of change.

Such sameness theorems are core tools in the study of how functions spread their values. They tell when data pin a function down in full. The pair prove three results. Each one sharpens and broadens a 2011 theorem by Qi. Stronger rules help analysts see when shifted forms, common in difference equations, cannot pose as each other.
arxiv-2512-02151:
Integrating an increasing function once gives its accumulated area; integrating the result again and again builds a tower of smoother curves. Maxim Burke and co-authors characterize in 2025 exactly which triples of values those repeated integrals can take at the endpoint, for increasing functions on the unit interval.

The question grew out of a problem about approximating smooth functions by entire functions in a comonotone way, keeping the same increasing pattern. Knowing the reachable set of first, second, and third integral values draws the boundary of what such functions can do. Results of this kind are the fine print of approximation theory, where they decide which approximation schemes can exist.
arxiv-2512-02251:
Farmers adapting to climate change need answers that are both scientifically accurate and readable, and those answers are scattered across papers and government data feeds. Liangji Kong, Aditya Joshi, and Sarvnaz Karimi present CAIRNS in 2025, a question-answering system for climate adaptation that tries to hold both virtues at once.

Adaptation strategies for sustaining food production live in unstructured literature and in structured climate data from official sources. A system that can draw on both must phrase findings plainly without flattening their accuracy. Balancing readability against precision is the central design problem, and it decides whether farmers and advisors can actually use the answers.
arxiv-2512-02351:
Unified multimodal models pack understanding and generation into one system, but most tasks use only a slice of that bulk. Shwai He and three co-authors study in 2025 how sparsity, running only the needed parts, can cure the inefficiency that unification creates.

A question about a picture may not need the model's generation machinery, and a caption may not need its deepest reasoning. Identifying and harnessing that sparsity means routing each task or sample to the capacity it actually requires. The work points toward unified models that keep their versatility without charging every user for all of it.
arxiv-2512-02551:
Songqiao Su and five co-authors attack matrix multiplication, the core math inside large language models. Fast multiplication kernels are hard to tune by hand. Each matrix shape rewards a different strategy, and tricks that help on one graphics chip often fail on another.

Their system, CUDA-L2, uses reinforcement learning to search for fast kernels on its own. The learning agent tests variants and keeps what runs fastest, aiming past the standard cuBLAS library. Automatic tuning at scale could speed up AI training and serving, where multiplication dominates both time and energy cost. Speed gains here flow straight to the cost of each task a firm runs on its chips.
arxiv-2512-02751:
Rakib Ahsan and three co-authors spot methane plumes from space with an attention based neural network. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and fast detection of leaks allows timely repair. Satellite images from Sentinel-2 already watch the whole planet on a regular cycle.

AttMetNet adds attention layers that teach the network where a faint plume is likely to hide. The framework targets plumes in Sentinel-2 imagery specifically. Automated detection at scale could help governments and firms find super emitters, a small set of sources behind much of the methane problem. Most leaks come from a few bad sites, so a fast sky scan is the quick way to find the worst ones first.
arxiv-2512-03051:
Ocean models stumble at coastlines, where their grids simply end. Treating fields near domain boundaries is a long standing problem in signal processing. New convolution based coarse graining methods and machine learned parameterizations have revived it, since both create artifacts at ocean boundaries.

The proposed method extends fields beyond the boundary by solving a Laplace boundary value problem. That harmonic extension is general and principled, not an ad hoc patch. Cleaner boundaries improve multiscale analysis and learned ocean models, where coastal errors now leak into open water forecasts. Coasts are where most of us live and work. Coast wise marks in a sea model are worth more than their share of grid points would first suggest to a glance.
arxiv-2512-03551:
Groups of users may need to prove membership all at once. Oylum Gerenli, Gunes Karabulut-Kurt, and Enver Ozdemir present a user centric group authentication scheme in this 2025 work. Group schemes verify many users simultaneously without a certification authority.

Past schemes fall into three generations based on their math foundations. The authors aim for a scheme centered on user needs for secure communication. Efficient group checks matter for chat, IoT networks, and shared workspaces. Removing a central authority can cut cost and single points of failure. User centric design aims to ease enrollment, a common pain point in group schemes.
arxiv-2512-03951:
Tensor products multiply mathematical objects together, and algebraists have long wanted a version that works inside abstract categories, not just for vector spaces. Bo Shan Deval, Manfred Hartl, and Tim Van der Linden build one in a 2025 category theory preprint. Their product is defined intrinsically for objects of a semi-abelian category, using a construction called the cosmash product.

Applied to abelian objects, the construction recovers the classical tensor product in many cases. A recognition theorem then characterises exactly which pairing operations arise this way for varieties of algebras. The authors develop the product's basic properties, compare it with the older Brown-Loday non-abelian tensor product. They go on to prove a categorical analogue of Ganea's six-term sequence. They also give explicit descriptions for representation categories. There, their product of modules generalises how group and Lie algebra representations are combined.
arxiv-2512-04051:
Training large models in low precision saves enormous computing, but the usual recipe computes updates in full precision and rounds them afterwards. Paul Wilson, Fabio Zanasi, and George Constantinides propose cutting out the rounding step in a 2025 machine learning preprint. In their schemes, the update rule itself is discrete, producing integer steps by design rather than by discretising a continuous update.

The authors prove that a general class of such schemes converges. As a concrete member, they present a multinomial update rule, backed by empirical evaluation. The framing matters most for models whose structure is inherently discrete, where pretending updates are continuous wastes effort. The work connects to a wider push for efficient training under hardware constraints. Giving discrete rules a rigorous footing may open design space that quantisation cannot reach.
arxiv-2512-04251:
A bilayer of the material Td-MoTe2 does something remarkable: flipping its ferroelectric polarisation with a displacement field switches its superconductivity on and off, with hysteresis. Yanfang Li, Xin-Zhi Li, and Wen-Yu He explain that coupling in a 2025 preprint. Why it happens matters because such switching promises low-power, non-volatile memory, yet its origin was poorly understood.

Their explanation centres on pairing between p and d orbital electrons within each layer. The effect sorts them into distinct layers, suppressing the intralayer pairing and killing the effect. A Landau-Ginzburg model shows hysteretic switching requires the remanent value to sit below a critical pair-breaking value, itself below saturation. The scenario makes testable predictions: an anisotropic, momentum-dependent pairing gap, and a possible transition into a pair density wave when the chemical potential is tuned.
arxiv-2512-04751:
Junhao Wei, Yanzhao Gu, Ran Zhang, and co-authors pair an improved whale-inspired optimizer with a gradient boosting model to flag promising computer science students early. The base Whale Optimization Algorithm mimics how whales circle prey, but it searches narrowly, converges slowly, and can stall in local traps. Their 2025 arXiv paper upgrades it into NAWOA with several new strategies for exploration and balance.

Good-node-set starts, leader-follower foraging, dynamic encircling, and triangular hunting widen the search. A nonlinear factor steadies the landing. On standard test functions, NAWOA beat the classic optimizer in strength and robustness. The tuned XGBoost model then trained on records of hundreds of computer science undergraduates across a decade at Macao Polytechnic University. Early flags of academic potential could help advisors steer support to students before small struggles grow into failure.
arxiv-2512-04851:
Yirong Fang, Changfu Shi, and Jianwei Mei study one of the most violent events the universe allows: two black holes colliding at near light speed. Such head-on relativistic crashes could expose cracks in general relativity, since no merger of spiraling pairs reaches their energy. Nature rarely arranges them. Their 2025 arXiv paper finds a plausible stage: a triple system, where a massive black hole's gravity whips two smaller companions to relativistic speeds.

The team models collisions in the heavy hole's background and computes the gravitational wave signals they would emit. They then grade which current and future detectors could catch such a signal. The waveforms differ sharply from ordinary merger chirps. A detection would open a window on gravity at its most extreme, and even a null result across surveys would bound how often triple systems stage these crashes.
arxiv-2512-05051: Alberto Merici's short note computes a basic invariant for logarithmic motives, an advanced framework extending the algebra of geometric shapes to spaces with a chosen boundary. For a smooth, proper variety over a perfect field, he shows how to compute the zeroth homotopy group of its motive directly. He also proves the result is unchanged by the theory's standard homotopy deformation. Applying the method to the projective line, he shows the functor that forgets the logarithmic structure loses no information.
arxiv-2512-05151: Bojan Žunkovič's lecture notes introduce quantum machine learning to an audience of computer scientists. Quantum machine learning applies quantum computing ideas, superposition, interference, and quantum circuits, to the tasks of machine learning, and it is usually taught to physicists.
