These notes take the other door in, presenting the subject for readers whose home ground is algorithms rather than laboratory physics. As lecture notes, they form a structured teaching text meant to be worked through, lowering the entry barrier for computer scientists who want a route into the field.
arxiv-2512-05951:
Teofil Bodea and nine co-authors present Omega, a platform for running AI agents in the cloud without trusting the cloud too much. Agents read sensitive data, call tools, and talk to each other inside systems where some components may be hostile. Confidential virtual machines protect single programs, but say nothing about trust between the many parties an agent serves, nor about the graphics accelerators agents think with.

Omega builds a Trusted Agent Platform inside one confidential machine, using nested isolation to host many agents at once. Trust across principals is established by differential attestation. Every outside interaction is supervised under stated policies governing data access, tool use, and agent to agent talk, with provenance recorded. Built on AMD and NVIDIA confidential hardware, the system secures agent state end to end while staying fast and dense. The aim is cloud agents a bank could sign off on.
arxiv-2512-06351:
Zhiying Yang and five co authors present Luca, a scheduling system for smart factories that weighs both speed and carbon cost. In a flexible job shop, each job can run on several machines, and plans must shift as orders and conditions change. A plan that is fast but dirty, or green but late, fails the twin goals of modern plants.

Luca fuses two views of the shop floor. A graph network reads the web of jobs and machines, while a large language model, steered by a home grown prompt plan, adds context about the current state. The fused picture feeds a learning policy that issues scheduling choices in real time. Its score rewards both short total run time and low emissions. On made up and public data sets, Luca beat rival methods, cutting run time at the same emission level and gaining on both counts in public tests.
arxiv-2512-06551:
Jonas Britz and Monique Laurent study how to tell whether a quantum state shared by two parties is entangled or merely separable, a split that decides what quantum tasks it can power. Testing separability is a known hard problem. A hierarchy of semidefinite tests, the DPS hierarchy, approximates the set of separable states from outside, level by level, but can be too heavy to run.

The authors exploit structure to make it lighter. For states unchanged by diagonal unitary twists on both sides, they show the hierarchy breaks into blocks, which, joined with a moment based reading, gives a far cheaper implementation. For states with Bose symmetry, they characterize the dual hierarchy through sums of squares of polynomials. Two cones from optimization, the completely positive cone and its dual, turn out to run through both settings. The work brings a hard detection problem closer to routine computation.
arxiv-2512-06651:
Hayk Lekdar Gevorgyan revisits how to model a radio frequency helical deflector, a device that steers charged particles with a rotating field. Two helical conductors carry a radio frequency voltage, and the field they make sweeps an electron beam around in a circle or spiral. That sweep turns the time structure of a beam into a spatial pattern, which makes the device a fine timer for time of flight measures, with resolution reaching picoseconds.

Textbooks model the deflector one way; an older proposal by Shamaev models it another. Gevorgyan proposes a capacitor model, sets the three side by side, and works out what each really assumes. From his analysis come formulas for the electric field, the size and tilt of the ellipse the beam traces, and how much beam duration each stretch of the pattern encodes. He also treats the resonant case, where the pattern closes into a circle.
arxiv-2512-06851:
Ruijiang Ji, Yunbo Zhang, Shu Chen, and Zhihao Xu ask a counterintuitive question: can random disorder create orderly quantum behavior instead of destroying it? Their test bed is a chain of paired sites, the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, where links inside each pair vary at random. The randomness follows a flexible pattern whose values and odds can be tuned separately. In such chains, disorder can switch on a protected state known as a topological phase.

As the disorder grows stronger, the authors show, the region of that protected phase can split into several separate windows. The count, width, and place of the windows follow directly from the settings of the random pattern. Exact formulas for the window edges match computer checks using two other measures. A moving signal called mean chiral displacement can also spot the windows in real time, giving experimenters a practical handle on disorder-made order.
arxiv-2512-06951:
Ilia Larchenko, Gleb Zarin, and Akash Karnatak report the winning entry in the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge, a contest for robots that do household work in realistic simulation. The benchmark holds fifty long tasks that need two-handed handling, moving around rooms, and decisions that depend on context. Their entry builds on a vision-language-action policy called Pi0.5, which turns camera views and instructions into movement.

The team's main trick concerns the noise used while training the policy's action generator. By correlating that noise, they train faster and can patch action sequences smoothly, keeping motion coherent. Learnable attention that mixes layers helps too, as does a stage tracker that notes which step of a task the robot is on. Extra sampling during training calms erratic outputs, and compression plus hand rules tidy the final actions. The system topped both public and private leaderboards across all fifty tasks.
arxiv-2512-07051:
Adnan Munir, Muhammad Shahid Jabbar, and Shujaat Khan present DAUNet, a lean network for outlining organs and lesions in medical scans. Such segmentation guides diagnosis and treatment planning, but leading models are heavy, which shuts out clinics with modest computers. DAUNet reshapes the classic U-shaped design with two frugal additions: convolutions that deform their sampling grid to fit anatomy, and an attention scheme that needs no extra learned parameters.

The deformable kernels sit at the network's bottleneck, where they adapt to varied shapes, while the attention modules refine the decoding path and the skip connections that carry fine detail. On two demanding data sets, fetal ultrasound and chest scans for lung clots, DAUNet beat state-of-the-art rivals on overlap and boundary scores alike. It did so with fewer parameters than the competition. Tests removing each addition confirmed both pieces earn their place.
arxiv-2512-07351:
Sayeem Been Zaman and co-authors hunt deepfakes with a committee of agents rather than a single detector. Faked video now tampers with face and voice together. And detectors that fuse both senses inside one model can be thrown off when the two streams disagree, or when noise and manipulation hit unevenly. DeepAgent splits the work. One agent reads each video with a compact convolutional network, hunting the visual signatures of manipulation.

The second agent attacks from the audio side: it combines sound features, speech transcripts from a recognition system. And text read off the frames, looking for inconsistencies between what is said, heard, and seen. A random forest meta-classifier then weighs the two agents' decisions, exploiting the fact that they fail in different places.
arxiv-2512-07651:
Yuanye Liu and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 medical imaging report on liver fibrosis. Scarring of the liver is a heavy global health burden. Staging that scarring correctly decides how each patient should be managed.

The report introduces LiQA, a dataset built for the CARE 2024 challenge. It gathers MRI scans from hundreds of patients across several centers. The scans come in multiple phases and reflect messy real-world conditions. Domain shifts, missing scan types, and misaligned images all appear in the data. Algorithms are benchmarked on two tasks against that backdrop. One task segments the liver; the other stages its fibrosis. The report also describes the challenge's top-performing method in detail. It pairs semi-supervised learning with outside data for sturdy segmentation. For staging, it seeks agreement across views and regularizes with activation maps. Using many data sources and anatomical rules clearly boosts robustness.
arxiv-2512-07751:
Shoham Letzter and Arjun Ranganathan wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on cycles in hypergraphs. A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex of a graph exactly once before closing. In hypergraphs, edges hold many vertices, and cycles can overlap in varied patterns.

The authors seek the exact density that forces such a cycle to exist. Their condition is a new flavor called minimum supported co-degree. It counts, for sets of vertices inside an edge, how many edges contain them.  Under that condition, large enough hypergraphs must contain the desired cycle. The bound they prove is tight for infinitely many parameter choices. For all other choices it misses the truth by at most one. Earlier work had only an asymptotic version of the statement. One special case settles a conjecture from a recent team of five authors. A new tiling method powers the proof.
arxiv-2512-07851:
Sansrit Paudel wrote this 2025 paper on cleaning up biological signals before machines learn from them. Heart and body sensors produce streams that real life constantly corrupts. Motion artifacts and wandering baselines spoil stretches of otherwise good data.

Some corrupted segments are too degraded for any filter to rescue. Paudel's goal is to sort the stream rather than save every piece. The sorting runs in two stages of increasing detail. First, clean segments are separated from noisy ones as a binary call. Second, the noisy pile is divided by kind: motion, sensor failure, and others. The tool is K-means clustering, an unsupervised method needing no labels. It groups clean segments from noisy ones with notable reliability. Clean data, in particular, is identified with strong consistency. Keeping only high-quality segments sharpens the features fed to later models. Downstream learning on biosignals should then grow more precise.
arxiv-2512-08151: Jeremie Brieussel and Ryokichi Tanaka, mathematicians, posted a short research paper on arXiv in December 2025. They study random walks on virtually abelian groups, a family that behaves almost like a grid of integers. Their question is noise sensitivity: does a tiny random disturbance to the walk change where it ends up, measured in total variation? They prove a clean criterion: such walks are noise sensitive exactly when the group has no nonzero homomorphism onto the integers, tying a probability property to a purely algebraic one.
arxiv-2512-08351:
Ngoc Tan Nguyen, Thi Thu Hoang, and colleagues, wireless researchers in Vietnam, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is jamming, where an attacker floods a wireless channel to block communication. Drones make the threat worse: a flying jammer can move, aim with line of sight, and adapt, while defenders run on tiny power budgets.

Their defense turns the attack into a resource. A transmitter in an ambient backscatter system learns through deep reinforcement learning. It chooses when to transmit actively, when to harvest energy from the jamming signal, and when to backscatter data using the jammer own emissions. The team models the choice as a Markov decision process and solves it with a deep Q network. In simulations, the learned policy converged faster than plain Q learning and beat a greedy defense on throughput, packet loss, and delivery ratio.
arxiv-2512-08751:
Kuniko Paxton and coauthors present a pruning method to shrink large vision models for skin lesion work on edge devices, while learning across sites without sharing data. Top vision models can beat specialists at lesion classification, but they are too large and compute heavy for small devices. Privacy rules also block central collection of medical images, which motivates federated learning.

Their method prunes parts of a multimodal Swin transformer based on the skewness of output distributions, targeting attention and feed forward layers. In a horizontal federated test, the pruned model keeps its accuracy while its size falls by about a third. That balance matters for real deployment. The study shows that careful compression and privacy preserving training can coexist for multimodal medical systems that must run on limited hardware at the point of care.
arxiv-2512-09151:
Anna Chlingaryan, Arman Melkumyan, and Raymond Leung address a practical problem in mining: estimating the chemistry of rock underground from drill samples. Blasthole samples do not measure a single point. Each one averages the rock along a drilled interval, and standard models that treat them as points lose that information.

Their method, IntegralGP, uses Gaussian processes, a statistical model that predicts values with uncertainty, built to handle interval data directly. They work out the changed mathematics the idea requires, including the formulas needed to train the model and the numerical care it demands. The method then merges blasthole results with an existing block model of the deposit to forecast iron grades in the bench of rock below. In validation tests, the fused model predicted grades more accurately and made fewer costly mistakes, such as calling waste rock high-grade ore.
arxiv-2512-09751:
Keyu Wei and colleagues use gate tuning to settle a debate about tantalum nickel selenide. It may be an excitonic insulator, a state where electron-hole pairs condense and open an insulating gap. Proving that mechanism has been difficult because a structural change occurs alongside it, and the two are hard to separate. The team studies flakes from bulk to a layer with Raman spectroscopy.

It survives to the monolayer limit. Its temperature rises as the material gets thinner. In bilayer samples, electron and hole doping both suppress the insulating state, though they shift it in opposite ways. The quasi-elastic scattering signal blamed on exciton effects grows across the doping range, opposite to what screening of exciton links should do. The authors conclude it is a coupled electronic and structural change, not excitonic, and offer doping as a test for such insulators.
arxiv-2512-09851:
Yuyang Li and colleagues build a robot sensor that sees and feels at the same time. Their see through skin sensor pairs a camera view through soft material with touch signals from the contact surface. Earlier designs could not capture both senses at once, and their touch tracking was unreliable. The new sensor, called TacThru, uses a transparent elastomer, steady illumination, and keyline markers. A matching system, TacThru-UMI, feeds both signals into imitation learning.

The learner uses a transformer based diffusion policy, a method that generates robot actions from demonstrations. On five hard real world tasks, the combined system succeeded about eighty-five percent of the time on average. That clearly beat a touch only policy and a vision only policy. It did especially well where contact sensing is decisive, such as detecting contact with thin or soft objects, and in precise tasks needing vision and touch together.
arxiv-2512-10351:
Georgi Bebrov asks a basic question about quantum key distribution, the method that uses quantum physics to share secret keys. How can anyone tell whether a given system is running as well as it possibly could? His 2025 paper sets out to give that question a precise, testable answer.

Bebrov defines a quantity he calls optimality, the best total efficiency a key distribution setup could reach under any settings, judged in the long-run limit of many uses. He then shows how that best case could be reached by pairing a top-performing quantum channel with a fully compressed classical channel. He closes by giving optimal versions of two known protocols, BB84 and twin-field distribution.
arxiv-2512-10451:
Le Tuan Minh Trinh and co-authors borrow a concept from human psychology: metacognition, knowing how much to trust your own judgement. Deep learning models give confidence scores, but those scores are often badly calibrated, claiming certainty where the model is actually weak. Their paper, presented at a NeurIPS 2025 workshop, asks whether a model's self-trust can be measured and then put to work.

The team defines a sensitivity measure, drawn from cognitive science, for how well a model's confidence tracks its own accuracy. That score then guides a bandit-style arbiter that picks, task by task, which of several expert models to believe at test time. Across varied datasets and model pairings, including image networks and vision-language models, the metacognitive route beat simply using any single model on its own.
arxiv-2512-10751:
Charlie Lloyd and Robert Dorrell simulate what offshore wind turbines do to layered seawater. New wind farms are pushed into deep, seasonally stratified water, where a turbine's foundation sits in a two-layer sea and its wake stirs the layers together. How much mixing follows, and by what mechanism, was poorly understood, caught between crude field-scale models and sparse measurements.

The authors ran the first structure-resolved direct numerical simulations of two-layer stratified flow past a vertical cylinder. Two wake regimes emerged, set by the flow's Reynolds and Richardson numbers. Weak stratification gives a narrow, energetic wake ruled by horizontal shear, the regime of today's wind farms. Under strong stratification, a recirculation cell spans the layer boundary. Strong vertical motions develop there. They launch large stationary internal waves, which carry a real share of the energy far downstream. That explains puzzling field reports about wake persistence.
arxiv-2512-10951:
Samuel Goldstein and J. Colin Hill report the first robust evidence that galaxy clusters rotate, seen through a faint signal in the cosmic microwave background. As background light scatters off hot gas inside a cluster, the gas motion leaves a two-sided pattern aligned with the cluster's spin. Finding that pattern required careful separation from much stronger background noise.

The team combined Planck satellite measurements with galaxy redshifts from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey for a sample of massive nearby clusters. The dipolar signal lined up with each cluster's estimated angular momentum and was very unlikely to be chance. Its size and shape matched advanced simulations, giving astronomers a new tool for probing how clusters move and evolve.
arxiv-2512-11251:
Yunkai Zhang and a large team build Insight Miner, a multimodal model that explains time series data in plain language across many domains. Charts of measurements drive decisions in fields from farming to finance, but extracting insights usually takes scarce expert time. Their system generates detailed descriptions enriched with domain knowledge, after training on a new paired dataset.

The companion dataset joins one hundred thousand time series windows from twenty forecasting collections with written trend descriptions. An agentic workflow built it by first extracting statistical features with tools, then having a large model weave those features into coherent narratives. After instruction tuning, Insight Miner beat leading multimodal models, including a top commercial system, at describing series and drawing insights. The authors frame the work as a first step toward models that read time series as a native input.
arxiv-2512-11451:
Joshua Althüser, Ilya Eremin, and Götz Uhrig report an unexpected strengthening of superconductivity when many electronic states pile up near the Fermi energy. In the standard BCS theory, phonon mediated attraction between electrons matters mainly right at the Fermi surface, so the superconducting order away from it is usually tiny and ignored. A closer derivation shows the attraction acts whenever two electron energies differ by less than the phonon energy.

When the density of states has a peak close to the Fermi level, that neglected region lights up. The order parameter near the peak can exceed its Fermi level value at moderate coupling strengths. A softening collective mode announces the effect, resembling a second phase transition. The authors predict concrete signatures in thermodynamic and spectroscopic measurements. Their analysis turns a textbook approximation into a search strategy for enhanced superconducting behaviour.
arxiv-2512-11751:
Andy A Shen and co-authors improve a causal inference tool by letting outcomes choose what to balance. In observational studies, fair group comparison needs balanced background traits. Kernel balancing picks a similarity measure, then balances a summary of it, but that summary is chosen blind to the outcome.

Their forest kernel balancing uses random forests and BART, two tree based learners. Trees group units that land in the same leaf, and that grouping defines a kernel shaped by outcome relevant patterns. In simulations and real examples the method beat standard kernel balancing on speed and accuracy. It offers a practical way to fight hidden bias in health and policy studies.
arxiv-2512-12251:
Saneesh Babu, Gabriele Di Stefano, and Aparna Lakshmanan S study graph coloring in a 2025 math paper. Their version uses mutual visibility: points with the same color must be able to see each other along a shortest path with no other same color point in between. The goal is the fewest colors that can do this.

They prove that finding that number is NP-complete, a sign of a hard problem, even for graphs with diameter four where the answer is just two. They also find exact values for glued binary trees and glued t-ary trees. Such exact cases help map where the problem stays tractable.
arxiv-2512-12451: Vladimir Guletskii presents a claimed proof of the Bloch conjecture, a statement in algebraic geometry first made by Spencer Bloch in 1975. The conjecture deals with smooth projective surfaces. In plain terms, these are curved two dimensional shapes that are cut out by polynomial equations and have no sharp edges or gaps. The conjecture says that the Albanese kernel of such a surface is zero. That holds as long as the second cohomology group of the surface is algebraic in nature.
arxiv-2512-12551:
Dewen Suo and four co-authors test Android security tools against anti-runtime analysis tricks in a 2025 paper. Android draws many new apps each year, and malicious apps increasingly use anti-runtime analysis, or ARA, techniques to block dynamic examination. Such tricks detect analysis setups and hide bad behavior, complicating the work of security professionals who run apps to watch what they do.

Their empirical study measures how well widely used dynamic analysis tools bypass varied ARA techniques. Results reveal a critical gap: current tools often fail against these countermeasures. The authors call for more robust solutions and offer their findings as a map of where existing tools fall short, to guide improved defenses.
arxiv-2512-13651:
Taishi Sano and Yuki Yokokura study Schrödinger symmetry in small, simplified gravity models with matter fields. Such mini-superspace models keep only a few degrees of freedom of a full spacetime. Past work found this symmetry emerging in a fluid limit, and the authors test how robust that emergence is.

They study two spherically symmetric, static models at the classical level: one with a Maxwell field and a cosmological constant, and one with many massless scalar fields. For the first, 3D symmetry emerges and the solution is the de Sitter Reissner-Nordström spacetime. For the second, symmetry in 2+n dimensions appears, with a generalized Janis-Newman-Winicour solution. They also offer a physical reading of what the symmetry generators do.
arxiv-2512-14051:
Mengzhang Cai and the OpenDataArena team introduce OpenDataArena, an open platform for benchmarking the value of post-training data sets for large language models. Model quality depends on post-training data, yet that data is usually a black box: opaque composition, uncertain provenance, and no systematic evaluation. That blocks reproducibility and hides how data traits drive model behavior.

The platform combines a unified training-evaluation pipeline, a multi-dimensional scoring framework, an interactive data lineage explorer, and an open-source toolkit. Experiments cover over 120 training data sets, 22 benchmarks, more than 600 training runs, and 40 million processed data points. Findings include trade-offs between data complexity and task performance, plus redundancy in popular benchmarks found through lineage tracing.
arxiv-2512-14251:
Nat Sothanaphan improves a lower bound for a classic distance problem in a 2025 note. Erdos, Herzog, and Piranian asked whether, for points in the plane with a fixed largest distance, a regular polygon makes the product of all pairwise distances as large as possible.

For even counts, a regular polygon was recently shown not to be best, but the gain was tiny. Sothanaphan proves the best arrangement beats the regular polygon value by a factor above 1.037 for large even cases, settling a stated conjecture. Some other arrangements look even better but lack proofs. Whether the ratio can grow without bound remains open, and no such arrangements are known.
arxiv-2512-14651:
S. Saoud and four co-authors study quintessential inflation inside the inert doublet model, a particle physics setup with an extra scalar doublet. A quintessence field with an exponential potential is coupled in, with the aim of covering both early inflation and today's accelerated expansion in one story.

Using a conformal transformation from the Jordan frame to the Einstein frame, they derive an effective Starobinsky-type potential reshaped by an exponential factor. They then test the scenario against the swampland bounds, conjectured limits on which theories can sit inside quantum gravity. The paper links a concrete particle model to those wider consistency checks.
arxiv-2512-14851:
Aslak Djupskås and two coauthors test a popular shortcut for judging how unsure a neural network is. The shortcut, Monte Carlo dropout, runs a network many times with random parts switched off and treats the spread of answers as uncertainty. It is widely used because full Bayesian methods are too slow for big networks.

The team compares the shortcut with Gaussian processes and Bayesian neural networks on test problems. Monte Carlo dropout often failed to show more doubt in the zones where doubt should grow, such as far from the training data or between clusters. Bayesian methods did show that growth. The authors conclude that, as tested, dropout based doubt is not as trustworthy as classic Bayesian doubt, a caution for safety critical uses.
arxiv-2512-15051:
H. M. Florez gives the first microscopic account of how hot atomic vapor can create entangled light in many spatial modes at once. Multipartite entanglement, links among many parties, is a resource for quantum information work. Earlier experiments showed alkali atoms could generate it in a single device through four wave mixing, a nonlinear process where pumps trade photons.

Florez extends a double Lambda model of single pump mixing to a two pump setup in dense vapor. A Floquet expansion solves how the modes gain strength and how much noise they carry. The model captures how the output depends on angle and on pairs of photons, and describes the quantum correlations among modes. It matches the main traits of past experiments, and can predict gain patterns and correlations across the range of settings labs actually use.
arxiv-2512-15151:
Yuki Nakayama and three coauthors release a large corpus of hotel reviews for language research. The Rakuten Travel Reviews collection holds 7.29 million customer reviews spanning 16 years, from 2009 to 2024. Each record pairs the review text with the hotel's response.

Records also carry an anonymized reviewer ID, the date, IDs for the hotel and the plan, the room type and name, the trip purpose, and who traveled along. Guests rated six aspect categories plus an overall score. The authors present statistics for the corpus and study how the data drifted between 2019 and 2024, using statistical tools to find what drove the shift. A long, rich, and openly described dataset like this supports work on sentiment, dialogue, and changing travel taste.
arxiv-2512-15451:
Addhyaya Sharma and co authors report a new way to build polaritonic circuits that work at room temperature in a 2025 paper. Polaritons are hybrid states of light and matter that can carry signals, and they may serve in analog computing. Older ways of shaping the host cavity gave designers little freedom after the fact.

The team etches circuits of chosen shapes into a finished organic microcavity using a focused ion beam. They show polaritons condensing and moving through straight and trapezoid guides at room temperature. Test devices include a ring guide, a Y splitter, and a Mach Zehnder interferometer. The work is an early step toward full polariton circuits.
arxiv-2512-15851:
Naoto Nakatsuji, Jennifer Cano, and Valentin Crepel present a high throughput workflow for twisted moire homobilayers in a 2025 paper. Stacking two layers of the same material with a twist creates moire patterns that can host designer quantum phases. Experiments have sampled only a narrow slice of the possible materials and angles.

The workflow pairs small scale density functional theory with perturbation theory to extract moire band gaps, valley Chern numbers, magic angles, and relaxation thresholds quickly. It also parameterizes a continuum model for each material for deeper study. The survey flags chromium based dichalcogenides for high temperature quantum anomalous Hall effects, nitride halides for mixed superconducting and moire physics, and thin III-V semiconductors for room temperature scale effects.
arxiv-2512-15951:
Shih-Yu Chang advances a theory program in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum mathematics. It is the third part of a project building a unified algebraic foundation for operator theory and quantum processes. The language is multicategories and operads, tools for describing how operations with many inputs combine.

Chang introduces n-adjoints, a ladder of generalized adjoint operations for multi-input settings, and proves a version of Stinespring's theorem with them. He then shows that standard quantum channels, the allowed transformations of quantum states, form algebras of a single monad built from an interaction operad. Finally, he encodes famous no-go rules, such as the ban on cloning quantum states, as algebraic constraints. The results tie operator theory, category theory, and quantum information into one framework.
arxiv-2512-16051:
Sidharth Kannan and three co-authors apply graph neural networks to gravitational wave hardware in an arXiv paper made public in 2025, presented at a NeurIPS 2025 workshop. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, detects ripples in spacetime with complex optical instruments. Simulating those optics with standard software is accurate but slow.

The team trained graph neural networks to mimic the simulations for three interferometer layouts. The networks captured the intricate light physics well while running 815 times faster than state-of-the-art simulation packages. The authors also released their high-fidelity simulation data as a benchmark for future work. The study opens a new use for these networks: helping design scientific instruments, not just analyzing the data they produce.
arxiv-2512-16351:
Anshu Kumar and three co-authors survey water simulation in a paper published on arXiv in 2025. Computer models of fluid flow are now a cornerstone of water engineering. They help predict and manage rivers, pipe networks, and treatment systems. The survey reviews the math models and numerical methods behind that practice.

Coverage runs from shallow water equations to full three-dimensional Navier-Stokes models. The history and math structure of each model are explained. The authors compare the main ways to solve them on a grid. They also cover practical headaches. These include source terms, wetting and drying fronts, turbulence, and free surfaces. Data assimilation, uncertainty estimates, and machine learning add-ons get their own sections. Case studies from large water systems show how modeling choices change outcomes. The survey is a unified reference for researchers and practitioners.
arxiv-2512-17051:
Haoye Lu, Yaoliang Yu, and Darren Lo study how to restore a true distribution from many noisy, partial samples when clean samples are rare and dear. The corruption process is known only as a black-box generator.

They frame the task as one-sided entropic optimal transport and solve it with an EM-like algorithm. A test tells whether the true distribution can be recovered under the given per-sample loss, and in lost cases a few clean samples can make it largely recoverable. Their bridge model, SFBD-OMNI, maps corrupted samples back to ground truth for arbitrary measurement models, past Gaussian cases. Benchmarks show clear gains in quality and scores.
arxiv-2512-17251:
Madhava Gaikwad designs AlignDP, a guard meant to stop people from copying what a large language model knows. Attackers can extract training data, distill a model into a cheaper copy, or fine-tune it without permission. Older defenses such as watermarks only react after the leak has already happened.

AlignDP acts earlier, at the point where data enters or leaves. It splits fields into rare and common kinds and treats each kind in its own way. Rare fields get a strong shield that hides them almost fully, while common fields get measured noise so counts stay useful. A global tracker watches the total privacy budget. In a small test, rare groups stayed hidden and common groups were recovered with little error.
arxiv-2512-17451: Noam Berger, Anders Johansson, and Anders Öberg settle a threshold question for the Dyson model. In that model, a chain of spins feels every other spin, with a grip that fades with distance. The team proves the freezing point is the same either way. Stated as a critical inverse temperature, it matches whether the chain stretches one way or both ways. The proof covers fade powers between 1 and 2. They conjecture the same match holds at the borderline power 2.
arxiv-2512-17651:
Andreas Kirchner and three co-authors ask whether one fluid story can cover a nuclear smash from first touch to final spray. When heavy ions collide, they melt into quark-gluon plasma, and modelers usually start their fluid math a heartbeat after impact. Everything before that moment gets guessed, and those guesses are the biggest error source in the field.

The team tests whether a second-order fluid theory can stretch backward to cover the incoming nuclei themselves. They set out the needed equations and check how entropy grows along the way. The results are first steps, not a finished model. The larger prize is a single description where the only unknowns left are the plasma's own material traits.
arxiv-2512-17751:
Dimitrios Chatzis, John M Marley, and Daniel C Thompson revisit a claimed bridge between theories in six, four, and two dimensions. A diagram nicknamed the twistor diamond links a six-dimensional theory at the top to integrable two-dimensional models at the bottom. Coupling two copies of the top theory was proposed to switch on gaugings, extra symmetries, all the way down, but the proof covered one special case.

Recast in Cartan geometry, the mechanism now works for generic setups, the hidden gauge structure made plain. Applied to the lambda-deformed WZW model, the coupling does induce gaugings, with a twist: extra multiplier fields force the gauged connection flat. The two-dimensional children are thus non-Abelian dualisations, not mere gauged models. The diamond's plumbing needed relabeling, and dualities gain.
arxiv-2512-17951:
Kaijie Chen, Zhiyang Xu, Ying Shen, Zihao Lin, Yuguang Yao, and Lifu Huang presented SuperFlow, a faster way to train flow based image generators with reinforcement learning. The framework varied how many trial images each prompt received and scored credit step by step, matching the flow of the model. Reported tests used far fewer training steps and beat a strong base model by wide margins on text and layout tasks.

Readers should know that this paper has been withdrawn from arXiv. The withdrawal note states it was submitted without the consent of all listed authors. Because the submission itself lacked full author approval, the reported gains should not be relied on. The entry is kept as the record of a withdrawn submission.
arxiv-2512-18151:
Cesar Fierro Cota studies six dimensional supergravity theories that come from F theory built on elliptically fibered Calabi Yau threefolds. For such a theory to make sense, its gravitational, gauge, and mixed anomalies must cancel, and that demand ties geometry to counting problems.

The counting side is the Gromov Witten theory of the fiber curves, and its generating series are quasi Jacobi forms. Cota shows how the modular behavior of those forms fixes the Green Schwarz counterterms that cancel the anomalies. One outcome is a modular anomaly equation for four point couplings, driven by the second Eisenstein series. In this family of compactifications, the cancellation conditions turn out to follow on their own from the holomorphic anomaly equations of topological string theory.
arxiv-2512-18951:
Patrick Batsell, Satoshi Tsutsui, and Bihan Wen ask whether AI models raised on infant-scale data learn attributes the way babies do. Children master not just categories but color, size, and texture from little experience. Earlier baby-scale vision-language models were tested mostly on object naming. Their benchmark, posted to arXiv in December 2025, renders 67 everyday object classes synthetically, varying attributes independently of identity.

Infant-trained models like CVCL form strong visual representations for size and match others on texture, but they discriminate color poorly in images and ground color words weakly. Web-scale models show the mirror image: strong color grounding from text, weaker visual size discrimination. The split shows visual and linguistic attribute knowledge develop on separate tracks, a clue for both developmental science and training-data design.
arxiv-2512-19051:
S. Di Matteo and C. Mazzoli re-examine a 2025 experiment that was presented as a challenge to Bohmian mechanics, a version of quantum theory with hidden particle paths. Their focus is the transient regime, the brief settling phase before a steady state forms. That phase, they argue, changes how the data should be read.

In the steady regime's fading state, they prove the data can still be read in Bohmian terms. Bohm's quantum potential can also be recast as a kinetic energy term in Nelson's stochastic version of quantum theory. Since standard quantum theory fits the data too, the experiment cannot rule any framework out.
arxiv-2512-19451:
Nitin Kumar Singh, Arie Rachmad Syulistyo, Yuichiro Tanaka, and Hakaru Tamukoh recognize sign language with a computing style built for small devices. Deep learning sign readers work well but eat far too much compute for edge hardware. Their system pairs MediaPipe hand tracking with parallel bidirectional reservoir computing.

MediaPipe extracts hand joint coordinates in real time, and two bidirectional echo-state reservoirs, run in parallel, turn the motion stream into rich features for a classifier. On the word-level American Sign Language video set, scores reached about sixty-one percent top-one accuracy. Training took under twenty seconds, against nearly an hour for deep rivals.
arxiv-2512-19551:
Jiawen Wang and four co-authors set language models a lifelong task: keep learning to generate emotional human motion in brand-new settings. Existing generators train once on one fixed dataset, be it dance or sport, and stall when a new scenario appears. Real agents, the authors argue, should grow their empathic motion skills continually.

Two hurdles define the task: pulling emotion apart from motion content, and adapting to new scenarios without forgetting old ones. Their ES-MoE design answers with a causal-guided emotion decoupling block and a block that builds scenario-specific experts. The goal is a closed-loop agent whose embodied empathy keeps evolving in unseen worlds.
arxiv-2512-19651:
Filippos Ventirozos, Peter Appleby, and Matthew Shardlow test a prompting trick for reading the fine print of customer reviews. Their task is aspect-category sentiment analysis, which names the themes inside a review and the feeling attached to each. Labeled training data for new domains is scarce and pricey, so they ask whether large language models can do the job zero-shot, with no examples.

Their method inserts a Unified Meaning Representation, a structured sketch of meaning, into chain-of-thought prompting before the model answers. They compare it against ordinary chain-of-thought across three models, from Qwen variants to Gemini-2.5-Pro, and four datasets. Results look comparable for a mid-sized model, but the authors stress the pattern seems model-dependent and needs more study, especially for smaller models.
arxiv-2512-19751:
U. S. Idiong, U. N. Bassey, and O. S. Obabiyi study the Brioschi-Halphen equation. It is a second-order complex equation. It comes from the Lamé equation after two changes of form. The Lamé equation serves in the study of how planets move. This work looks at the radial part of the new equation, for large radius and one set limit for the angle.

They find the far-field form of the radial wave function. It is written with canonical polynomials. They also get solutions in two more senses. One uses spherical functions on the group SL(2,R) with a point change of form. The other is a solution in the sense of distributions, found by a Fourier method. The work sits in the field of quasi-exact solvability. There, only part of a problem gives way to closed forms.
arxiv-2512-19851:
Aditya Bhosale and Laxmikant Kale bring supercomputer-scale stencil work to Python users. Stencil sums are the bread and butter of physics codes. Python tools for them tend to stop at one node. Yet modern machines have graphics chips spread across many nodes. Their tool runs stencil work across multi-node GPUs. It is built on CharmTyles, over the adaptive Charm++ runtime. Its syntax stays close to NumPy, to ease the move from draft to full code.

The tool can rescale a live run across more or fewer nodes. The authors measure what that rescaling costs. In speed tests, the tool beat a special stencil language built for the task. It also beat a general NumPy stand-in. The point is that being flexible need not cost speed.
arxiv-2512-19951:
Yufei Zhou's submission on computing with encrypted data has been withdrawn by the author. The record gives the reason in the author's own words. The current version needs extensive modifications. What the withdrawn text presented was a way to run the modulo operation in the CKKS scheme. That scheme for homomorphic encryption supports only arithmetic. So remainder sums on ciphertexts are a standing hard problem.

The proposed fix approximated the mod function. It used polynomial interpolation and Chebyshev series. The aim was accuracy at each integer point of a bounded input range. Past methods were exact only on subranges. Two packing schemes for small-integer data were also described. So were uses in rounding and in turning secret shares into ciphertexts. Tests reported very high accuracy. All of it should be read as superseded, pending the author's revised version.
arxiv-2512-20051:
Hedibert Lopes, Nick Polson, and Vadim Sokolov reframe hyperparameter tuning as a generative problem. Tuning picks regularization strength, model size, and robustness knobs. Cross-validation can cost too much at scale. Full Bayesian learning stalls on the cost of sampling the posterior. Their approach joins two ideas. One is to use randomized, weighted objectives as stand-ins for Bayesian posteriors. The other is to amortize the repeated optimization across many settings.

A learned transport map does the amortizing. It takes hyperparameters, with random weights, straight to the matched optimizer. That forms a generator look-up table for estimators. Grids or smooth ranges of settings can then be scored fast. The table serves both predictive tuning and rough Bayesian uncertainty checks. Links to weighted M-estimation round out the frame.
arxiv-2512-20551:
Miltiadis Karakikes and co-authors build a dictionary between arithmetic geometry and topology. On one side sits the arithmetic homotopy exact sequence of a variety and its absolute Galois group. On the other, the Birman exact sequence of a surface and its mapping class group. Their unified group-theoretic approach treats both in parallel.

Classic notions such as descent of varieties and covers gain topological twins. Groups of moduli, definition, and invariance are defined on both sides, and some proofs become purely group-theoretic, yielding results in both worlds at once. Applications include a topological analogue of Weil's descent theorem and cohomological obstructions to descent, adapted from work of Débes and Douai. The Weil cocycle condition is shown equivalent to a linearization in equivariant categories.
arxiv-2512-20751:
Renan J. S. Isneri, Eric B. Santiago, and Severino H. da Silva study how moving systems settle down over time. Their systems follow the slope of a potential, like a ball rolling in a bowl, while damping steadily drains energy. The question is whether motion always fades to the resting point, and how fast.

Using a Lyapunov function shaped to the geometry, they prove the equilibrium is stable for all small damping values. When the potential behaves quadratically near its bottom, the approach decays exponentially fast. Semigroup arguments add a global attractor, and simulations show paths near rest in both energy-losing and energy-keeping cases.
arxiv-2512-20951:
Jiangen He, Wanqi Zhang, and Jessica Barfield test whether the biases people apply to human workers follow them when the worker is a robot. In two experiments with just over a thousand participants, people chose among artificial agents that varied in skin tone and human-likeness for jobs in construction, healthcare, education, and athletics.

The choices were not neutral. Healthcare and education scenarios favored lighter-skinned agents, while construction and athletics accepted darker-toned ones more readily, and participants' own race shifted the patterns further. A second experiment showed that first seeing human professionals of a particular racial background moved later robot preferences in stereotype-consistent directions. Bias, in short, transfers from human-human judgment to human-robot choice, which means careless deployment could entrench the inequalities it inherits.
arxiv-2512-21251:
Martijn Dekker's lecture names a slow disease he believes is overtaking cybersecurity: cyber senescence, the aging of the security ecosystem into an operational risk. The problem is not complexity alone but accumulation, layer upon layer of controls whose actual risk reduction nobody has verified. Overlapping frameworks pile up like waste in cyberspace, and a system stuffed with controls of uncertain value may eventually collapse under its own weight.

The lecture opens with a historical sketch of how the field arrived here, then lays out the research agenda the worry dictates, centered on the role of uncertainty in security decisions. Dekker's prescription begins with pruning: unless control frameworks are deliberately thinned, removing measures that cannot justify themselves, the waste keeps compounding. For security leaders, the argument reframes maturity: an older control stack is not a stronger one, and confidence should be earned by measurement, not by count.
arxiv-2512-21351:
Code agents trained one way can freeze when the world shifts, a library changes, an API moves. Santhosh Kumar Ravindran's CosmoCore-Evo borrows evolution to stay loose. Building on his earlier dream-replay framework, it treats reinforcement-learning trajectories as genomes that mutate and face selection during an overnight replay phase.

The fitness scores are tuned for enterprise concerns: efficiency, compliance, and scalability beside raw success. Tests used shifted HumanEval variants, BigCodeBench, and a custom PySpark simulation. The evolved agent made up to thirty-five percent more novel solutions. It adapted a quarter faster than the first version and standard baselines. Ablations confirm the evolutionary parts do the work. Replication code, with a toy simulation, comes with the report.
arxiv-2512-21951:
Where channels connect reservoirs of different salinity, diffusio-osmotic flow arises, and hydrostatic pressure can reshape it. Elena F. Silkina, Evgeny S. Asmolov, and Olga I. Vinogradova analyze the flow in a uniformly charged long slit thicker than the Debye screening length, under a finite concentration difference and an imposed pressure drop.

They recover the classical local slip formula at a single wall, then write the total flow rate as diffusio-osmotic plus pressure-driven parts. The pressure drop leaves the diffusio-osmotic term itself unchanged but strongly modifies the concentration and surface potential profiles along the slit, and hence the local slip. Because the flow rate is easily tuned by pressure, the theory explains recent measurements and turns flow data into information about surface potentials.
arxiv-2512-22051:
Yotam Gafni asks a self-referential question about voting rules: what happens when a voting method must also decide votes on replacing itself? Voters judge each proposal by whether they would rather have the current rule or its challenger decide it. A rule that no challenger can displace this way is called self-maintaining, and Gafni studies what self-maintenance implies about centralization of power.

Building on earlier work by Barbera and Jackson and by Koray, the paper drops their anonymity and neutrality restrictions. One headline result says that, for simple games under unbiased beliefs and worst-case tie-breaking, only a dictatorship is self-maintaining. Other results characterize stable weighted majority games, and extensions cover forward-looking voters, two-level rules, and changes to voting rights.
arxiv-2512-22251:
Pascal Passigan, Kevin Zhu, and Angelina Ning model how drugs change gene activity, a window into drug methods, side effects, and repurposing chances. Earlier graph-based models handled simpler tasks like link prediction or drug-disease association, not full perturbation profiles. The team merges PrimeKG++, a biomedical knowledge graph with rich node embeddings, with LINCS L1000 data on drug and cell line responses.

A graph attention network with a prediction head learns the change in expression across 978 landmark genes for any drug and cell pair. It beat multilayer perceptron baselines under both scaffold and random data splits. Shuffling tests showed the knowledge graph's edges genuinely help prediction. The authors frame the work as a step toward mechanistic, gene-level drug modeling.
arxiv-2512-22751:
Yoshiaki Sofue and a large team from the ALMA CMZ Exploration Survey, called ACES, map the gas disk circling the center of the Milky Way. Molecular line data from the ALMA telescope reveal the disk's shape and motion. From those motions the team works backward to the gravitational pull and mass distribution in the inner twenty parsecs or so around the galactic nucleus.

Test-particle simulations show the central potential is close to spherical, and a rotation curve built from position-velocity diagrams gives a cusped density profile that falls steeply with distance. Tidal forces from that potential keep the gas disk stable against collapsing under its own gravity inside a critical radius. That stability helps explain suppressed star formation and an unusual mix of stellar masses near the center.
arxiv-2512-23451:
E. Malik, P. Kaigorodov, D. Kovaleva, and O. Malkov audit how reliably binary star catalogs can be merged. Catalogs built from the Gaia mission's third data release list more than two point six million binary pairs, over ten times the previously known population of about one hundred forty thousand pairs. To do statistics on the combined ensemble, the pre-Gaia compilation catalog must be cross-identified with the Gaia-based catalogs by matching coordinates, and that matching is where systematic errors creep in.

The analysis shows identification quality depends on the source catalogs and on sky position. In dense fields, especially the Galactic disk, false positive matches should be expected to rise. Systems with large proper motion carry the opposite risk, false negatives, as the star moved between catalog epochs. The authors propose method modifications that would suppress both failure modes.
arxiv-2512-23551:
Chawit Sakkawattana, Chatchai Promsiri, and Supakchai Ponglertsakul compute how light bends around a compact object in Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton gravity, a theory that adds a scalar dilaton field to Einstein's gravity and electromagnetism. Their object is spherically symmetric and q-deformed, characterized by the dilaton coupling, the integrated dilaton flux, and its magnetic charge. Such objects are candidate black hole mimickers worth comparing with observations.

Using the Hamilton-Jacobi method, the authors derive the photon orbit equation and effective potential, then map the total deflection angle against impact parameter as the three parameters vary. They relate the photon ring's width to its Lyapunov exponent, model the glow of a thin accretion disk with three emission profiles to build images. They also compute the innermost stable circular orbit for massive particles. The study shows how each of the three key settings bends light in its own way.
arxiv-2512-23651:
Károly Bezdek and Zsolt Lángi revisit a geometry problem Erdős posed in 1945 about arrangements of convex bodies. A family of bodies is called non-separable when every hyperplane that cuts through their convex hull also cuts through at least one of the bodies themselves. So the family cannot be cleanly split by a flat cut. Recent work concentrated on minimal coverings of such families by scaled copies of one shape.

The authors strengthen those results by extending them to weakly non-separable families of convex polytopes. They add stability results, which describe how the property behaves under small perturbations, and analyze maximal weakly non-separable families of cubes in detail. A further extension treats weakly k-impassable families, a graded version of the same idea, for polytopes in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2512-23751:
Lorenzo Pirovano computes a thermodynamic price for watching the vacuum. Landauer's principle says erasing information costs heat, and Pirovano applies it to a detector that continuously records, bin by bin, whether photons are present or not: a vacuum or no-vacuum measurement. Each time bin's click or no-click outcome lands in a classical register that is then reset, incurring the Landauer cost.

Modeling the monitoring with finite bandwidth, he derives a working lower bound on the lost heat rate, set by the Shannon entropy rate of the measurement record itself. The analysis discusses coarse-graining, extends to many monitored modes with correlations and compressibility, and gives rough numbers for photon monitoring in circuit quantum electrodynamics. A far-fetched example with horizon-based bookkeeping closes the paper, connecting measurement thermodynamics to gravitational analogies. The cost is small, but it cannot be dodged.
arxiv-2512-24051:
Alessio Basti and Fabio Camilli prove error bounds for numerical schemes. The schemes solve convex Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Such equations appear in control theory and physics. The domain here is a multi-dimensional torus. The schemes are the standard monotone ones used in practice.

The proof uses the adjoint method. Semiconcavity estimates support the argument. First comes a first-order error bound in the mean. It covers classical monotone schemes of Crandall-Lions type. Semi-Lagrangian schemes are covered as well. Two assumptions do the heavy lifting. The driving term must be convex. The starting data must be semiconcave. Interpolation with the classical worst-case bound finishes the job. Error estimates then follow in every intermediate norm. Numerical analysts gain a clear statement of how fast these schemes converge.
arxiv-2512-24351:
Asja Attanasio, Francesco Corso, Gianmarco De Francisci Morales, and Francesco Pierri study a shock to an online community built around conspiracy claims. After Jeffrey Epstein's death, the subreddit r/conspiracy drew a surge of mainstream attention. New users met established narratives directly. The authors ask what such visibility does to a group like this. Who joins, how long they stay, and how their language adapts are the questions.

Twelve months of data feed a computational analysis. Toxicity scores, survival analysis, and word-level measures combine. Users who joined around the arrest period resembled core members closely. Their language matched group norms, and their engagement stayed stable. Users who arrived at peak visibility looked different. They stayed distant in style and left sooner. Visibility acted more like a filter than an amplifier. Passing exposure rarely produced integrated members.
arxiv-2512-24751:
Panchugopal Bikram, Hariharan G, and Sudipta Kundu prove maximal inequalities and ergodic theorems for group actions in non-commutative probability spaces. The groups are amenable, locally compact, and second countable, and the actions preserve a given state on tracial spaces of integrable maps. Such results control averages along group orbits, the core of ergodic theory.

Combined with the Neveu decomposition, their inequalities yield a random ergodic theorem for amenable group actions. Readers in map algebras get ergodic tools extended beyond standard measure spaces. Maximal inequalities matter because they turn pointwise convergence questions into estimates that can actually be proved.
arxiv-2512-24851:
Xunyi Zhao, Gengze Zhou, and Qi Wu introduce VLN-MME, a benchmark for testing multimodal language models as navigation agents that follow language instructions. Acting as an embodied agent needs multi-round dialogue, spatial reasoning, and sequential action choices, beyond static vision tasks. Their framework converts traditional vision-and-language navigation datasets into a standardized, modular test.

Models are probed as zero-shot agents, without task-specific training. Readers in multimodal AI get a flexible harness for diagnosing where navigation fails, whether in grounding words, planning routes, or choosing actions. A shared benchmark makes competing models comparable on the same embodied challenge.
arxiv-2512-24951:
Wollenberg, Perona, Palaci, and co-authors introduce laser intracavity uptake magnetometry, a precise way to measure magnetic fields using nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. Intracavity uptake spectroscopy already detects weak uptake with very high sensitivity by placing the sample inside a laser. Extending that idea to magnetometry keeps the sensor inside the laser cavity, where small uptake changes are boosted.

An electrically driven edge-emitting diode laser runs self-sustainably, and highly precise operation under ambient terms is shown. The concept also fits other optical quantum sensors, including optically pumped magnetometers. Quantum sensing readers get a route to compact, precise magnetometers without cold or lab-bound hardware.
arxiv-2601-00151:
Ali Devran Kara, writing alone, studies reinforcement learning when the world does not follow the Markov rule. In that rule, the present state holds all that matters for the future. Real state and cost streams often break it. Kara uses linear function approximation, where values are built from a small set of features. He first asks when policy evaluation still settles down.

Under suitable ergodicity limits, the method does converge. Its limit is a fixed point tied to an auxiliary Markov process. The picture for Q learning is less kind. Convergence fails in general, just as in the Markov case. But one special choice of features, built from quantization maps, restores it. Kara then applies the results to partly observed problems. Memory based states get explicit error bounds there. The work maps where learning stays safe without Markov cover.
arxiv-2601-00351:
Xiuli Bian leads five coauthors in writing out higher multiplication rules for the cohomology of a finite group algebra. Tate Hochschild cohomology mixes algebra and group symmetry deeply. Its cochain complex splits into additive pieces. The team builds a computing frame on that split. Each planar tree breaks into small local parts. Two child and three child nodes carry the local work.

All second level formulas are given on that basis. Explicit higher formulas follow for Hochschild cochains. The chain complex gets the same full treatment. Abelian groups close the paper with their own formulas. Such A infinity structures encode far more than a product. They record how associativity holds up to higher corrections. Concrete formulas are rare and laborious to derive. Algebraists gain a ready computational scheme here. Abstract definitions become objects that can be computed with.
arxiv-2601-00551:
Shuang Li and a nine-author team speed up three-dimensional photoacoustic imaging, a technique that turns absorbed light pulses into sound waves to picture tissue. Arrays of sound detectors shaped to fit a body region could give good images with fewer detectors, saving space and cost. Standard iterative reconstruction, though, struggles with such irregular arrays, demanding heavy computation, memory, and time.

Their algorithm, SlingBAG Pro, grows from an earlier point-cloud iteration method and extends it to arbitrary array geometries. It keeps reconstruction quality high while reducing the number of detectors needed, and a hierarchical optimization strategy cuts the computing burden. Faster, cheaper reconstruction of this kind matters if photoacoustic imaging is to move further into clinics.
arxiv-2601-00651:
Nicola Bortolotti and six co-authors report a 2026 test of an idea about gravity and quantum rules. The idea says that tiny jitters in space itself slowly blur quantum states. It comes from a model first put forth by Karolyhazy, here in a broad form. The team used data from the VIP group in Italy.

From the data, they set a floor on how far the space jitters stay in step. That floor is more than four and a half metres. It is more than ten times the best past limit. Yet a twin bound from how matter settles puts a cap below two metres. A floor above the cap leaves no room for the model to be true. The broad model is thus ruled out, and so is a close kin of it. The work shows how quiet, deep labs can test deep claims about nature.
arxiv-2601-00851:
Emily Lu and a twenty-four-author team propose letting an AI pilot run battery experiments at large research facilities. Understanding battery degradation is critical to the energy transition, but experiments that watch batteries while they work suffer from weak reliability, representativeness, and reproducibility. Bespoke hardware and pre-programmed routines miss fleeting failure events such as the first growth of a dendrite, a metal spike that can short a cell.

Using a multi-modal toolkit at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory as a case study, the authors show conventional experiments systematically miss such transient phenomena. Their heuristic operando framework instead steers the beamline actively, guided by physics-based digital twins, to predict and capture rare events deliberately rather than by luck.
arxiv-2601-01051:
Koustav Mallik studies a workhorse method of statistics called expectation-maximization, or EM, which fills in hidden data step by step to fit a model. Two snags motivate the work. Real data rarely match the model exactly, and some model settings describe the same thing, so the fit has no single right answer to aim at.

Mallik handles the second snag by working on a space where settings that mean the same thing count as one point. He measures error with a broad family of distance measures between data patterns. The main results give a sharp rate for how fast the method settles near a solution, and tight bounds on the error when only a finite sample is at hand. The bounds rest on careful control of random swings in the data.
arxiv-2601-01151:
Yu Qiang, Zhibo Li, and Junchen Pei simulate the fission of a spinning plutonium nucleus to learn how the two fragments get their spin. Fragment spin is a clue to how the nucleus pinches apart, but the details are still debated. The team uses time-dependent density functional theory, a microscopic method that follows every nucleon in effect, and varies the starting spin and heat of the nucleus.

They find the ratio of light to heavy fragment spin stays fixed even at high spin, but shrinks as the nucleus gets hotter. That means the sawtooth pattern in fragment spins would fade with heat, not with spin. Their analysis shows a bending mode of splitting dominates at low heat. Fast spin also stretches the neck between fragments and knocks out nucleons sideways. The results add a missing piece to how fission works in spinning nuclei.
arxiv-2601-01451:
Yong Song, Jiaqi Fu, and Yiting Cen bound the size of a black hole's photon sphere, the shell where light itself can orbit. That shell shapes the black hole's shadow, its lensing of background light, and its ringing after a disturbance. The authors work in Einstein gravity with any number of space dimensions from four up, for still, round, isolated black holes.

Under stated conditions on the surrounding matter, they prove an upper bound set by the black hole's mass, which in four dimensions matches the classic limit of three mass units. A lower bound, needing one extra assumption about the matter's pressure profile, ties the shell to the horizon's radius and also matches the known four-dimensional answer. Such bounds are guardrails: any proposed black hole solution outside them must break an assumption. Extending them beyond four dimensions tests whether familiar intuition survives in higher-dimensional gravity.
arxiv-2601-01751:
Search evaluation increasingly uses large language models to judge whether documents are relevant, replacing costly human assessors. Samaneh Mohtadi and Gianluca Demartini ask a sharper question than average accuracy: do these models make patterned mistakes, judging wrongly in predictable kinds of cases?

Their method embeds each query-document pair as a single point in a shared space. It then clusters the pairs. Relevance is treated as a relation, not a property of one text. On TREC Deep Learning data from 2019 and 2020, disagreements between models and humans clustered in specific groups, especially definition-seeking, policy-related, and ambiguous queries. Pinpointing these hotspots lets evaluation designers target model weaknesses instead of trusting a single average score.
arxiv-2601-02451:
Subhankar Mishra adapts a recent transformer idea, manifold constrained hyper connections, to graph neural networks, which learn from data arranged as nodes and edges. Deep graph networks suffer over smoothing, where node features blur into sameness, and their power is bounded by a classic test of graph difference. The adapted method expands each node into several parallel streams and mixes them only through matrices kept doubly stochastic by a Sinkhorn Knopp procedure.

A proof gives a layer wise lower bound on how fast node differences can decay, far slower than the standard collapse rate tied to the graph spectral gap. The analysis splits into two regimes depending on depth versus stream count. With random stream starts, the method can also separate some graph pairs that the classic test cannot.
arxiv-2601-02551:
Christopher J. R. Clark, Roberto J. Avila, Alyssa Guzman, and Norman A. Grogin mine twenty three years of data from the Hubble Space Telescope's solar blind channel to learn what background light levels observers actually face. Backgrounds in that ultraviolet channel vary a lot between observations. For several filters the spread exceeds a factor of ten, apparently driven by changes in airglow. The faint glow of Earth's upper atmosphere, while filters dominated by detector dark rate vary far less.

For the airglow dominated filters, measured backgrounds sit well below what the telescope's exposure time calculator predicts. Its average airglow estimates exceed the median measured values by factors ranging from about two and a half to more than one hundred, depending on the filter. A preliminary look blames certain oxygen airglow lines that are usually fainter than the calculator assumes, which would let future observations plan for lower backgrounds.
arxiv-2601-02751:
Yuetian Chen and six co authors strengthen membership inference attacks, the tests that ask whether a specific text was inside a language model's training data. Most attacks average a model's loss over the whole text, which dilutes the faint, local traces of memorization. The authors argue membership signals concentrate in short stretches, where a model that saw the text behaves measurably differently from one that did not.

Their method slides windows of many sizes across the text. Each window votes on membership by comparing losses between the target model and a reference model, and votes are combined across scales from single tokens to whole phrases. Across eleven data sets the window based comparison beats established baselines clearly, with higher detection scores and several times better performance at low false positive rates. The result underlines how much fine tuned models leak about their training data.
arxiv-2601-02851:
Samuel Pawel and Leonhard Held make it easier to plan studies that use Bayes factors, a standard way to weigh evidence for one hypothesis against another. Such studies often stop early once the evidence looks conclusive, which suits clinical trials and animal experiments. Until now, working out how a design would perform usually meant slow computer simulations, since no fast formulas existed.

The authors borrow results from classical group sequential design and restate the Bayes factor stopping rules in terms of a familiar test statistic. Probabilities of stopping can then be computed with standard multivariate normal tools, quickly and without simulation. Worked examples cover clinical trials, animal studies, and psychology, and free software in the R package bfpwr lets researchers design such studies with ease.
arxiv-2601-03451:
Nassim Helou, writing alone, builds an economic foundation for learning systems that act inside markets. In such settings, data, behavior, and incentives all shape each other, so a model cannot treat its world as fixed. Helou studies a principal and an agent who both learn over time inside a Markov decision process, a standard model of choices over time, with effects each has on the other.

The proposed mechanism works in two phases: first it estimates which payments can actually be put in place, then it uses them to steer long-run behavior. Under mild conditions it reaches near optimal social welfare over time. Simulations show even rough incentives can fix wasteful learning. The lesson is that safe AI in markets and insurance needs incentive-aware design.
arxiv-2601-03751:
Chuang Yang, Deyou Chen, and Yongtao Liu study spinning particles orbiting a charged Reissner-Nordström black hole and test a proposed universal bound on chaos. The bound links how fast a system scrambles to the black hole's surface gravity. Earlier work found violations near black holes in some field settings, and this team asks whether particle spin changes the story in a spinor field.

For a neutral particle, once its spin passes a threshold, the chaos exponent exceeds surface gravity and the bound is violated. Spin direction matters too: anti-aligned spin gives a larger exponent than aligned spin at fixed total angular momentum. For charged particles, the electromagnetic force shifts values but not the overall trend for large angular momenta. Such tests probe whether the chaos bound is truly universal.
arxiv-2601-07051:
Michael Neumann and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers between policy and practice. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Context: The rapid emergence of generative AI (GenAI) tools has begun to reshape various software engineering activities.

Yet, their adoption within agile environments remains underexplored. Objective: The work investigates how agile practitioners adopt GenAI tools in real-world organizational contexts, focusing on regulatory conditions, use cases, benefits, and barriers. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07751:
Aloïs Demory studies real solutions of special polynomials built from squared monomials. The broader field concerns the topology of real algebraic hypersurfaces: which shapes these equations can form. Since Harnack and Hilbert, the field has split into two directions. One finds restrictions on possible topology. The other constructs hypersurfaces that reach those limits. Demory's 2026 preprint works on real critical points of TT-polynomials.

Sums of squared monomials have special structure that may control their critical points. Critical points shape how the hypersurface bends and connects. Counting and locating them constrains the topology the surface can have. The paper serves real algebraic geometers. It adds to the long effort, started in the nineteenth century, to map which shapes algebra allows. Both the restriction and construction traditions inform the questions asked here.
arxiv-2601-08051: Jay Gopalakrishnan and Gabriel Pinochet-Soto wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to gauge error in eigenspaces found by a code. An eigenspace is a set of modes that a linear map scales but does not turn. The authors reuse error tools made for source problems to bound the gap between the true set and its computed copy. The maps in view are unbounded and not self-mirror in form, with compact inverses. As a first step, the team studies modes of ratio-based forms of such maps.
arxiv-2601-08151:
Shezheng Song, Shasha Li, and Jie Yu ask where vision meets language inside multimodal models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that multimodal large language models now score well on vision-language tasks. Yet how visual information is integrated across layers remains poorly understood.

The authors run layer-wise masking experiments to trace that integration step by step. Masking layers shows which stages carry visual detail into the language side. Their title points to contrastive attention as a tool for refining the fusion process. For model builders, a clearer map of visual fusion could guide leaner designs and better fixes when images are misread.
arxiv-2601-08351: R. S. Hombal and co-authors evaluate radio interference removal methods for single pulse searches. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that artificial and terrestrial signals plague astronomical data. Interference can obscure real signals and trigger large numbers of false detections. Searches for pulsars, rotating radio transients, and fast radio bursts all suffer from this problem. The team compares how well removal algorithms protect single pulse searches. Reliable cleaning could raise the yield of rare transient discoveries from existing telescope data.
arxiv-2601-08651: Pouriya Torkinejad Ziarati constructs critically cyclic functions in Dirichlet spaces of the ball. The 2026 arXiv paper works in the Dirichlet space on the two-dimensional unit ball. The author builds holomorphic functions with a sharp cyclicity threshold. Each example has an index between one half and two such that the function is cyclic exactly up to that index. Cyclic functions can approximate every function in the space through shifts. Sharp examples map the border between cyclic and non-cyclic behavior for analysts studying these function spaces.
arxiv-2601-08951:
Jing-Jing Li and six co-authors build a test for how folk judge harm from AI acts. Most safe frames treat harm as a yes or no call. Real folk oft split on edge cases. One group may call an act rude but safe. The next may call it a true harm. A test that hides that split can mislead builders.

Their test is called PluriHarms. It holds the full spread of human calls, not just the most common one. It tracks where splits arise and why. A reader who builds safe AI gets a more true scale. It lets a tool learn that harm calls can be plural, and plan for the split.
arxiv-2601-09251:
Qin-Yi Zhang and eight co-authors build a learn solver for systems where a fluid and a solid move each other. A wing bends in wind, and its bend shifts the wind. Each side obeys its own rules, and they meet at a face that moves. Grid sims of such pairs are true but slow. Past learn solvers treat both sides as one stuff, and miss their split traits.

Their solver is called HGATSolver. It uses a mixed graph focus net, with nodes for fluid and solid in one graph. Focus weights let each side keep its own voice at the meet face. A reader in sim work gets a fast solver that still hears the split of the pair.
arxiv-2601-09551:
Zhicong Lin and four co-authors settle a counting conjecture about Young tableaux with walls. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on work by Banderier, Marchal, and Wallner. These tableaux look like standard Young tableaux, except that entries may decrease at certain walls.

Fuchs and Yu had conjectured a formula for two classes of three-row tableaux with walls. The authors prove that conjecture. Enumeration results like this feed the wider theory of lattice paths and symmetric functions. A proof also validates the methods used to guess the formula, which can now be trusted on harder cases.
arxiv-2601-09651:
Timothy J. Krogmeier, Anthony W. Schlimgen, and Kade Head-Marsden model how molecular spins lose their quantum coherence. Their 2026 arXiv paper gives a perturbative, non-Markovian treatment of low-temperature spin decoherence. Molecular spins are promising carriers for quantum sensing and computing.

Their coherence is eroded by nuclear spins in the molecule and its surroundings. At low temperatures the bath has memory, so Markovian models miss the physics. The authors build a treatment that keeps that memory while staying tractable. Better decoherence models can help chemists design molecules that hold their quantum states longer.
arxiv-2601-09951:
R. Malarchick and A. Steed run a key quantum task on a fast chip set. The task finds the low point of the energy of a molecule. It mixes quantum steps with classic steps in a loop. The team used the PennyLane set of tools for the run.

They ran the task for the hydrogen molecule. They swept one bond length at a time, for a full range of lengths. The run used a high end cluster with four large GPUs. The paper is about speed tricks. Just in time code builds and work split across GPUs let the loop scale up.
arxiv-2601-10151:
