Such signals usually die within tens of nanometres, limiting chiral spintronics. The team induced chirality in a semiconductor polymer and built it into a transistor device.

In darkness with a magnetic field, the chiral signal traveled up to ten micrometres, already far beyond the norm. Under light, spin-selective effects switched the signal into another form and stretched its range to the millimetre scale, a leap of orders of magnitude. Gate voltage, temperature, and polarized light each tuned the signal, giving detailed control. The authors expect the long range and light switching to advance chiral spintronics theory and devices.
pmc-13267351:
Lauren Angel and colleagues describe a 2026 workshop that let patients help design a vulvar cancer trial. Standard care removes lymph nodes in the groin, which can cause lasting swelling and harm. The planned ANVU trial, across several countries, will test whether ultrasound checks can safely replace that surgery for some women.

Patients with lived experience of the disease joined the research team for a structured session. Short-term, they prized full cancer removal and accepted some side effects. Later, quality of life, fear of the cancer returning, and avoiding chronic swelling mattered most. These views set the trial's main outcome, survival after node spread at 30 months, and added patient-centered measures such as return to daily life.
pmc-13267551:
Saleck Choumad and colleagues present a 2026 case report on brain inflammation in a child after a viral illness. Their patient was seven years old and developed behavior changes two weeks after a flu-like illness, along with vomiting and tiredness. Spinal fluid tests were normal, so imaging carried the diagnosis.

Brain MRI showed bright patches on both sides of the deep gray nuclei, the basal ganglia, on water-sensitive sequences. Blood tests suggested a recent herpes-family infection, though no direct virus test was done. The child got supportive and anti-inflammatory care and slowly improved. At three months the child had no lasting problems, and a repeat MRI showed the patches fully gone. The authors stress MRI's central role in such cases.
pmc-13268051:
C R Horsburgh and colleagues wrote a 2026 scoping review of community-wide tuberculosis screening. TB still kills more people than any other single infection. Many infectious people have no symptoms, so waiting for clinic visits misses them. The team gathered studies since 1945 where whole communities were actively screened, keeping those that measured TB rates before and after or against an unscreened community.

Eight studies qualified, spanning nine countries from China to Zimbabwe. Starting TB rates varied widely. Five studies cut TB prevalence by 44 percent to over 80 percent. The winners shared a trait: over several years they found well over the number of cases first estimated to exist. Two studies failed to cut rates and found far fewer. The authors conclude that repeated full rounds of screening can break transmission.
pmc-13269151:
Daniele Napolitano and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on family carers of adults with inflammatory bowel disease in Italy. Carers help with daily self-care for a long-term gut illness. The study asked whether giving more of that help goes with better or worse quality of life for the carer.

Surveys from 275 carers at nine centers were analyzed. Help with upkeep, watching, and managing care showed no clear link with physical quality of life. Only upkeep help showed a link with mental quality of life, and the link was curved rather than straight. Carers in the upper middle of upkeep help scored 6.58 points higher on mental health than those lower down.
pmc-13269251:
Vitor Heidrich and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on how microbe strains pass between the mouth and gut, and between people living together. A strain is a close variant of a germ species. The team compared mouth and stool samples taken in pairs.

Across 1,644 paired samples, housemates shared far more strains than strangers, in both mouth and gut. Romantic partners shared the most mouth strains, even more than their gut sharing. Within one person, 74.5 percent of species found at both sites were the same strain, pointing to saliva as the route. One gut species was an exception, never matching between sites. Some highly shared gut species linked to poorer heart and metabolic health.
pmc-13269651:
Sarah Aljefri and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 59-year-old woman treated with topiramate for pressure inside the skull. Eight days after starting the drug at 25 milligrams twice daily, she developed painless blurred vision and faded colors in both eyes. Eye exams found fluid lifting the retina, the light-sensing layer, in several spots.

Tests for infection and inflammation found nothing. The drug was stopped, and over three months the fluid cleared fully and vision improved to 20/30 in both eyes. Detachment of this fluid type is a rare side effect of topiramate, which is used for seizures and migraine. The authors stress fast drug withdrawal when it is suspected.
pmc-13269751:
Noa Scholz-Murcia and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a web tool that calculates where places sat on Earth in deep past time. Plate models describe how continents drifted, but using them often needs coding skills. Their tool, PACA, lets users upload located data and pick a model.

Reconstructions appear in three dimensions, layered on classic world maps of past eras. Checks against desktop software showed near-perfect agreement, with median position errors under 17 meters. Statistical tests found no systematic bias across models. The authors say the tool widens access to these reconstructions and makes Earth science work easier to repeat and check.
pmc-13269951:
Yan Xu, Jing Ye, and Shuaiqing Chen published a journal article in 2026 on remnant cholesterol, a lesser-known blood fat, and gout in United States adults. National survey data from 2007 to 2018 covered 11,685 adults aged 20 and over. Statistical models adjusted for age, lifestyle, and health factors, and tested the shape of the link.

Higher remnant cholesterol went with more gout, in a straight rising line. Each small unit increase raised gout odds by a factor of 1.01. People in the top quarter of levels had 65 percent greater odds than those in the bottom quarter. Body weight explained 23 percent of the link, and uric acid, the chemical that builds up in gout, explained 40 percent.
pmc-13270251:
Akino Inagaki and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on wild boars responding to a dead female of their own species in Nikko City, Japan. Camera traps watched the carcass from October 1 to November 11, 2023, through its full decay. Three boars visited, and animal responses to dead group members are rarely documented in this way.

One adult male mounted the carcass, a necrophilic act counted as only the 11th documented case in mammals. His interest lasted about 17 days after the first visit, including stepping on the carcass and resting beside it. No visitor ate soft tissue, so feeding did not drive the visits. The authors argue that watching carcasses reveals behavior shifts across decay stages.
pmc-13271151:
Andrea Brandstetter is lead author of a 2026 journal article mapping the human bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, a small deep brain structure involved in stress responses and anxiety. The structure has distinct parts, but routine MRI cannot show them because it is tiny and low in contrast, making it hard to locate in living brains.

The team mapped the nucleus across its full extent in stained tissue slices from ten human brains, making 1,130 annotations and identifying four subdivisions: central, dorsal, medial, and posterior. They produced probability maps in a standard brain space, plus ultra-detailed maps in a high-resolution model brain. Both sets are openly available as references for imaging studies.
pmc-13271751:
Bridget O'Sullivan is lead author of a 2026 methods article on co-designing technology-supported integrated care with the people who will use it. Integrated care pathways and new technology both fail often when built without deep knowledge of local users and settings, and reviewers have called for earlier, more continuous stakeholder involvement, reported in detail.

The study develops and tests a method combining participatory rapid appraisal with focus groups, applied in the GERONTE project on older people's care. It was designed to engage many end-users in different places, allow quick feedback between users and designers, and flex around users' time. The article reports the process, the application, and the core steps so other teams can adopt or adapt it.
pmc-13272651:
Yutaka Akikusa leads a 2026 study of why fission yeast stops growing well at high heat, focusing on how cells make proteins. Earlier work found two proteins that hinder heat growth. Here the team shows they form a pair and work with a larger complex that controls RNA fate.

The pair normally holds down genes needed to build ribosomes, the cell's protein-making machines. When the pair is lost, those genes become more active, protein making improves, and heat growth recovers. The authors argue that the heat sensitivity of protein making itself may set the upper temperature limit for this yeast. Gene activity data support that view.
pmc-13272951:
Xiaoli Li leads a 2026 genetics study seeking treatment targets for two blood disorders marked by excess blood cell production. In essential thrombocythemia, platelets run high; in polycythemia vera, red cells run high. The team used a post-GWAS framework that joins gene data with causal inference methods to rank molecular drivers.

Higher predicted levels of five proteins linked to risk of both disorders, while one gene, MYB, linked only to the platelet disorder. Several markers also changed platelet, red cell, and white cell counts in distinct patterns. Two DNA marks lowered one key protein and raised risk for both disorders, pointing to shared and separate pathways for therapy.
pmc-13273151:
Gustavo Rey Alvira-Arill leads a 2026 cross-sectional survey of antimicrobial stewardship programs in children's hospitals in the United States. Such programs promote optimal antibiotic use in children. The survey, run in late 2024, asked about structure, staffing, activities, and after-hours on-call coverage.

Twenty-two programs replied, most from academic centers. Physician staffing rose with hospital size, from 0.1 full-time equivalents in the smallest to 0.8 in the largest, while pharmacist staffing rose to 2.25 in the largest. Nearly all programs did audit and feedback during work hours. Only six programs, 27.4 percent, offered on-call coverage, mainly for urgent approvals and inquiries on evenings, weekends, and holidays.
pmc-13274551:
Reina Murasawa and a large team report a 2026 case report of a newborn's abdominal tumor that masqueraded as a different cancer. A fast-growing mass above the right adrenal gland was spotted late in pregnancy and first read as neuroblastoma, the commonest malignant tumor of this age. Its mixed cystic and solid look, plus nonspecific blood tests, fit that guess.

After birth the mass kept growing, yet scans showed no abnormal tracer uptake and hormone byproducts stayed normal. Repeat imaging over time revealed new calcium deposits and fatty parts, classic teratoma clues that were missing at first. Surgery removed the mass completely, and testing confirmed an immature retroperitoneal teratoma with no adrenal involvement. The authors stress watching such masses evolve over time.
pmc-13275151:
Daniele Sciuto, Madeline C MacKechnie, and Michael J Terry report a 2026 case series on limb-saving flap surgery in Samburu County, Kenya, performed by an orthopedic surgeon rather than a plastic surgeon. Severe leg wounds need prompt soft-tissue cover to prevent bone infection and amputation, but reconstructive specialists are scarce in low-resource regions. The surgeon had taken a short-term training course in flap techniques.

The series covers fifteen procedures in thirteen patients between 2018 and 2024, most for severe open shin fractures with exposed bone. The reverse sural artery flap was used most often. Overall flap success reached 86.7 percent. The authors present short, hands-on orthoplastic training as a scalable way to close the reconstructive care gap in austere settings.
pmc-13275551:
Yasuharu Suga and co-authors present a 2026 case report of eye ulcers in two kittens traced to their own vaccine strain. The two-month-old littermates received a core feline herpesvirus vaccine at six weeks old, then developed sneezing and eye discharge within days. Another clinic misread it as allergy and gave steroid eye drops for a week, which can worsen herpes eye disease.

On presentation, each kitten had branching dendritic ulcers in one eye and a shallow ulcer in the other. Genetic testing matched the virus to the vaccine's F2 strain, with no wild strain present, though a second virus, calicivirus, shared the shallow ulcers. Branching ulcers healed in six days on antiviral treatment. The shallow ones later grew crystal deposits and deep blood vessels, ending in scarring complications in both cats.
pmc-13276051:
Dieta Hanson and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on counting visitors to public lands in the United States. Land managers need visitor numbers for planning, but counters are costly at remote sites with many entrances. The team tested whether phone and online data could stand in for on-site counting.

They gathered counts from seventy Bureau of Land Management sites, totaling over thirteen hundred site-months of data. Three computer models combined site features with mobile phone locations, geotagged social media, and nature observation records. Models using site features beat models using digital traces alone. Accuracy on new sites varied, depending on whether similar sites were in the training data. The authors advise blending many data sources rather than trusting phone data by itself.
pmc-13276251:
Karen Kai-Lin Hwang and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a flexible way to watch cell health in real time. Reporter proteins that glow can track acidity, stress chemicals, and energy levels inside cells. But hard-to-grow primary cells resist the usual DNA delivery, and making stable reporter lines for each use is impractical.

Instead, the team delivered the reporter instructions as messenger RNA, the short-lived molecule cells read to build proteins. Uptake was high in primary skin cells, cancer cells, and stem cells grown from adult tissue. Three ratio-based reporters worked as intended, sensing acidity, hydrogen peroxide, and ATP, the cell's energy currency, in specific cell compartments. The authors say the approach frees metabolic studies from commercial kits and suits patient-derived cells.
pmc-13276451:
Shuaikang Hao and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on measuring light-activated drug levels inside tissue more precisely. Photosensitizers gather in tumors and glow under light, guiding surgery and powering light-based therapy. Tissue bends and dims that glow, so raw brightness misstates the true drug amount.

Their deep learning system, called HS-QFNet, learns from both the glow's full spectrum and reflected light images. It was trained on lab phantoms, fake tissue blocks with known drug levels and varied optical traits. An attention mechanism helps it model how distortion depends on tissue properties. In phantoms it cut measurement error by about two thirds versus traditional correction. In mouse tumors its estimates stayed close and tracked true levels tightly. The authors see uses in drawing tumor margins and personalizing light therapy doses.
pmc-13278051:
Medha Sridhar Rao wrote a 2026 reflective essay on a student medical elective at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Australia. The essay, chosen among the best submissions from Queen's University Belfast students for 2025, contrasts past and present children's bone and joint care. In Victorian London, conditions such as clubfoot and scoliosis drew stigma and care was mostly non-surgical.

Modern practice centers on function and quality of life, though resources and place still shape what children receive. Cases during the elective included a thirteen-year-old with severe cerebral palsy who had never walked despite custom supports. The reflections weigh what the specialty offers beyond the bones themselves, in the author's phrase.
pmc-13278451:
Moemen Khalifa leads a 2026 study of thyroid harm after breast radiotherapy given in fewer, larger doses. Radiation to the breast area can expose part of the thyroid gland, causing underactivity months or years later. The team followed 109 women with normal thyroid function who received regional breast radiotherapy and retested them six months after treatment.

About eight percent developed radiation-induced hypothyroidism, an underactive thyroid, by that check. Risk rose with higher maximum and mean thyroid doses and with smaller thyroid lobe size on the treated side. A key dose measure, the share of thyroid receiving forty gray, passed clear thresholds tied to higher risk. The authors propose planning limits to spare the thyroid and call for larger, longer studies.
pmc-13278851:
Yangha Kim reports 2026 surveillance figures on seat belt non-use among adolescents in Korea, drawn from the twenty-first Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey of 2025. Non-use means riding while wearing a belt seldom or never. The note tracks three settings: front seats, rear seats, and express buses, over the period from 2016 to 2025.

In 2025, non-use stood at thirteen percent for the front seat, about forty-three percent for the rear seat, and twenty-seven percent for express buses. Rear seat non-use has fallen substantially over the past ten years, the report notes, yet it remains by far the highest of the three. The figures are published in both English and Korean by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.
pmc-13279751:
Bruna Mezzomo Bejes and colleagues report a 2026 study of drug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa from hospitals in south Brazil. The germ is a major hospital threat that shrugs off many drugs. Carbapenem drugs, a last line class, fail when germs make carbapenemase enzymes that break them. The team read the genomes of clinical isolates from Parana and Santa Catarina states. They matched gene finds with drug test results.

Eight isolates, eighty percent of the set, ranked as extensively drug resistant. They beat back beta lactam drugs, carbapenems and paired inhibitor drugs alike. Type reads showed a mixed clone scene, with ST1560 the top type at thirty percent. Many beta lactamase genes showed up, held both on chromosomes and on plasmids, small DNA rings that can jump between germs. Gene spread by plasmids raises the stakes for hospital control.
pmc-13280351:
Shuling Wu and colleagues report a 2026 case of long survival in a rare chest cancer after immune and vessel therapy. Mediastinal sarcomatoid carcinoma arises in the chest centre and often ends poorly. No past work tested immunotherapy plus anti angiogenic therapy, which starves tumour vessels, for it. Their patient was a seventy four year old woman. Tumour tests showed high PD-L1 expression, an immune brake protein, with a score of eighty.

She first got two cycles of chemotherapy and one cycle of radiotherapy with anlotinib, a vessel blocker, for stable disease. Two cycles of durvalumab immunotherapy with anlotinib then gave a partial response. Immunotherapy stopped due to severe side effects, while anlotinib went on. She stays alive with no disease progression past forty two months. The pair of therapies may suit PD-L1 high cases of this rare cancer.
pmc-13280451:
Linda G. Franken and colleagues report a 2026 study of guanabenz dosing in children with vanishing white matter disease. Vanishing white matter is a leukodystrophy, a white matter decay illness, that causes neurological decline and early death. No treatment exists for it. Guanabenz, a blood pressure drug that acts in the brain, eases the disease in mouse models. The team built a translational dosing model from rodent and adult data for a phase one two trial in children.

The estimated target dose was two milligrams per kilogram per day. The minimum effective dose was one, and the maximum was ten, in the same units. Pharmacokinetic modelling used thirty two trial participants aged about two to thirteen years. The study also explored links between drug levels and side effects, and estimated brain levels via a biological effect marker. Model based dosing can spare children trial and error in rare disease trials.
pmc-13280651:
Luiz E T Avelar and colleagues shared a 2026 case series on face care after weight loss from GLP-1 drugs. These drugs treat diabetes and obesity, but fast weight loss can hollow the face and deepen lines. The series followed fifteen women, aged thirty to fifty, in four Latin American countries. Each woman got two kinds of filler shots to restore the face.

Photos taken about ninety days later showed less loose skin and softer wrinkles. All fifteen women said their looks had improved, and most said they were pleased. No one had a serious side effect. Mild bruising and swelling cleared on their own within three days. The authors say the paired fillers may help patients who lose weight on these drugs.
pmc-13281351:
Laurence Cobbaert wrote a 2026 letter on harm caused by eating disorder care itself. Talk therapy can ease eating disorders, but gain is not proof of safety. Harms from care are poorly defined and rarely tracked, the author argues. So no one can say how often harm and gain occur side by side. When patients report harm, staff may brush it off as resistance or poor insight. That dismissal can deepen the wound and block learning.

Harm also falls unevenly, the letter says. Care that ignores culture, body diversity, or social barriers can hurt marginalized patients in distinct ways. Cobbaert calls for tracking harms from the start in every study. Patient reports and open-ended checks should count as core data. People who lived the harm should help design care and define what repair means. Claims of proof, the author warns, must cover safety too.
pmc-13281951:
Yingchao Ma and colleagues built a dosing model for a last-resort antibiotic in a 2026 study. The drug revives old power against germs that resist modern standbys. Its safe band is narrow, and levels swing widely between patients. The team enrolled fifty-one very ill patients with drug-proof infections at a Hebei hospital. Care ran from 2021 to 2023. Blood readings, one hundred twenty-three in all, fed the model. Computer runs then tested doses across kidney strength and germ toughness.

About six in ten patients improved in care, and about half cleared their germs. Kidney harm was rare, in two patients. A one-room model fit the drug's path, with kidney strength as the key dial. Standard doses hit the target zone reliably only for the most sensitive germs in normal kidneys. Tougher germs or weaker kidneys broke the target. The authors offer it as a dosing guide.
pmc-13282151:
Sana M Salih and co-authors wrote a 2026 case report and literature review on fertility during long-term treatment with a targeted lung cancer drug. The drug, osimertinib, blocks a faulty growth signal in some lung cancers. Older chemotherapy is well known to harm the ovaries, but newer targeted drugs are far less studied. Their patient was a thirty-year-old woman with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, an inherited condition that raises cancer risk, plus lung cancer.

Over thirty-six months of therapy, her ovarian reserve stayed normal. Blood hormone tests and repeated ultrasound counts of small follicles, the sacs that hold eggs, remained stable. Still, hard choices remain. Pregnancy is not allowed during the drug treatment. Gene testing of embryos may be used to avoid passing on the cancer-risk mutation, and a surrogate carrier may be considered. A preserved reserve lets patients delay fertility treatment until a better time.
pmc-13282251:
Emily R Shertzer and co-authors report a 2026 field study on how nestling traits shape death risk after young songbirds leave the nest. Early conditions can carry over into later life stages. The team tracked three sagebrush songbird species in the post-fledging period, the weeks after leaving the nest. They recorded causes of death and tested which nestling body traits predicted each cause.

Carryover effects differed by species and by cause of death. Leg length, unexpectedly, had an outsized effect on predation risk in the two sparrow species. Most deaths fell in the first five days, when young birds could not yet fly. At that stage they likely escaped by running or scrambling, so leg traits mattered more than wing traits. The authors say growing birds face trade-offs, since body investment that helps against one risk may not help against another at a different stage.
pmc-13282351:
Jie Wang and co-authors present a 2026 analysis from a lung cancer drug trial on how patient-reported symptoms relate to survival. The trial tested an immune therapy drug, tislelizumab, added to chemotherapy, against chemotherapy alone. Patients had advanced squamous non-small cell lung cancer, a common lung cancer type. Earlier results favoured the combined treatment for survival and quality of life.

pmc-13311251:
Katarzyna Pogoda and co-authors analyze the 2026 cohort on how HER2 status shifts in breast cancer after drug treatment given before surgery. Such shifts can change which follow-up drugs make sense.

The team compared tumor samples before and after treatment in 736 patients treated from 2019 to 2024. HER2 class changed in 34.2 percent of patients, and drops in HER2 level were more common than rises. New HER2-positive status after treatment was rare. Knowing how often the marker moves helps doctors decide when retesting the leftover tumor is worth doing. That timing question matters for drug choice after surgery.
pmc-13311951:
Shivana Neeta Modi and co-authors present their 2026 London cohort study on what counts as a successful move from child to adult epilepsy services, and whether success improves seizure outcomes.

The study followed patients aged 20 to 24 who had moved from a pediatric service between 2009 and 2023. Success needed four marks: timely start, full preparation, a joint clinic visit, and adult follow-up within six months. Of 59 eligible patients, 72.9 percent met all four in this cohort. Successful movers had over fourfold adjusted odds of better seizure control or staying seizure-free by age twenty.
pmc-13312051:
Juan Yang and co-authors follow, in a 2026 longitudinal study, how symptom groups and quality of life change around surgery in women with cervical cancer. They tracked 183 patients at a hospital in northwestern China from admission through the days after their operations.

Using symptom and quality-of-life questionnaires at three time points, the team found five symptom clusters, covering pain and fatigue, mood, hot flashes and nerve symptoms, digestion, and low energy. Most clusters peaked one to three days after surgery and then eased, while quality of life dipped and only partly recovered. Worse cluster scores went with worse quality of life, which supports watching symptoms as shifting groups rather than one by one.
pmc-13312151:
Caio César Gonçalves Silva and co-authors report a 2026 three-dimensional study of how Le Fort I osteotomy changes the nose and sinus region. This jaw surgery, which frees the upper jaw so it can be repositioned, is widely used to correct midface deformities. Moving the bone also disturbs the walls of the maxillary sinus and nasal cavity.

Comparing scans from before and after surgery, the team found that breaks in the continuity of the sinus walls, nasal cavity, and septum were common after the operation. The lining of the maxillary sinuses thickened more in the postoperative period, while the air volume of both the sinuses and the nasal cavity shrank. The authors suggest watching factors that could upset sinus balance after surgery, since lasting swelling raises the risk of sinusitis.
pmc-13312251:
Jay Olivet and colleagues present a 2026 program evaluation of rapid molecular testing for bloodstream infections caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. This severe infection does best on targeted beta-lactam drugs such as cefazolin. Many patients sit on vancomycin while conventional cultures crawl, and late switches are tied to slower clearance, more failures, and kidney harm.

The study compares care before and after the hospital adopted a blood culture identification panel, run on an automated platform, that names the organism directly from a positive culture. Patients are then ranked by a combined desirability score weighing treatment success, kidney injury, and survival, with secondary measures such as time to optimal therapy and length of stay. The authors set out to learn whether faster identification leads to earlier targeted treatment and better overall outcomes for these patients.
pmc-13312551:
Mohamed Mahmoud Shalaby and Fatma Aboalsoud Taha follow, in a 2026 prospective study, the hearts of newborns born with a left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia around the time of surgical repair. Babies with this defect face lung and circulation trouble, and a small, strained left ventricle often decides how they fare, yet serial heart measurements across the operation were scarce.

Thirty term newborns at a tertiary center had detailed ultrasound heart scans within a day before repair, again two to three days after, and once more at one month. Significant pulmonary hypertension was present before surgery in 70 percent of the babies. After repair, left ventricular dimensions, both raw and size-adjusted, grew significantly at the early and one-month checks, while several measures of pumping function dipped significantly in the early period. The authors chart a heart reshaping itself as circulation normalizes.
pmc-13315451:
Jinmei Gao and colleagues studied in 2026 how high homocysteine in mother mice affects the fertility of their daughters. Mothers fed a high-methionine diet developed the condition, defined by blood homocysteine above 15 micromoles per liter, and the team then checked the ovaries and eggs of female offspring.

Resting follicles switched on too early, driven by stronger signals through proteins including mTOR, AKT, FOXO3a, and RPS6. Mature eggs held fewer mitochondria that worked less well, with more reactive oxygen, more DNA damage, and more spindle faults. Together those changes lowered egg quality and help explain reduced fertility in the offspring.
pmc-13316651:
Yang Zhang and colleagues report 2026 lab work on Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that switches between free floating growth and sticky biofilm life on skin and inside cells. Acid stress is common in those niches, and the team asked how a secretion machine part called EssC shapes the switch.

Deleting the essC gene made biofilms grow thicker and heavier at acid levels near skin, even though fewer bacteria inside stayed alive. The mutant stuck faster, clumped more, and leaked more DNA from self-digested cells, all changes that cement a biofilm. Gene control circuits shifted in step, turning down a biofilm brake and turning up glue making paths. EssC emerges as a quiet governor of survival strategy.
pmc-13316751:
Maureen Norah Nabulime and colleagues offer a 2026 protocol for sorting and testing city solid waste from many sources, so towns can judge energy recovery options on solid data. Waste differs by source, and sloppy sampling ruins the math for digestion or gasification projects.

Called MSW-CAP, the framework standardizes collection, sorting, and lab checks, building on an existing ASTM method. Trials ran on home, grocery, restaurant, and school waste across five United States states. Samples split by moisture level, sending wet waste toward digestion and dry waste toward gasification paths. The shared recipe lets cities compare results fairly and pick recovery routes with fewer surprises.
pmc-13318051:
Mathieu Hénault and co-authors build, in a 2026 yeast study, a unified model of how wrong chromosome counts arise, persist, and sometimes fix themselves. Extra or missing chromosomes cause many birth and tissue disorders, and oddly, a second sorting error can restore balance.

The team measured gain and loss rates for each chromosome in budding yeast, weighed the fitness of each state, and fed the numbers into population models. True back-errors proved too rare to matter for most chromosomes. A few chromosomes that seemed to revert fast instead passed through a brief unstable state, with stuck-together chromosomes breaking and being repaired across divisions, as sequencing and live imaging confirmed. Chromosome-specific routes, they conclude, shape genome change.
pmc-13318251:
Giovanna Spina leads a 2026 retrospective study of total elbow replacement for older patients whose lower arm bone fractures near the elbow could not be rebuilt with plates and screws. Records covered operations done between January 2017 and December 2024.

Thirty-seven patients, averaging 80.4 years old, were followed for a mean of 107 months and assessed for movement, pain, function scores, imaging findings, and complications. Final results showed good elbow motion and function, with a revision rate of 11 percent and implant survival of 94.2 percent at five years in this group. Other health problems did not clearly change outcomes, supporting replacement as a primary option for selected older patients.
pmc-13318551:
Adriano José Pereira and a large team set out a 2026 protocol for TELESCOPE 2, a trial testing whether telemedicine support can shorten stays in intensive care units in Brazil. Earlier work showed remote intensive care is safe and workable, but its effect on patient outcomes is unproven.

Twenty-five units will join in a stepped-wedge design, starting the programme at staggered times in five randomised sequences between January 2024 and January 2026. The package combines daily remote rounds led by intensive care doctors, coordinated input from nurses, physiotherapists, and pharmacists, and a quality and safety programme. Length of intensive care stay is the main measure, backed by death rates, ventilator-free days, readmission, and tube accidents.
pmc-13319651:
Şeyba Sara Mansuroğlu and co-authors compare rinse methods for killing germs deep in tooth roots in a 2026 lab study. Germs that hide in tiny tubes in root walls are a main cause of lasting tooth infection. Five ways to stir rinse fluid were tested for how deep their kill reached into those tubes.

Sixty pulled human teeth with one root canal each were filled with a hardy germ type, then rinsed by needle, soft tip, sound, or pulse methods. Slices at three depths were viewed under a strong scope to measure the kill zone. Pulse rinsing reached deepest at both top and tip ends, while plain needle rinsing reached least. No method cleared germs in full.
pmc-13320351:
Wanyue Li and co-authors study sleep habits and spine curve risk in a 2026 long follow up study from a British health bank. Sideways spine curves can arise in adult life, yet forward looking proof on sleep as a risk factor was near absent. A five part sleep score joined bed time type, sleep length, sleeplessness, snoring, and day sleepiness into one habit grade.

Among 408870 adults free of the curve at the start, 2976 new cases arose over a mean span near sixteen years. Each added healthy sleep trait cut risk by about a tenth in the adjusted counts, and those with all five traits faced far lower risk than those with almost none. The link held across most subgroups, which hints sleep care may aid spine health.
pmc-13320451:
Kamran Dousti and co-authors survey public knowledge of invasive mosquitoes in Saarland, Germany in a 2026 study. The region has no settled tiger mosquito yet but faces rising invasion risk as the insect spreads in Europe and can carry tropical fevers. A public form ran from February to June 2024 through digital and paper routes to gauge awareness, habits, and knowledge.

Of 1064 replies, 623 met the study rules for a close look in the counts reported. More than half knew that clearing still water blocks breeding, yet fewer than one in five did it on a regular basis. Most had heard of the tiger mosquito, but fewer than half tied it to one fever it can carry. Seasonal teaching drives may slow the insect foothold, the team argues.
pmc-13321251:
Ernestina Melicoff, David Moreno McNeill, and Christian Benden look ahead for children's lung transplantation in a 2026 review. The piece opens a special issue on paediatric chest transplantation and covers donor access, graft failure, and how fitness shapes outcomes. Lung transplant is a settled option for a small group of children with severe lung disease.

In the United States, 1511 paediatric lung transplants were reported from 1988 to 2024, and 46.8 percent were for cystic fibrosis, long the leading reason. New cystic fibrosis drugs are reshaping who needs a transplant. The authors argue that donor supply, long term graft health, and frailty checks will decide the field's next gains.
pmc-13322751:
Zengchun Xie and co-authors tune reflected colour in laser written nanocomposites in a 2026 study. Ordered layers of tiny silica particles can produce structural colour without dyes, much like patterns in nature. Direct laser writing was used to arrange the particles in stacked tiers inside a composite material.

By adjusting particle size, particle type, loading, and laser settings, the team widened the reflected colour range across the visible spectrum. Electron microscopy showed the neat, non-packed order survived the writing process, with features below a micron made reliably. Colour measures matched the tuning, and the method produced tiny three dimensional multicolour images, including versions with plasmonic coated particles.
pmc-13322951:
Zrinka Greblo Jurakić and colleagues study team climate and well-being in teen handball, in a 2026 survey of 522 players aged 14 to 17 years. Players rated the motivational climate set by their coaches and completed scales for anxiety, depression, stress and self-esteem.

Teams were seen as more task-focused than ego-focused overall, though boys reported a weaker task climate than girls. A task focus linked to lower anxiety, depression and stress and to higher self-esteem, while an ego focus showed the reverse pattern. Among girls, those coached by men saw a weaker task climate and stronger ego climate than those coached by women. The authors advise coaches to reward effort and learning over comparison.
pmc-13323151:
Angana Mukherjee and co-authors study the transcription factor FOXI3 in prostate cancer that has spread to bone, in a 2026 tissue and cell study. FOXI3 helps normal bone develop, and the team had earlier found it raised in prostate cancer without knowing its role.

Staining of human tumours linked FOXI3 to worse pathology and higher grade, and public gene data showed it markedly raised in bone metastases alongside FGF8. Adding FGF8 lifted FOXI3 in bone-derived cancer cells but not in a brain-derived line. Movement and growth of bone-derived cells depended on FOXI3 in their tests. The authors cast the FGF8-FOXI3 link as a bone-specific driver worth targeting.
pmc-13324251:
Ekhlas Qays Al-shawway and Zohre Balak test a two-layer high-entropy ceramic composite, in a 2026 materials study. One layer joins five metal carbides with graphite and silicon additives, while the other forms medium-entropy borides in place from oxides with carbon sources.

Spark plasma sintering pressed the layers at 2,000 degrees Celsius under pressure for ten minutes. The carbide layer densified almost fully, reaching far higher density and hardness than the boride layer in their measures, with hardness near 15 GPa against about 1.2 GPa for the boride side. Grain sizes sat in the hundreds of nanometres for both. Microscopy and diffraction mapped how additives shaped each microstructure.
pmc-13327651:
Mingyang Wei and co-authors describe a 2026 case where a slipped upper back disc caused belly pain for years. A 65-year-old woman had right lower abdominal pain for more than five years, worse over the last three months, with back pain and pain down her left leg. Repeated belly, gynecology, and urinary checks found nothing to explain it.

Back scans showed wear at several levels, including a disc slip at L2-3 and narrowing at L4-5. A guided numbing injection at the L2-3 nerve root cut her belly pain score from 7 to 3, naming the level, and keyhole removal of that disc dropped it further to 2. A later fusion at L4-5 eased the leg pain, showing how spine disease can masquerade as abdominal illness.
pmc-13327951:
Kristine Santos and co-authors update a comparison of two pain methods for chest wall surgery in a 2026 meta-analysis. The Nuss procedure fixes sunken chests, and pain control comes from either freezing chest nerves or an epidural catheter. Fifteen studies covering 1,391 patients were pooled, with 823 receiving the freezing method.

Freezing lengthened operations by about 29.1 minutes and raised hospital costs by about 1,655.3 US dollars on the pooled estimates, yet patients left hospital 2.7 days sooner, reported less pain on day three, and used far fewer opioids. Matched and randomized subgroups backed the same pattern, with no clear difference in complications. Recovery gains may justify the higher upfront cost.
pmc-13329751:
Christian Kim and co-authors review breast cancer spread to the eye socket and add four new cases in a 2026 article. Breast cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and the most common source of such spread. The team searched medical reports from 2011 to 2025 for biopsy-proven cases.

Of 220 records screened, 63 articles with 69 cases met the rules in the reported counts. Most patients were women, with an average age of 60 years at eye symptoms. In 43 percent of cases, eye spread was the first sign of breast cancer in those summaries. Double vision and blur were the top complaints. Care varied widely. The authors advise doctors to weigh spread when patients with breast history show eye signs.
pmc-13332451:
Man Wu and colleagues tested a wake-up-and-kill strategy against Epstein-Barr virus linked stomach cancer in a 2026 laboratory study. The virus hides silently in these tumor cells, and forcing it into its active cycle can make the cancer vulnerable to antiviral drugs.

The HDAC inhibitor nanatinostat switched on the virus's early and late genes in two representative cancer cell lines and raised overall histone acetylation across the genome. It also suppressed the growth drivers c-MYC and BCL2, halting the cell cycle and killing tumor cells. Combined with ganciclovir, the pairing showed strong antitumor effect and acceptable safety in cell and animal models. The authors note the same pairing already looked promising in EBV-positive lymphoma trials, and argue stomach cancer of this subtype deserves the same precision approach.
pmc-13333351:
Ainhoa Andueza and colleagues describe a gene therapy pairing in a 2026 commentary on their Cancer Cell study: radiation first, then a virus that delivers immune-stimulating genes into the tumor. Radiation kills tumor cells and spills their antigens. Yet it switches on immune suppression, so immune attacks rarely follow.

The team found radiation reshapes the viral genome's packaging in tumor cells. It strips methyl marks and adds the mark H3K27ac at the switch, which boosts how much the genes are read. A protein, YY1, binds the DNA after radiation and matters for the boost, since mutating its landing site cut expression. To keep the payload time-limited, they used a switch that answers to interferon, itself raised by radiation. They injected the vector into tumors irradiated, and mouse imaging confirmed it stayed at the target. The authors frame the alliance as a way to reprogram the irradiated tumor.
pmc-13334951:
Joel Mwanga and co-authors studied exclusive breastfeeding and child malnutrition in Mwanza, Tanzania, in a 2026 field study that also studied how health workers teach feeding practices. Malnutrition in its many forms still threatens young children's survival and growth.

Five hundred mothers with children aged 6 to 24 months joined the study, plus 15 healthcare providers. Bayesian logistic regression, run with Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, weighed how exclusive breastfeeding relates to malnutrition measures such as stunting and wasting. Provider interviews and observation cross-checked how feeding education is actually delivered along the maternal care sequence. The joint design links home feeding behavior with the clinic support meant to sustain it, pointing to where teaching can be strengthened.
pmc-13336451:
Yanyu Su and co-authors mapped drug heteroresistance in the yeast Candida glabrata in a 2026 fungus study. Heteroresistance, where a stubborn subgroup survives drug levels that kill the rest, had rarely been recorded in this species.

From a many-center collection of 156 isolates, 25 percent showed heteroresistance specific to caspofungin and tied to 37-degree growth. Gene activity scans of the survivors under rising drug pressure showed an adaptive program around cell cycle and cell wall integrity, centered on the calcineurin pathway. Blocking calcineurin with drugs or deleting its genes erased the trait. Survivors also spawned descendants with a range of stable resistance, marking heteroresistance as a reservoir. Machine learning on genomes found a known mutation and a new candidate gene loss.
pmc-13336851:
Mahni Fatahi and colleagues decorate a blue light emitter to raise OLED performance in a 2026 study. Efficient, stable blue screens made by solution printing remain hard to achieve. Their strategy adds bulky carbazole donor units at two spots on a known delayed-fluorescence emitter.

The new emitter dissolved better and moved holes better while keeping its blue color. In doped films it reached a light yield of 93% with a tiny energy gap of 0.01 eV and a short delayed lifetime of 2 µs in the reported measures. Printed devices hit a top external quantum efficiency of 29.4% at blue coordinates of (0.145, 0.211) in the study runs. Wider charge spread and faster recycling curbed wasteful collisions.
pmc-13336951:
Sanbao Zhang and co-authors map the sheep rumen microbiome one cell at a time in a 2026 atlas study. Tough microbial walls had blocked fair single-cell profiling of this gut community. A tuned 25 min enzyme lysis method let them profile 60 748 cells across 21 samples, resolving 213 genera and 662 species in the dataset.

Seven cross-species functional clusters emerged, tying lifestyle to metabolic specialty. In heat-tolerant hosts, energy clusters switched on fast, and one species shifted toward sugar-burning in a way that spared nutrition for the host. The atlas gives rumen ecology a reference map and a method for probing how whole communities flex under stress like heat.
pmc-13337451:
Jiaoru Liu, Denise Manahan-Vaughan, and Josué Haubrich compare how mouse strain and age shape reward-guided learning in a 2026 study. Juvenile mice aged 2–3 months and mature mice aged 7–8 months, from CBA/CaOlaHsd and C57BL/6 lines, learned a T-maze where one arm paid rewards first reliably, then with falling odds.

CBA mice chose faster, reached high performance earlier, and held up better as rewards thinned. Aging slowed choices in both lines and bent strategies in strain-specific ways, which reinforcement learning models helped expose. The work warns that age and genetic background jointly script decision behavior, so mouse studies of memory and aging must report and plan for both factors.
pmc-13337651:
Zhiyan Zou heads a 2026 mouse study tracking gut bacteria as Alzheimer's disease develops. Three common transgenic models were followed: APP/PS1, 3xTg, and 5xFAD. The question was whether gut communities change in the same way as each model ages and worsens.

Stool samples collected at 2, 4, 6, and 8 months were read with 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Diversity and community structure shifted over time, but the pattern differed by model. Each strain showed its own set of changing bacterial groups. Those differences matter for anyone using mouse gut findings to reason about human disease, since model choice shapes the result.
pmc-13338851:
Yi-Fen Li and colleagues issued a 2026 correction to a laparoscopy study comparing endometriosis with and without painful periods. Several values in Table 1 were wrong as published. The corrected table is given in full, covering 345 patients with painful periods and 144 without.

Corrections fix the deep nodule shares in the group without painful periods to 50.7 percent without nodules and 49.3 percent with nodules as stated in the notice. The matching p-value becomes 0.047 instead of 0.04 as reported there. Age, hormone, and severity stage rows are also restated, so readers should use the corrected table for any comparison.
pmc-13341451:
How esophageal cancer patients hunt for nutrition advice at home is explored by Xinhui Song and coauthors in their 2026 qualitative study. Semi-structured interviews with 15 patients recovering after surgery at a Guangdong tertiary hospital ran from November 2025 to January 2026.

Four themes emerged: wide-ranging information needs, many different sources, barriers while searching, and patterns in applying what was found. Seeking proved symptom-driven and fragmented, with real difficulty in reaching, understanding, and using guidance. The authors recommend continuous, individualized, family-inclusive nutrition support after discharge instead of one-off advice at the hospital door.
pmc-13341651:
Difficulty naming feelings may carry early trauma into adult emotion trouble, in a 2026 study by Angel Vásquez-Romero and Carlos Miguel Pérez-Lara. The Trujillo project surveyed 108 adults aged 18 to 25 with forms on childhood adversity, alexithymia, and emotion regulation.

Medium levels led across all three measures, in 62%, 56%, and 72% of participants. Mediation analysis found alexithymia clearly linked the trauma and regulation scores, with an indirect effect whose confidence interval ran from 0.04 to 0.31. Helping young adults identify and voice emotions could thus be a practical point of help after early harm.
pmc-13341951:
Konstantinos Prokopidis and co-authors relate testosterone levels to muscle mass and grip strength in middle-aged men, using United States national survey data from 2011 to 2014. Their 2026 study examines 1,001 men aged forty to fifty-nine, split into two age bands, comparing lean soft tissue in the limbs and handgrip strength across hormone levels.

Higher total testosterone was associated with stronger grip, with the link clearest in men aged fifty to fifty-nine, who also had higher odds of being in the stronger group. Men above the deficiency threshold for testosterone had substantially higher odds of greater lean tissue than men with deficiency, and normal-range levels showed a similar but weaker pattern. Linear analyses confirmed a modest lean tissue advantage above deficiency. The authors conclude that non-deficient testosterone in midlife, especially in the fifties, tracks with better muscle mass and strength.
pmc-13342051:
A new workplace wellness questionnaire is validated by Christine E. Garver-Apgar's team in their 2026 psychometric study. The Work and Well-being Inventory separates personal wellness from employer-supported wellness across eight dimensions each, aiming for scores managers can actually read.

Staff (949 people) from four large behavioral health organizations in four states filled in the survey in 2022 or 2023. Factor analysis on split samples backed a final 106-item inventory with 16 separately usable subscales and good internal consistency. Links with established measures matched expected theory. Organizations wanting to track wellness programs get a tool built for that exact purpose.
pmc-13343851:
Jan V. Henkel and a large team study bacteria clinging to magnetic minerals deep in Baltic Sea mud in 2026. Acetate breakdown below the sulfate-methane boundary seems to run through teamwork fed by electron flow. Conductive minerals such as magnetite may host the partners, so the team pulled magnetic grains straight from the sediment.

Tracer tests confirmed acetate oxidation matched methane formation rates, a signature of syntrophic teamwork. Magnetic particles ran through every layer and hosted communities ruled by relatives of Desulfatiglans, sulfate breathers whose recovered genomes oddly lack sulfate-breathing gear. Instead they may oxidize acetate and dump electrons onto the minerals. Cytochrome-rich ANME-1 archaea shared the grains, though their exact partner role stays open.
pmc-13344251:
Mehreen Zaigham, Ines Nunes, and Bo Jacobsson frame maternal and newborn health for the era after the 2030 development goals in a 2026 commentary. A woman still dies every two minutes from pregnancy or childbirth causes, with 260,000 maternal deaths in 2023 and 2.3 million newborn deaths in 2022, most of them preventable.

Progress toward the Sustainable Development Goal targets has slowed badly, and the global average death ratio sits far above the goal line. The authors introduce the Lancet Commission on Maternal and Newborn Health, launched in 2025, which gathers researchers, clinicians, policymakers, and advocates to set post-2030 priorities. Grounding advice in frontline realities, they argue, matters as much as the evidence itself.
pmc-13345851:
Zhan Tang and co-authors build a forecasting tool for severe childhood shortsightedness from school screening histories in 2026. Single snapshots miss how a child's refraction travels, so the team used repeated Binchuan County screenings from autumn 2023 to autumn 2025 and stacked several classifiers under expert guidance.

The resulting EGS-Net pairs an ensemble of models with a clinical rule override designed to catch risky children other tools miss. Recall reached 0.9533 with precision of 0.9211 on held-out students, beating the false-alarm burden of a near-perfect but sloppier rival. Importance analysis confirmed that trajectory features drive the calls. The system suits mass school screening where missed high-risk children cost the most.
pmc-13346851:
Sunyoung Choi reviews how implant surfaces shape bacterial sticking and biofilm growth, in a short literature review from 2026. The review notes that gum disease around implants starts with film forming on the surface. That tissues around implants lack the ligament found around natural teeth, which raises the risk of colonisation.

Adhesion is traced from loose first contact to firm binding and mature film, with rough surfaces giving bacteria sheltered spots while polished neck areas stay easier to clean. Zirconia tended to draw less bacterial adhesion than titanium in lab reports, though patient factors also matter. Design that limits film is presented as key to long implant life.
pmc-13347151:
Mohammad Reza Shadmand Foumani Moghadam and a large team test links among activity, work, mood, and muscle loss in a registry feasibility study published in 2026. A total of 766 healthy adults gave activity and job histories and took mood scales, with muscle loss judged by European working group rules for sarcopenia.

Past and current activity, sports time, and being in work were each tied to lower odds of muscle loss. Swimming plus some traditional Iranian sports stood out in the reported links. Higher depression, anxiety, and stress scores went the other way, raising odds in the same models. Combined models kept activity and mood as separate signals, supporting a broad registry approach.
pmc-13349751:
Laura Menchetti and colleagues trial a quality-of-life frame for free-range chickens based on felt experience, in a methods study from 2026. Four slow-growing types were watched over five weeks outdoors, acts were sorted as good or bad feeling signs. A balance score gave the share of good acts among all acts for each type across the full watch.

Good acts outweighed bad acts in every type, with balance scores from 73.7 percent to 92.5 percent and no clear split among types in the reported values. Tricky acts such as sheltering and attacking resisted fixed labels, so the authors urge judging each act by timing, pattern, and setting rather than by name alone.
pmc-13349951:
Wenming Zhang and colleagues evaluated a gentler CT angiography method in 2026 for checking dialysis access in the arm. Patients on haemodialysis often need repeat scans of their fistula or graft, and standard scans bring heavy radiation and dye loads.

One hundred and two patients with suspected access problems were randomly assigned to routine-dose scanning or a low-dose version using less dye and an AI image rebuilding method. Image quality and readings were compared, and 44 patients also had the reference dye test through a catheter. A reliable low-dose option would ease the burden on patients who face these scans again and again.
pmc-13350351:
Han Yajuan and a large team studied abnormal cortisol levels in people living with HIV in a 2026 retrospective analysis of 117 patients seen between 2017 and 2025. Nearly half, 47.9 percent, showed unusually high morning cortisol.

Patients were grouped by low, normal, or high morning cortisol. The low group had longer-standing HIV, higher treatment use, and higher diastolic blood pressure, while the high group carried higher triglycerides. Different antiretroviral regimens were checked for links to the hormone patterns. As people with HIV live longer, hormone and metabolic side effects of lifelong therapy deserve the same attention as virus control itself.
pmc-13350451:
Siyuan Ding and colleagues reviewed surgery through the nose as the sole treatment for early cancer of the nasopharynx in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Four retrospective studies covering 164 operated patients were found.

Most patients, 58 percent, had stage I disease, and two studies reported three and five year survival of 100 percent for that group; pooling all stages gave five-year survival of 90.6 percent. Comparisons in two studies set surgery against modern radiotherapy or open surgery, and quality of life and complications were extracted. Avoiding radiation would spare patients lasting side effects, but the thin, retrospective evidence base limits certainty.
pmc-13353351:
Ronak J Mahatme leads a 2026 database study of smoking and clot risk after joint arthroscopy. Smoking drives clotting, inflammation, and heart-lung harm, yet its short-term effect after keyhole joint surgery was ill-defined. Patients having shoulder, hip, or knee arthroscopy in the TriNetX network were matched one-to-one by age, sex, health conditions, and procedure type.

Ninety-day rates of clots, lung embolism, emergency visits, readmission, infection, and wound opening were compared. Among 18,948 shoulder patients, smoking showed no clear link to clot outcomes, with a risk ratio of 1.086 for venous clots. Emergency visits, though, ran higher in smokers, with a risk ratio of 1.627. Joint-specific results guide counselling before elective keyhole surgery.
pmc-13354651:
Edward Willow and co-authors reviewed studies in 2026 on dextromethorphan, a common cough drug sold without a prescription in the United States. At high doses the drug can cause psychedelic-like effects, which has raised interest in it for hard-to-treat mental illness. The review asks what doses cause which effects, and how safe those doses are.

Only eight studies, with 104 people in total, met the review rules. Effects began near 100 mg, while nausea, slow thinking, and trouble moving grew above 200 mg, and stronger visions came at higher doses. The authors say the proof is too thin to set a safe dose range, so larger dose-finding studies are needed.
pmc-13354951: Eran Gefen and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study of sprinting and surface activity in scorpions. The note fixes how running speed was scaled: speed was split by body length, not by shell length as first stated. It also fixes a count in a figure, raising one species group from 39 to 40 animals. The authors state that the values and findings of the study do not change.
pmc-13355151:
Adnan Ur Rehman and co-authors studied 160 patients with acute pancreatitis in Pakistan in 2026 to see if diabetes made the illness worse. Pancreatitis is a sudden, painful swelling of the pancreas, and it can range from mild to deadly. Patients at a medical college hospital were tracked from April to September 2025 for severity, complications, and death.

About 42 percent of patients had diabetes, and severe illness was about twice as common in that group. Organ failure, dead pancreas tissue, intensive care stays, and death were all higher, and hospital stays were longer by about three days. The authors say spotting diabetic patients early may help improve their care.
pmc-13356551:
Menghan Zhou and co-authors built a glucose-responsive microneedle patch in 2026 to treat diabetic wounds, which often stall in a state of lasting inflammation. The patch carries a plant compound, isoliquiritigenin, tied into a framework that releases it when sugar is high. The needles push the drug deep into skin, past the surface barrier.

pmc-13358451:
Richard C. Oude Voshaar and Radboud M. Marijnissen wrote a 2026 review on death wishes in older adults. As societies age, more older people say they wish to die, even when they are not ill or depressed. The authors pull together past research to explain where such wishes come from.

They sort the causes into layers: loss of meaning and self, loneliness and feeling like a burden, and wider views on ageing and dependence. Laws on assisted dying form the last layer. The review helps doctors and families hear these wishes with care and not rush to treat them as a sign of mental illness alone.

Vladislav Muldiiarov and co-authors review a rare condition in a 2026 paper: lung hernia, where part of a lung pokes out through a gap in the chest. Once tied mostly to injury, it now shows up more often after surgery, including lung transplant, or after long spells of heavy coughing that spike chest pressure.

The authors searched the medical literature through the end of 2025 and gathered what is known on causes, signs, scans, and treatment. Most of the evidence comes from single case reports and small series. Even so, the review gives doctors a practical guide to spotting this uncommon problem and choosing between watchful care and repair.
pmc-13358851:
Tomoki Makino and co-authors wrote a 2026 reply in a debate over surgery for advanced esophageal cancer. Their earlier paper reported 90 cases where the cancer had grown into nearby organs and surgeons removed those organs along with the esophagus. Two groups of commentators questioned how far such extended surgery should go.

Makino and co-authors stress they do not propose the operation for every such patient. They argue it can be done safely in a carefully chosen few at experienced centers, where drug and radiation treatment leaves stubborn local disease. Their reply sharpens the line between bold surgery that helps and surgery that only harms.

Hanwei Zhang and co-authors survey exercise habits among adults with a migration history in Germany in a 2026 study. Staying active protects health, yet little was known about activity levels in this large group. The nationwide GEDA Fokus survey interviewed 6,038 adults holding Croatian, Italian, Polish, Syrian, or Turkish citizenship between late 2021 and mid-2022.

About 70 percent of participants met at least part of the World Health Organization activity guidance. The team also mapped which social, migration-related, and mental factors track with more or less activity. Such detail helps health promoters design programs that fit the lives of specific communities rather than guessing.
pmc-13359951:
Kun Guo and co-authors study how a farmed fish handles sudden cold in a 2026 paper. The Aral barbel is a promising aquaculture species, but cold snaps in farm water can damage health and output. The team kept fish in cold water for four days and checked several body systems at once: liver and blood chemistry, gut bacteria, and the small molecules of metabolism.

Cold-exposed fish showed weaker defenses against cell damage, higher stress signals, shifted gut microbe balance, and disturbed energy and membrane processes. The harm spread across connected systems rather than striking one organ. Knowing the pattern can help farmers plan cold-season care and cut losses.
pmc-13363551:
Salvatore Michele Carnazzo and colleagues present a 2026 review pooling trials of probiotics given to babies to prevent chest and airway infections. Parents and doctors alike hope friendly bacteria can cut the colds and lung infections of the first two years. The team kept nine randomized trials of probiotics or synbiotics started before age two, checked their quality, and graded the overall certainty of the pooled proof.

Overall, supplements did not significantly cut upper airway infections, and the trend toward fewer infections of any kind stayed short of proof. Two specific strains hinted at benefits in side analyses, but each rested on very few studies. No serious harms were tied to the products. The authors advise against routine use for this purpose until strain-level trials firm up.
pmc-13363951:
Ran Cao and colleagues present a 2026 study on how carrier recipe steers polymer nanopesticides in plants. These tiny loaded particles promise precise pest control with less spray, but polymer strength and surface charge were untested levers. Using a near-infrared dye tracer that glows through tissue, the team varied polymer levels and block types, then tracked release speed, light stability, and movement inside model plants.

More polymer slowed release and shielded the load from light, at the cost of carrying less pesticide per particle. In plants, the particles rode the stem quickly and pooled at wound sites, where they fought fungi. The authors turn the trade-offs into design rules for nanopesticides that release on schedule and survive sunshine.

Luis A Arce-Saenz and colleagues present a 2026 study on classifying road surfaces in real time from vibration sensors inside a moving car. It runs on an embedded automotive computer, and the team tuned the deployment for speed at city driving pace.

Its score dipped modestly versus the offline model but stayed fair, and mapping pinned surface faults to places regardless of light, a known weakness of camera methods. Highway speeds are the next test.

Suhel Khan and co-authors tested a sound-wave tool to measure gum tissue in a 2026 study. Dentists need to know how much tissue holds each tooth, since loss there can harm the tooth. The old way uses a hand probe, which can be off the mark.

The team used a tiny high-pitch sound probe on pig jaws, dead human jaws, and live people. Sound measures sat closer to true photo measures than hand probe reads. Zheng and colleagues test two ratios calculable from routine blood tests as warning signs that a child's sepsis is tipping into septic shock, in 2026 pediatric critical care research. The ratios combine C-reactive protein with albumin, and neutrophils with lymphocytes, both reflecting how inflammation and immune balance shift. The retrospective study covered 174 hospitalized children between June 2022 and November 2025: 123 with sepsis and 51 with septic shock under the 2024 Phoenix criteria. Blood was drawn within 24 hours of admission.

Combined, the two ratios discriminated better than either alone, reaching an accuracy score of 0.802 with sensitivity of 74.50 percent and specificity of 74.80 percent across the cohort. Mohamad Hadla and co-authors found a salt-free path for kidney water take-back in a 2026 study. The known path uses a hormone that tells the kidney to hold water. Their path turns on fruit sugar kin called urate, held in kidney duct cells.

pmc-13379151:
Ameen Suhrawardy and a large team introduce a 2026 pilot program called Six Steps to Squats, for recovery after a broken leg bone. Squatting uses the hip, knee, and ankle together, so it reveals strength and control better than single-joint checks. No standard squat-based program existed for trauma patients.

The pilot enrolled adults healing from a single leg fracture at a major trauma clinic. Patients followed a structured, step-by-step squat program whose difficulty rose over time. The article reports how workable the program was in clinic and describes the squat form of the first patients enrolled. Comparisons between groups will follow when the pilot finishes.
pmc-13381051:
Zayar Aung and colleagues present a 2026 report of two patients whose partial knee replacements were followed, years later, by fractures next to the implant. Partial replacement of one side of the knee is popular because recovery is faster and movement feels more natural. Most fractures linked to it occur within three months.

One woman, aged 79, fractured seven years after surgery; another, aged 73, fractured after four years and then fractured again after a plate repair. Both were finally treated by converting to a full knee replacement with a stem, after which the fractures healed and function improved. The authors suspect age-related bone thinning and stress shielding by the implant, and urge long-term follow-up.
pmc-13382051:
Shuiling Zhao and colleagues report a 2026 study of an enzyme that destroys certain RNA messages in cells stressed by excess fat. The enzyme, called RNASET2, sits in the cell's recycling compartments and is needed for fat-induced cell death. Which messages it destroys to drive that process was unknown.

When the enzyme was reduced in human cells, three specific messages lasted longer and produced more of their proteins. Those messages reach the recycling compartment through a transporter in its membrane. Two of the three proteins had not been linked to fat stress before. Testing their roles showed they protect cells against fat damage, so destroying their messages removes a shield.
pmc-13383051:
Kawakami and colleagues provide the first test of whether a spontaneous chemical change in a protein can trigger amyloid disease, in 2026 protein research. The protein, beta2-microglobulin, builds up in long-term dialysis patients and forms amyloid fibrils that damage joints, a condition called dialysis-related amyloidosis. An age-related change, isoaspartate formation, was suspected but untestable because chemists could not build the modified protein. The isoaspartate-17 variant formed fibrils even more readily than the known pathogenic truncated variant. Microscopy and spectroscopy confirmed amyloid fibrils. The position-42 variant did not share that potency, localizing the effect to one specific aging site on the protein. Kawakami argues it is a general driver of pathological protein aggregation, and casts the disease as one of accumulated damage that healthy kidneys would normally clear.
pmc-13386951:
Xu Wang and colleagues propose microbe-based wastewater recycling for long-term space habitats in a 2026 perspective. Closed-loop water recovery is essential off Earth, and microbe systems promise lower energy use than chemical systems. Habitat wastewater, though, brings high ammonium, a low carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and stacked stresses that break standard setups.

Their answer joins synthetic microbiology with single-cell Raman spectroscopy, a light method that fingerprints single cells. Paired with isotope tracing, it can pick out hardy working microbes without long enrichment cultures. The same tool could watch the system live, giving early warnings and smarter control for resilient space water loops.
pmc-13387751:
Anshuman Panda and colleagues report urine leaking into the chest in a man with blocked kidney drainage in a 2026 case report. A 30-year-old man arrived breathless and needed intensive care for the fluid around his right lung. Scans showed ureter stones with kidney swelling and fluid tracks running from the kidney area up to the chest space.

Chest fluid carried very high urea and creatinine, confirming urine as its source, a condition called urinothorax. Both urine and chest fluid grew the same drug-resistant E. coli, treated with meropenem. Stents placed in both ureters addressed the blockage at the root of the problem.
pmc-13390551:
Mahmoud Issam Salameh, Amani Anwar Khalil, and Majed Alamri assess, in 2026, genomic skills among nurses through a genetics and genomics nursing practice survey. In intensive care, genetic information can clarify diagnoses, tailor drug choices, and trigger referral to specialist genetics services.

The authors argue that nurses need not only basic genomic knowledge but also positive attitudes, confidence, and sound judgement to take family histories, spot genetic risk, and teach patients. Nursing educators gain a competency snapshot that shows where intensive care nurses feel equipped and where training should focus.
pmc-13390851:
Rui Wang leads a 2026 analysis sorting younger Chinese patients with high blood pressure into distinct medication literacy profiles. Knowing how to use medicines safely varies widely among patients, and averages hide the groups most at risk of misuse.

They also examined which personal and clinical factors predict profile membership. Hypertension clinicians gain a segmentation they can act on: education efforts can target the profile that struggles most. That may mean help with dosing schedules or side-effect judgement. It beats giving every patient the same leaflet.
pmc-13391051:
Hiroshi Shimizu reports, in 2026, a stitch-free method for re-fixing a dislocated man-made lens together with its capsular bag, years after cataract surgery. Late dislocation of this lens-bag complex is a key delayed problem that leaves patients with blurred, decentered vision.

A 75-year-old man developed a shifted lens with symptoms about two years after cataract surgery. He had also had a laser cut to the lens bag since then. Through small corneal openings, and after limited removal of vitreous gel, the surgeon anchored the complex using a standard shop-bought iris hook with a flanged end, avoiding stitches. Eye surgeons gain a single-case method note with shop gear. It may help where special fixation tools are not at hand. One case shows the move can be done, though more cases must show it lasts.
pmc-13392151:
Sevil Yasar leads a fifteen-year look, in 2026, at whether blood markers of the renin-angiotensin system predict later cognitive decline. This hormone system, best known for blood pressure control, is implicated in Alzheimer's disease processes, but long-term human evidence has been thin.

In a secondary analysis of 310 community-dwelling adults who began cognitively healthy in a randomised trial cohort, the team measured angiotensin compounds and converting enzymes. They then followed new decline and impairment over time. Geriatric and dementia researchers gain long-horizon evidence on whether a blood pressure pathway doubles as an early dementia risk signal, which could connect two common prevention agendas.
pmc-13393151:
Charbel Saad, Thadeu Rangel, Juan Pablo Menendez, and Gregory Nicolas reviewed how surgeons rebuild the face in the same operation that removes the parotid gland and sacrifices the facial nerve to cancer. pmc-13394651:
Srikrishna Sulgodu Ramachandra leads a 2026 study of skin illness among metal casting workers in Goa, India. Casting exposes staff to heat, fumes, dust, and harsh chemicals. About one third of workers had a job-linked skin problem. Contact rash and prickly heat led the list, ahead of ringworm and burn scars. pmc-13394851:

The team sorts who got these tools by age, sex, illness load, town or country home, and plan type. Gaps in use raise fair-access worries, they argue. Rules and payment choices shape which tools reach which patients. The authors call for study and policy that spread gains more evenly.
pmc-13395251:

pmc-13395351:
Winifred Maduko and colleagues listen, in 2026, to communities in Enugu, Nigeria, about antibiotic use and drug resistance. Many people buy antibiotics without prescriptions from chemist shops. The team surveyed 1,281 people and added interviews and group talks. Well over half had used antibiotics in six months, often for malaria, cough, or fever.

Nearly half of users dosed themselves, and few had heard of resistance. Many mistook it for fake drugs or allergy. New habits surfaced, such as use to end pregnancy or as a cleanse. Poverty, poor access, and loose rules drove the pattern. Locals suggested radio jingles, faith leader teaching, and tighter shop rules.
pmc-13395451:

Top speed, sprint, and easy running rose everywhere over the span. Total distance rose in some regions but not in South America. Hard running fell in Asia, South America, and Europe, with little change in Africa. The authors read a global shift toward speed over sheer volume. Training plans may need region-wise tuning.
pmc-13395551:

Surveys before and after scored confidence in each skill.

Confidence rose sharply for nearly every skill. The biggest jumps came in tasks new to classroom students, such as sterile gowning and tube work. pmc-13396451:

pmc-13396551:

The publisher obtained the raw, uncropped images and the authors' explanation, which the editor found plausible but not enough to uphold the claims. pmc-13396851:

His point is a distinction he calls necessary: physical capacity and physical function are not the same thing, though clinics often swap the words.

A cardiopulmonary exercise test, he notes, measures capacity, the body's ceiling under full effort, and its target value is that peak. Most bedside tests measure function instead: the sit-to-stand test chiefly reads leg strength and power, and even the six-minute walk stays below maximum for most patients. Mixing the two, he argues, can mislabel what a test result means.
pmc-13397451:

The bright state that normally absorbs ultraviolet light sits very close in energy to gold's own excitations. The two mix, splitting the state, shifting its color toward the red, and boosting absorption around it, a coupling designers of light-driven surface chemistry must reckon with.

pmc-13400751:
Xuming Zeng, Mengdong Zhang, Xuanxuan Liu, Xionglei He and Li Liu show, in 2026, that selection acting during meiosis itself can swiftly reshape the gene pool of a yeast population. Evolution is usually credited to differences in survival and reproduction. But biased inheritance during spore formation can skew gene frequencies directly.

Tracking a hybrid yeast group over six meiotic generations, and checking single gametes, the team saw fast shifts at many DNA sites. A chromosome swap from one parent formed four-way structures that favored one sorting pattern. That made more unbalanced gametes and shifted nearby gene frequencies. Because such swaps are common, the authors argue this meiotic selection is a broader force than appreciated.
pmc-13401651:

The cohort split by calendar time at the patient level: a development set from 2019 to 2023 and a later prospective validation set from 2024 to 2025. pmc-13402251:
Isabella Pereira Pesenato and a large team report frogs in Bahia, Brazil, carrying two kinds of parasites at once: soft ticks and chigger mites.
