The mites proved new to science and are described as Hannemania diamantinensis, raising the known Brazilian Hannemania count to eight. pmc-13402651:

Heavy bleeding of 200 milliliters or more struck 2.5 percent of the inside-join group against 4.9 percent of the outside-join group, a gap the authors call significant. Total blood loss, lymph node harvest, and complication rates otherwise ran close, and inside joins tended to take longer, though the time gap flipped by surgical approach in subgroup checks. pmc-13402951:

Released sharks swam hard for a while, then settled back to normal behavior within about 10 hours, and at least 90 percent survived the 30 days when capture deaths usually strike. pmc-13403051:
Md Mohiuddin and Md Al Mamun Ahsan write a perspective on autophagy, the cell recycling system, as a double-edged target in cancer therapy. Early in cancer, recycling suppresses tumors. The balance shifts with tumor stage, which cell groups are present, and the surroundings, which is why simple on-off strategies disappoint.

First-generation blockers such as hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine sensitize some tumors in the lab and have reached trials, but they lack specificity and bring off-target toxicity. The authors spotlight narrower pathways, mitophagy and ER-phagy among them. They argue for precision approaches: selective blockers, markers that warn ahead, and nanoparticle delivery that controls where and when autophagy is touched. Their verdict is promise with discipline.
pmc-13403151:

pmc-13404251:

pmc-13404851:

pmc-13405451:

Centres in Singapore, Japan, South Korea and other wealthy settings offer advanced imaging, awake surgery and combined drug-radiation treatment. Many lower-income countries lack enough trained specialists to match that standard. The review sets out current obstacles and research horizons, framed around closing that regional gap.
pmc-13406951:
Meiqing Yang and co-authors review, in 2026, electrochemical sensors built to find antibiotic leftovers in fish and other aquatic animal foods. Leftover drug traces threaten food safety, so quick, cheap, small-scale tests carry real value for producers and inspectors.

The review covers eight antibiotic families, from fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines to beta-lactams, and sorts sensors into four kinds: direct devices, antibody-based sensors, aptamer-based sensors, and molecularly imprinted versions. Attention goes to how each target behaves electrically, how sensing surfaces are built, how signals get amplified, and how samples are prepared before testing. Stubborn problems remain, notably messy real-world samples and uneven preparation methods, and the authors sketch where development should head next.
pmc-13407951:
Chady Ghnatios and Kazem Fayazbakhsh model, in 2026, why composite tape warps while a robot prints it. Continuous-fibre thermoplastic printing promises strong light parts, yet feedstock deformation during deposition seeds defects and defeats path planning. The team therefore combined experiments with physics-based and learning-based modelling to pin down the drivers.

Residual stress relief, drying, crystallisation, and thermal stress were separated using thermal and mechanical test data. A viscoelastic physics model handled the prepreg mechanics while a stabilised neural differential-equation model captured drying and ordering behaviour. Fitted together, the hybrid reproduced tape conduct well beyond the temperatures it was trained on, a strong sign of validity. Robotic printing trials then validated the model in real printing settings.
pmc-13408051:
Cahit Ucar and co-authors probe, in 2026, a stress-defence protein as an early warning of heart trouble in lupus. It was read alongside heart tracings, heart ultrasound, and neck-artery thickness scans.

In adjusted modelling, lower Sestrin-1, a wider left atrium, and longer QT each independently accompanied lupus status, with every unit of Sestrin-1 lowering the odds substantially. The authors propose the protein as a marker of the subclinical cardiovascular alterations accumulating silently in lupus.
pmc-13408151:
Li Wang and co-authors report, in 2026, a phase II trial of a two-in-one immune antibody plus chemotherapy. pmc-13408351:

Responding tumours were rich in resident CD8 and CD4 T cells that had multiplied and switched on killing programmes, while resistant tumours showed exhausted cells stuck in chronic interferon signalling. pmc-13409551:

Brushing, interdental cleaning, diet, and follow-up attendance were each recorded for the period before and after treatment, and statistical models hunted for what predicts actually adopting prevention.

Daily interdental cleaning stayed low at under a quarter of patients, while about three fifths reported changing their diet and just over half kept follow-up appointments. Most demographic traits predicted nothing. pmc-13410551:
Sarah Jasat and co-authors update in 2026 a review of what helps or blocks physical activity for people on dialysis. Exercise improves health for these patients, yet few stay active and clinics offer it unevenly. The review uses behavior theory to turn scattered views into a plan for lasting change.

Five databases yielded 17 papers with views from patients and staff. Barriers and supports were mapped onto a standard framework of behavior domains. Patient and staff views lined up closely, and every broad driver of behavior played a part. Training, reshaping clinic settings, teaching, showing examples, and practical support came out as the most workable levers for routine care.
pmc-13410851:
Stephen Olaide Aremu and colleagues survey in 2026 hepatitis B vaccination among adults at a hospital in Nasarawa State, Nigeria. The virus remains a major health threat in sub-Saharan Africa despite a safe vaccine. Awareness ran high, and about 94 percent reported at least one vaccine dose. Finishing the full three-dose course was another story: only about 22 percent had done so. Most people said they were willing to complete the course. Cost, poor access to facilities, and fear of side effects topped the barriers named. Knowledge and attitudes scored well overall, which suggests access, not awareness, is the binding problem.
pmc-13410951:
Verena Petzer and co-workers search in 2026 for a simple clue that flags men carrying mutations behind VEXAS, an inflammatory illness described only in 2020. The mutation hides in blood-forming cells and can mimic many diseases, so picking who to test is hard. Oversized red blood cells are a near-constant sign of the syndrome.

The team traced men who had both a blood protein disorder and available marrow samples, narrowing over a thousand cases to 160 for gene testing. They compared mutation rates in men with and without those enlarged red cells. Pairing the size clue with the protein disorder may preselect patients far better than either sign alone, sparing many men an unneeded gene hunt.
pmc-13411151:
Di Zhang and Jing Zhou mine in 2026 a United States side-effect database for safety signals of three drugs used to trigger ovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome. The condition is common, and each drug carries its own risk profile. Knowing those profiles apart can guide personal prescribing.

Of 21,730 reports tied to the condition, letrozole accounted for the vast majority, then tamoxifen, with clomiphene rarely reported. Fatigue surfaced as a shared signal, and tumor progression plus joint pain appeared across all three drugs. Tamoxifen and letrozole reports clustered around tumor-related terms, while clomiphene leaned toward psychiatric and gut events. The authors stress matching drug choice to each patient's risk profile.
pmc-13413451:
Zlatko Kirovakov, Angel Yordanov, and Vasilena Dimitrova gather in 2026 what is known about pregnancy in women with myasthenia gravis. The disease weakens muscles when nerve signals fail at the muscle door. Pregnancy can stir it up or calm it down, with little warning. Their review searched four large databases for group studies, case sets, and strong case reports. The mixed designs ruled out pooled sums, so the team wove the finds into a story form.

Birth results were most often good when care teams watched closely and tuned treatment to each woman. Flares bunched in pregnancy and just after birth, most in wide-spread disease or weak breathing. Past thymus surgery may lower flare rates and brief weakness in newborns, though data stay thin. Joint care by nerve, birth, sleep-drug, and newborn staff is the core advice.
pmc-13415151:
Irene Zapata-Martínez leads a 2026 systematic review of physical activity in people with celiac disease. Gluten triggers immune damage in this condition, and a gluten free diet is the only proven treatment. The reviewers searched five databases for studies linking activity levels or exercise programs to health outcomes.

Fourteen studies qualified, most of them one-time surveys rather than trials. Higher activity sometimes matched better body composition, calmer inflammation, and stronger quality of life. Findings for metabolism and bone density conflicted across studies, often tied to diet differences. The authors call those findings preliminary and ask for long term trials, especially in children.
pmc-13415551:
Abdulhusein and co-authors test, in 2026, whether curcumin, the compound in turmeric, helps broiler chickens withstand coccidiosis, a gut parasite disease, and whether the oil source matters. Their 42-day trial placed 660 one-day-old male Ross 308 chicks into five treatments with six replicates of 22 birds each, crossing soybean or canola oil diets with curcumin at 0.02 percent, and challenged the birds with mixed Eimeria parasites on day 14.

Among challenged birds, curcumin improved weight gain and feed efficiency, trimmed abdominal fat and relative liver and spleen weights, and raised post-challenge antibody levels. It shifted gene expression protectively, suppressing the inflammatory switch NF-kappaB and interleukin-6 while boosting interleukin-10 and the antioxidant master gene NRF2 in the factorial analysis. Gut counts moved the right way too, with more Lactobacillus and less ileal E. coli. The canola oil plus curcumin group showed the clearest recovery, while canola oil alone gave endpoint-specific effects.
pmc-13415751:
Laure Inçaby and co-authors publish the first complete mitochondrial genome of the Pacific spiny dogfish, in 2026. This small North Pacific shark is taken in commercial and bycatch fisheries. pmc-13415851:
Roman Jerala and Duško Lainšček comment in 2026 on a molecular velcro trick for precise genome repair, discussing work by Mu and colleagues. Base editors rewrite single DNA letters without cutting both strands, yet the editors are too large for the adeno-associated virus carriers used in gene therapy. Split editors solve size, provided the halves find each other inside cells.

Delivery limits have stalled base editing's clinical path, so a modular self assembling design could widen treatable diseases.
pmc-13416751:
Eisendrath and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare heart event during a hip replacement operation. A 63-year-old man had an elective right total hip replacement, and monitoring later showed his ventricles had stopped contracting for twenty seconds during surgery. This event, called ventricular standstill, means the heart's main pumping chambers pause completely.

This patient stayed asymptomatic, with steady blood pressure before, during, and after the pause. No treatment emergency followed, and the event was found only on the heart monitor record. The authors discuss possible triggers, including a vasovagal response, where a nerve reflex slows the heart, and inflammation linked to surgery and anaesthesia. They note that no earlier case in their search described standstill during an operation. The report adds a data point on how long a pause a stable patient can tolerate.
pmc-13418051:
Ma and colleagues report a 2026 study of a chemical tagging system that restrains sugar burning and bowel cancer growth. Many tumors run aerobic glycolysis, a fast but wasteful way to burn sugar. The work names a new control point in cancer metabolism and a drug pairing ready for further testing.
pmc-13418251:
Yanli Lin, Marne L White, Jihong Zhang, and Todd S Braver track brain networks during mindfulness training, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Sixteen beginners completed up to 24 lab sessions of two meditation styles: focused attention on one object, and open monitoring of whatever arises. Brain waves and self rated mindfulness quality were collected each session, then modelled as networks over time.

The two styles produced distinct brain and experience networks, supporting their theoretical split. Both shared strong carry over of mindfulness skill between sessions, plus opposing effects of front versus back brain alpha rhythms. One size EEG markers mislead, the authors argue; meaning depends on practice type and stage.
pmc-13420651:
Yasunaga and co-authors describe a surgical technique for controlling blood flow during open repair of a chest-and-abdomen aortic aneurysm. Their patient was a man whose aorta had earlier been treated from inside with a stent graft. Clamping the old graft directly looked difficult. So they used inflatable occlusion balloons to seal the aorta from within.

The patient was a 76-year-old man whose earlier repair had developed a pseudoaneurysm, a contained leak beside the original stent. Guided by X-ray imaging, the team placed balloons into each graft limb through leg artery sheaths. Blood kept flowing to the legs through side branches during the operation. A composite graft bridged the size mismatch, and an inner cuff stopped bleeding at the lower join. He survived without major complications. Scans at 12 months showed no recurrence.
pmc-13421151:

pmc-13421251:

pmc-13421451:

pmc-13422351:

The strain proved far milder in mice and protected most animals against three different serovars. pmc-13422751:

Its growth marker stayed near two percent of cells in samples taken both before and after treatment began. pmc-13423151:

Mismatches led to small wording and cultural adjustments, including debate over the answer scale and items reflecting United States health care. pmc-13425851:

A speaking valve redirects air through the upper airway, supporting speech and breathing mechanics, and the team tested whether valve use speeds early mobilization. Reports from the trial link valve use with improved respiratory measures during recovery.

Care teams can fit the valve check in with the daily round, since the gear is small and the steps are few once staff learn the way.
pmc-13425951:

pmc-13426351:
Mohammed Ali Qasem Al-Soufi and coauthors surveyed complementary medicine knowledge among health students in Sana'a, Yemen, in a 2026 single-centre cross-sectional study. Their questionnaire reached 318 final and pre-final year medical and pharmacy students at the University of Science and Technology, a 53 percent response.

Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores were split at sixty percent of the maximum to define good knowledge and positive attitude. Results show how prepared Yemeni graduates feel to counsel patients who already use traditional and alternative remedies.
pmc-13427751:

pmc-13428151:

Only half felt happy with the training they now get, though most felt at ease managing symptoms and talking with patients. Residents felt unsure about local resources and about discussing feeding tubes with patients and families. Senior residents praised hands-on learning but cited weak role models and timetable clashes, and backed required rotations and case-based teaching.
pmc-13428251:

pmc-13428351:

In epilepsy those identities survived, but three of the four proteins shifted in amount and place, pointing to faulty glutamate clearance and water control. pmc-13428451:

Two indices stood out consistently: the visceral adiposity version and the body roundness version of the combined score. Each standard deviation rise in the visceral version carried a hazard ratio of 1.36, and the roundness version a hazard ratio of 1.32 at baseline. pmc-13428551:

The highest urgency level covered about one in ten patients yet accounted for about four fifths of emergency deaths. pmc-13433951:
Amin Sharifi and co-authors brewed a soap-like flood mix in 2026 to squeeze more oil from tight chalk rock under hot, salty strain. Such rock holds vast oil yet yields poorly to plain water floods. A screen chain ran from shelf life through mix acts, touch angles, phase play, rock soak, and core floods. The best mix cut oil-water skin pull to a whisper and halved the wet angle, while holding firm at fierce salt and hardness loads. Core floods won near a fifth more oil past sea water. A cheap plastic cut the hero part's rock loss to a low mark. Full checks backed the wet shift and its gears.
pmc-13434151:

The study covers 1,276 old shophouses in Chinatown. Its groups differ from the time order set by city planners in the 1990s. The new order gives more weight to the mixed roots of the buildings across ethnic groups. Urban historians get a model for joining field study with computing.
pmc-13434451:
Leoš Shivaya Valášek and coauthors review a surprise in cell biology in 2026: RNAs long classed as non coding can in fact make small proteins. These long RNAs were once seen as mere regulators that never build anything. New tools now catch tiny products that old screens missed.

The review asks which products are real, how cells choose to build them, and what jobs they do in growth and disease. Some tiny proteins may add a second role to RNAs already known for control work. The authors suggest a fresh name for the coding subset. Field leaders get a map of open tests to run.
pmc-13434651:

The piled up carrier harms the cell power units and sparks a rust like cell death. Tumors shrank in mice, immune attack rose, and a common immune drug worked better. Blood levels of the carrier track better outcomes in lung cancer patients. A heart drug that hits the same enzyme mimics the benefit.
pmc-13436451:
János B Biró and coauthors show that an mRNA cleanup system is vital for legume roots and their bacterial partners in 2026. The system, nonsense mediated decay, destroys faulty messages before they do harm. Roots of a model clover lacking the system were tested under low nitrogen.

Crippled roots grew poorly and formed far fewer working nodules. Partner bacteria normally move into root lumps and fix nitrogen for the plant. pmc-13436551:
Loizou, Aharonson, and Hajigeorgiou published a 2026 survey on AI tools in medical school. First-year students now meet chatbots and study apps from day one. Nearly all students knew the tools, and most used ChatGPT on a regular basis. Students rated the tools high for grasping hard topics and saving study time. Trust in medical facts from AI stayed middling, well below the usefulness scores. Wrong answers from chatbots were a common complaint in open comments. pmc-13437751:

Good responders carried far more of the receptor on these cells than poor responders or patients who could not tolerate the drug. Adding tocilizumab tended to trim receptor-positive monocytes, while pairing it with methotrexate nudged the pattern back toward the good-responder look. The authors float the receptor as a possible blood marker for likely response. They stress the work is exploratory, built on layered lab models rather than a patient trial.
pmc-13437851:

Electrical jitter testing of an eye muscle proved the transmission defect at the neuromuscular junction, while his muscle biopsy notably lacked the tubular aggregates typical of GFPT1 disease. pmc-13439351:
Shah and colleagues ask which early warning scores still work for liver transplants kept on a warm perfusion machine. Those livers had lower six month survival than the rest, 89 percent against 100 percent. Donor body weight, longer dying and sewing times, and weak pump readings, such as slow lactate clearing, tracked with dysfunction. Some livers past pump cutoffs still did well, so scores should guide, not dictate, organ use.
pmc-13439951:
Fu, in a solo 2026 study, measures whether stored barley seed quietly accumulates harmful mutations. Two variant-calling methods together identified 1,642 harmful variants spread across all seven chromosomes, mostly rare and carried in single-copy form. More variants appeared after regeneration than before. The estimates suggest each accession gained roughly 28 to 37 harmful variants over the period, showing such accumulation can be measured in practice.
pmc-13440051:

It also has a direct band gap, the energy needed to free electrons for current, smaller than in the cubic version. The authors trace the distortion to strong magnetic exchange interactions running along the stretched axis and to iron-oxygen-iron coupling between neighboring atoms. Strong mixing of iron and oxygen electronic states supports that picture. The result could change how the material's light response is modeled.
pmc-13440451:
Carlos Alberto Conceição Santana and colleagues review what happens when faulty cochlear implant electrodes are switched off, reporting a 2026 records study. pmc-13441851:

pmc-13442851:
Justine Gantzer and colleagues sort an ultra-rare tumor, PEComa, by its gene marks in a 2026 study. No gene-based class system guides care for these growths, which spring from vessel-wall cells. Full multi-layer profiling covered an unselected set of tumors from varied body sites.

pmc-13443851:

pmc-13444251:
Chuan Zhang and colleagues profile blood fatty acids in very preterm infants in the first day of life in a 2026 study. pmc-13446351:
Lizzy Olsen and colleagues watch what a lone fruit fly motor neuron does when every input to a patch of larval muscle is wiped out, in a 2026 study. The surviving tonic neuron sprouted fresh branches and built working junctions on the bare muscles, a reach across its own turf. Mere silencing of neighbors, without their loss, sparked no such growth, so physical loss is the trigger. The tonic cell grew its total contact patch only a bit, spreading it thin over home and foreign ground. The phasic kind barely remodeled, a split in talent by cell type.
pmc-13447351:
Aoyi Li and colleagues pool trials of music for people with disorders of consciousness in a 2026 meta-analysis. After severe brain injury, some patients remain in coma or minimally aware states for long periods. Music is safe, cheap and easy to deliver at the bedside, yet its effect on awakening needed a combined verdict.

Music groups scored higher on a standard coma scale than control groups and awakened at higher rates. pmc-13447451:
Bryan Ford leads a team expanding a web tool that links implementation science frameworks to measurement instruments in 2026 work. Researchers who study how proven practices reach real settings often struggle to find a fitting questionnaire or interview guide for each framework concept. Older repositories were scattered, narrow and uneven in access, prompting a rebuild of an existing models webtool.

The first phase holds fifty-one instruments spanning surveys, interviews and worksheets across quantitative, qualitative and mixed formats. pmc-13448051:
Lu Sun and co-authors review DNA methylation in bipolar disorder in a 2026 synthesis of mechanism and translation. The disorder cycles between mania and depression, with high relapse and suicide risk, yet its biology stays partly obscure. Methylation, a chemical tag that tunes gene activity without changing DNA code, may form a regulatory layer behind that variety.

Altered tags appear in genes for dopamine, serotonin and other messenger systems, plus growth and ion channel genes tied to brain plasticity and excitability. Candidate signatures include a growth factor pattern, specific sites in a receptor gene and faster epigenetic ageing. Mood stabilising drugs may partly act through such pathways, though evidence stays tentative. Most findings are associations, not causes, and blood tags may not mirror brain, the authors stress.
pmc-13448551:
Dandan Li and colleagues evaluate a one-week mindfulness plus ear acupressure programme before surgery for spinal metastases in a 2026 before-and-after study. Cancer spread to the spine fragments sleep and heightens anxiety and pain before an already major operation. A short, home-practised programme guided by phone audio offered a low-drug option worth testing against standard care alone.

Ninety-two patients treated at one hospital across two years split evenly between the programme era and the earlier standard era. Programme patients reached surgery with lower anxiety and pain scores and lower saliva cortisol, a stress hormone, than controls. Wearable sleep measures also favoured the programme on waking time and night awakenings in the reported results. Since groups came from different time periods rather than random assignment, the authors frame gains as associations needing prospective confirmation.
pmc-13448951:
Changyi Zhou and a large team trace in 2026 how dissolving artery scaffolds provoke the late inflammation that can re-narrow the vessel they were meant to open. These scaffolds, made of poly-lactic acid, support the artery briefly and then break down. Using gene profiling of stented pig arteries and tissue sections over time, the team found the late response dominated by neutrophil extracellular traps, webs of DNA that neutrophils cast out.

Breakdown products overload a calcium channel in neutrophils, triggering those traps, which then push vessel wall muscle cells into a growth state through the TLR2 receptor. To break the loop, the team coated a scaffold with C29, a selective TLR2 blocker. In rabbit arteries the coated device cut neutrophil buildup and reduced the thickened inner layer that causes restenosis. The authors offer the coated scaffold as a precise way to keep lumens open longer.
pmc-13449251:
S Lorena Ament-Velásquez and colleagues trace the evolution of NOD-like receptor genes, intracellular immune sensors, in the Podospora anserina fungus species complex. Some fungal versions of these receptors trigger regulated cell death when the fungus meets a non-self strain, but most remain uncharacterised. Their 2026 study asks how the repertoire changes over evolutionary time.

Most of the receptors carried domains known to execute cell death. Compared with random genes, they turned over faster, carried more protein-changing variation, and evolved more quickly overall. One subgroup, marked by repeat segments with very high internal similarity, arose independently several times. These genes sat near transposable elements, showed high diversity partly driven by a fungal mutation process, and carried signs of balancing selection, with repeat swapping between genes creating new variants. The authors argue fungal immune receptors evolve under diversity-enhancing pressure, consistent with a general immune role.
pmc-13449351:
Vincent Dutreuil and José Paulo Pinheiro present in 2026 full build plans for a laboratory device that stirs liquid samples while holding their temperature steady, printed largely on a 3D printer. Commercial circulation thermostats do this job but are bulky, slow to settle, and costly. Their open-source unit combines a magnetic stirrer with thermoelectric temperature control aimed at electroanalytical and spectroscopic measurements, where samples typically need holding anywhere between minus ten and eighty degrees Celsius.

One unit costs roughly 350 euros to build without chemical probes, controlled by Arduino electronics. The design files sit in a public repository under a Creative Commons license that allows reuse with attribution for noncommercial purposes. The authors frame the device as teaching and research infrastructure: a cheaper, faster-responding alternative that small laboratories can fabricate themselves, adapt to macroscopic or microfluidic cells, and repair without vendor support.
pmc-13449451:
Samuel Lam and a multispecialty panel publish in 2026 a systematic review and practice guideline on imaging children who arrive at emergency departments after blunt chest trauma. Computed tomography finds chest injuries superbly, yet injuries needing intervention are rarer in children than adults, and radiation carries extra lifetime risk for the young. The panel framed four structured questions about when screening chest X-ray or bedside ultrasound can stand in for the scanner.

Screening 10,447 articles left only three retrospective studies fit for pooling, and the quality of proof graded very low. On that thin base the group could answer just one question. For children under eighteen whose first screening chest imaging shows nothing or only minor findings, they conditionally recommend against routine chest CT to hunt injuries needing procedures or surgery. The guideline's honesty about its own limits is part of its message.
pmc-13449651:
Ramon Joel Seastres and colleagues pool in 2026 fifteen studies of 4,948 adults to find what predicts a good neurological outcome for people who survive a cardiac arrest inside a hospital. Predicting recovery in this group is notoriously hard, and the survivors are a selected slice of all arrests. Quality and certainty were graded formally, and most evidence landed at low certainty.

A first shockable heart rhythm tripled the odds of favorable recovery, the single strongest rhythm signal. Cardiac causes, an admission diagnosis of heart attack or heart failure, male sex, and shorter resuscitation all helped. After circulation returned, emergency heart catheterization carried the largest association, an odds ratio of 4.55, with intensive monitoring and membrane oxygenation also favorable. The authors stress that findings apply only to patients discharged alive, and that better prospective studies are needed before these factors guide family conversations.
pmc-13452151:
Pandey and colleagues reviewed in 2026 why HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria medicines run out in low- and middle-income countries, and what those stock-outs cause. Their systematic review screened over ten thousand records and included 56 studies on antiretroviral, anti-tuberculosis, and antimalarial drug shortages.

Causes clustered around inefficient supply chains, slow procurement, weak funding, poor governance, and bad demand forecasts. The harm was direct: patients missed doses, drug resistance grew, and illness and deaths rose, while families paid more out of pocket and programs paid emergency prices. Fixes ranged from emergency buying and redistribution in the short term to buffer stocks, more suppliers, and digital inventory systems for the long term. The authors stress that most causes are preventable with stronger, better financed supply systems.
pmc-13453951:
Alicja Braczko and nine co-authors show a way to watch mitochondria breathe in a piece of living human artery, in real time. The tissue is the left internal mammary artery, a vessel often borrowed for heart bypass grafts. Their 2026 study takes segments during bypass surgery and tests them on a Seahorse analyzer, a bench tool that tracks oxygen use.

A standard stress test read out the artery's base and peak breathing rates while the tissue stayed intact. In parallel, a liquid separation method measured the tissue's energy carrying nucleotides, which report on energy status and redox balance. Pairing the two reads gave a fuller picture of the graft's energy health than either alone. The authors present the workflow as a first for intact human vessel tissue and a base for vessel metabolism studies.
pmc-13454051:
Richard Chilipa and Clement Nyirenda review neuro fuzzy systems, which marry neural learning with fuzzy rule based reasoning, for the Internet of Medical Things. Half the papers used neural tuned designs, while hybrid and deep variants split most of the rest, and only seven used evolving systems that learn on the fly. Prediction tasks led the uses, ahead of detection tasks. Reporting was thin: 61.8 percent of papers never said where the system runs, and only 10.9 percent timed its speed. Nearly all proof was retrospective or simulated. The authors list open gaps in live adaptation, device fit, and bedside clarity.
pmc-13454651:
Hiroki Sato and colleagues, writing for a Japanese resuscitation study group in 2026, ask whether regions that test hearts more often suffer fewer cardiac arrests outside hospitals. Cardiac arrest away from care remains a major public danger, and rates vary by place. The team ran a prefecture-level ecological study covering 2014 to 2023.

Cases came from the national Utstein registry, which logs nearly every ambulance-treated arrest in Japan. The analysis kept arrests of presumed cardiac origin in adults aged 40 to 74. Testing intensity came from national insurance claims data, which record outpatient heart tests per prefecture. Risk profiles for each prefecture, such as metabolic health, came from the same source. By joining the two datasets, the authors test whether heavier local testing aligns with lower arrest rates after accounting for those risk profiles.
pmc-13454751:
Sofija Ivanova and six colleagues explore, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how diet relates to gut leakiness and inflammation in people with type 1 diabetes. Higher intake of hot drinks and legumes paired with higher levels of a key inflammation marker. Lower intake of protein, fat, energy, and fiber paired the same way. Red meat intake tracked with higher levels of a bacterial toxin marker in blood. Stool inflammation readings rose with protein intake. The authors call the study exploratory and ask for feeding trials that test whether changing diet can tighten the gut barrier in type 1 diabetes.
pmc-13454951:

pmc-13456651:

Eating less, the most reliable life-extending trick known, rewrites these RNA programs toward stress resistance and metabolic thrift. The review weighs that evidence species by species. It also tours the diagnostic promise of microRNAs floating in blood and urine, which could betray biological age without a biopsy. The authors close by imagining combined RNA networks and aging clocks as the next tools for measuring, and perhaps slowing, the aging process.
pmc-13457351:

Brains were classed by post death reads: one ill, the twin, both, or none.

Each ill alone left the mid time zone thin against clean brains. Both ills at once spread the loss to front and side zones too. The twin ill alone cut the front of the sea horse zone, the memory hub, most. Step ups in the twin ill shrank that hub more than step ups in the first ill. pmc-13457451: Heavier comorbidity burden steering initial treatment choices in older women with gynecologic cancer. Lin Tang, Yuhang Liu, and others study the retrospective cohort. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is gynecologic oncology. It links comorbidity burden to initial treatment allocation decisions in the cohort.
pmc-13458151:

pmc-13458351: The team construct a massive public database to support ending the HIV outbreak. The project provides thorough data resources for the national EHE initiative. pmc-13459251:

pmc-13459451:

pmc-13460051:

Compared with the other groups, these patients pumped far more blood per minute while their vessels offered unusually little resistance. Two patients improved despite starting with lower cardiac output.
pmc-13460951:
Shahdad Ahmadi and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a probiotic bacterium taken from camel milk can ease acute inflammatory pain in rats, benchmarking it against acetaminophen. pmc-13461351:
Federico Caporaletti and co-authors used an X-ray technique that watches molecular motion at specific length scales to settle how two kinds of movement in supercooled liquids relate. Their 2026 study examined a hydrogen bonded glass former. It found the two processes are not independent: the fast rattling is the prelude to escape.

Before diffusion begins, the mean squared displacement of molecules grows more slowly than linearly, the signature of this constrained rattling in their measurements. The team reads the secondary relaxation as molecules testing the cage walls just before breaking out, linking it directly to the onset of flow. pmc-13461851:

The authors conclude PLAU speeds the rebuilding of tissue around the tumor through that change, marking it as a target for blocking spread.
pmc-13462051:
Fukuda, Kobayashi, and Wakashima built in 2026 a scale to measure how Japanese adults explain mental disorders to themselves. pmc-13462251:
Baifeng Chen and colleagues reviewed how infected urachal cysts in babies respond to treatment without surgery. A urachal cyst is a leftover pouch near the bladder that can infect; the study covered first-time infections in infants under one year.

pmc-13462551:

pmc-13463151:

pmc-13463551:
Chi and colleagues build a star-shaped carrier that loads boron for a type of cancer care. The care, called boron neutron capture therapy, kills tumour cells with beams once boron sits inside them. It could dissolve at high strength in water too.

The carrier did not harm head and neck cancer cells in lab tests. A tagged form lit up on PET scans in healthy mice. Blood held the tag well, and the kidneys cleared it. That path sets up later tumour tests.
pmc-13464051:
Soares, Barbosa, and Stolf ask whether a host's immune response can change a parasite's strength in this 2026 study. Both mouse groups were infected for 13 weeks before parasites were collected from footpad lesions. Parasites from normal mice survived better and multiplied more once cultured. They also infected cells more aggressively, forming larger internal compartments, and caused stronger disease when placed into new hosts. The authors conclude that living under T-cell pressure had, paradoxically, produced hardier and more virulent parasites.
pmc-13464251:

pmc-13464751:
Abdilahi Abdi Ibrahim and three co-authors build a warning model for a rare flare-up after cryptococcal meningitis, a fungal brain infection. Small numbers mean the tool needs wider testing, the authors caution, before clinics can lean on it.
pmc-13466651:
Qiumei Gu and colleagues review eyes with wet macular disease that responded poorly to standard injections and were switched to double doses of the same drug, in a 2026 real-world study. The drugs block a vessel growth factor that drives leaking in the back of the eye. Eyes qualified only after at least three standard injections left active leaking or swelling.

Vision change and retinal anatomy after the switch form the main outcomes, with injection spacing as a secondary measure. Records captured the full treatment history, so the escalation decision reflects real clinic judgment rather than trial rules. Evidence for this doubling strategy has been thin, which is the gap the authors set out to fill.
pmc-13466751:
Linda Ficociello and colleagues compare hospital use between dialysis clinics that monitor blood volume during treatment and matched clinics that do not, in a 2026 study. The monitoring guides how fast fluid is pulled off during hemodialysis, a balancing act central to kidney failure care. Each of 165 high-use clinics was matched with a non-using clinic over the second half of 2022.

Nearly twenty-five thousand patients entered the analysis. Adjusted rates of hospital visits overall and of fluid-related visits ran lower where monitoring was routine, as did days spent in hospital. Monthly clinical measures were tracked as secondary outcomes. Real-world proof for this monitoring has been limited, which the authors aim to supply.
pmc-13466951:
Seal and colleagues ran a double-blind trial in 2026 to test whether bisphenol A, a chemical in many consumer plastics, directly lowers insulin sensitivity in healthy adults. pmc-13468851:
Marco Meloni and co-authors report in 2026 long-term results for injecting a patient's own blood cells into the legs of people with ischemic diabetic foot ulcers. No-option status was defined strictly, including failed revascularization and very low oxygen pressure at the wound. pmc-13469251:

pmc-13469751:

pmc-13470151:

pmc-13471151:

pmc-13471451:

pmc-13471551:

pmc-13471651:

pmc-13472851:

pmc-13473251:

pmc-13473751:

pmc-13474651:

pmc-13474851:

pmc-13474951:

pmc-13478051:

pmc-13478251:

pmc-13479551:

pmc-13479951:

pmc-13480051:

pmc-13480251:

pmc-13481751:

pmc-13481951:

pmc-13482551:

pmc-13482851:

pmc-13483051:

pmc-13483151:

pmc-13483551:

pmc-13483951:

pmc-13485851:

pmc-13486051:

pmc-13486451:

pmc-13486651:

pmc-13486751:

pmc-13486851:

pmc-13488151:

pmc-13488251:

pmc-13490351:

pmc-13491351:

pmc-13491451:

pmc-13491851:

pmc-13492551:

pmc-13493851:

pmc-13495151:

pmc-13495251:

pmc-13499651:

pmc-13500051:

pmc-13500351:

pmc-13500551:

pmc-13500851:

pmc-13501951:

pmc-13502851:

pmc-13503751:

pmc-13504051:

pmc-13507251:

pmc-13507351:

pmc-13508451:

pmc-13508551:

pmc-13509151:

pmc-13510451:

pmc-13512351:

pmc-13513151:

pmc-13514951:

pmc-13515151:

pmc-13518851:

pmc-13522051:

pmc-13523351:

pmc-13524551:

pmc-13526051:

pmc-13529051:

pmc-13529151:

pmc-13530251:

pmc-13530651:

pmc-13531751:

pmc-13533051:

pmc-13533851:

pmc-13534151:

pmc-13534451:
Majid Naseri and colleagues study in 2026 how adding titanium changes a low-cost, cobalt-free high-entropy alloy. Such alloys mix many main elements at once and can beat classic alloys, yet phase mix and segregation can hurt corrosion resistance. Tests ran in acid solution on the base alloy and a titanium-bearing version.

Titanium shifted the crystal mix toward a stronger phase set, refined grains, and formed titanium-rich zones between dendrites. The new structure supported a thicker, steadier protective oxide film in acid. Readers see titanium addition as a practical route to better corrosion behaviour.
pmc-13536251:
Ying Geng and colleagues test in 2026 whether human hunters can replace vanishing top predators in southwest China. Camera traps gave 30,778 records from 400 sites between 2017 and 2021, matched to control for habitat differences. Sites ruled by hunters, by top predators, or by neither were compared.

Predator sites held the richest and most abundant wildlife, with far more species than hunter or empty sites. Prey avoided hunters far longer than any predator, and food webs were weakest where hunters dominated. Hunters cannot fill the predator role, so wild predator protection stays essential for stable ecosystems and for prey communities across the wider region over time.
pmc-13536651:
Shan-Ru Feng and colleagues screen in 2026 cancer drugs to find one that makes liver tumours die in a way that wakes up the immune system. Most liver cancers stay cold to immune therapy, with low response rates to standard drug pairs. Cell, tissue, and mouse tests compared several kinase-blocking drugs for immune-style death signals.

Anlotinib stood out, releasing alarm signals from dying tumour cells through cell stress and self-eating pathways. Treated tissue drew in and switched on immune defender cells, which then primed killer T cells. The work sets up a pairing strategy for immune drugs in liver cancer.
pmc-13536851:
Michael Arthur Ofori and co-authors link pregnancy care visits, wealth, and low birth weight in Ghana in a 2026 analysis of the 2022 national health survey. Low birth weight remains a major newborn risk in the region. Data held nearly seven thousand observations, with missing values filled through repeated statistical imputation. Survey-weighted models and inequality indices tested how visit counts and wealth relate to birth weight.

Richer women used pregnancy care far more than poorer women, with the steepest gap for the highest visit target. Low birth weight clustered among poorer women. Too few visits and poor household wealth each raised low birth weight odds on their own. The authors call for targeted steps that lift visit attendance and ease wealth gaps to cut low birth weight.
pmc-13538551:
Kain S Saygan and colleagues quantify how test cycle values relate to live flu virus in patient nose samples in a 2026 study. Standard molecular tests report a cycle number that hints at viral amount but not contagious virus. Samples from patients positive for flu A or flu B were cultured, counted by precise digital methods, and checked against blood antibody levels in a combined analysis.

Cycle values tracked live virus amount closely and inversely. Cultures almost always grew virus below a mid-range cycle value, with growth odds falling to about one in ten near a high cycle mark. Antibody levels against a surface protein showed no tie to either measure. The authors endorse cycle values as a rough stand-in for infectious load in diagnosis and infection control.
pmc-13540851:
Zehra Koyuncu and six colleagues explore, in a 2026 study, how present-day psychiatric symptoms carry the long shadow of childhood attention problems into adult daily life. University students who recall strong childhood ADHD symptoms often report impaired functioning across study, family, and social domains.

One hundred ten students scoring above a clinical threshold on a childhood symptom scale completed measures of current symptoms and functional impairment. Childhood symptoms linked directly with family-domain impairment. Current symptoms, especially depression and anxiety, tied more strongly to problems with life skills, self-image, social life, and study. Statistical pathway models found significant indirect links through those current symptoms in nearly every domain.
pmc-13540951:
Yusuf Abdurrahman and colleagues report resistance genes in a 2026 study. The setting is fish farms in Katsina State, Nigeria. The fish is the African catfish, Clarias gariepinus. Gut bacteria from the fish carried the genes of concern. Data on resistance in Nigerian fish farms are scarce.

One hundred healthy fish came from five farms. Lab work yielded forty-nine Gram-negative isolates. Proteus species were the commonest find overall. Resistance ran highest against chloramphenicol and cefoxitin. It ran lowest against gentamicin and ciprofloxacin. Five isolates resisted several drug classes at once. Gene tests found beta-lactam resistance genes in most of those five.
pmc-13542251:
Toshihiro Magaribuchi and colleagues evaluated a 2026 surgical navigation system for robot-assisted partial nephrectomy, the operation that removes a kidney tumour while sparing healthy tissue. Their system projects a three-dimensional model of the patient's kidney onto the live surgical view. Models came from scan data, the actual surgical field was captured with a stereo camera, and the two were aligned only at moments when the organ was barely deformed.

Records from 29 patients at two Japanese hospitals were analysed. Cleaning noise from the camera data improved alignment substantially against the median error of 2.33 millimetres seen without it, and shorter camera distance improved accuracy further. The authors conclude that careful timing makes precise overlay possible, which could help surgeons find deep tumours and preserve kidney function.
pmc-13543351:
Mustafa Yalçın and colleagues published a 2026 imaging study refining how magnetic resonance scans distinguish harmless adrenal adenomas from other adrenal lumps. Chemical shift imaging detects the tiny fat droplets inside adenoma cells: tissue signal drops between two scan settings, and ratios built from that drop guide diagnosis. The retrospective Turkish cohort held 67 patients whose lesions were confirmed by pathology after surgery, 36 of them adenomas.

The chemical shift ratio performed best, and its ideal cut-off in this population sat notably higher than the value quoted in much of the literature, correctly classifying most lesions. The signal intensity index was less sensitive, partly because some adenomas here failed to suppress as expected. Signal from nearby back muscle emerged as a useful extra clue, and two readers agreed closely on all measures. Population-specific thresholds, the authors argue, beat imported ones.
pmc-13543451:
Guoye Lin and colleagues published a 2026 longitudinal study of maths anxiety in primary school children learning with AI-supported instruction, and whether executive function changes the story. Nearly five hundred pupils from grades one, three, and five used AI agent-supported maths lessons roughly twice a week for six months. Anxiety and ability were measured at two time points, and cross-lagged analysis separated which of the two predicts the other over time.

The relationship ran one way: higher maths anxiety foretold later declines in overall ability, computation, and logical-spatial skill, while earlier ability did not predict later anxiety. Executive function complicated the picture. Stronger executive function, and specifically stronger inhibitory control, actually deepened the harm anxiety did to overall and computation scores, contrary to a simple buffering story. Working memory and flexibility showed no such effect. AI classrooms, the authors imply, still need anxiety addressed directly.
pmc-13543551:
Ovie Martin Albert and Alexander Arthur published a 2026 analysis of polysubstance use, meaning use of several substances in the same year, in Canada's 2023 national substance use survey. Canadians aged fifteen and over living in the provinces reported their past-year use, and patterns were classed as single substance, several drugs without alcohol, or drugs combined with alcohol. Weighted estimates described prevalence, and survey models linked each pattern to self-reported harms.

Past-year polysubstance use reached 27.2 percent of respondents, and almost all of it involved alcohol. Drug-only combinations were rare at 0.3 percent. Alcohol with cannabis was the commonest pairing, followed by alcohol with stimulants. Compared with single-substance use, alcohol-involved combinations carried nearly five times the adjusted odds of reporting harm, a result that held under stricter definitions. Prevention and screening, the authors argue, must treat alcohol as part of the polysubstance picture rather than a separate file.
pmc-13546551:
Huang and co-authors apply machine learning to a DNA-repair weakness in this 2026 study of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer short on reliable prognostic markers. They asked whether the homologous recombination deficiency score predicts survival. The score gauges how badly a tumor's DNA repair is broken. They used gene and clinical data from 78 patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas.

High deficiency scores meant much poorer overall survival. Pitting 112 algorithm combinations against each other, a survival support vector machine won, reaching concordance indices of 0.741 in training and 0.708 in testing, and it distilled prognosis to six DNA-damage-response genes. A nomogram combining the gene risk score with clinical variables predicted one- to three-year survival with accuracy above 0.7 in the report. High-deficiency tumors also showed distinctive TP53 and TTN mutations and remodeled immune infiltrates, hinting at roles for PARP inhibitors and immunotherapy.
pmc-13548551:
Mehmet Sinan Saricicek and Ali Taylan Saricicek report a 2026 case linking a popular sports supplement to a migraine attack. Branched-chain amino acids are widely taken after exercise to support muscle recovery, yet their possible role in triggering headaches has barely been examined. Their patient was a healthy twenty-eight-year-old man with no chronic conditions.

Two hours after taking the supplement following a workout, he developed a severe one-sided throbbing headache with nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light. Scans and laboratory tests were normal, and the picture met the standard criteria for migraine without aura. Treatment settled the attack. He stopped the supplement, adopted preventive and lifestyle measures, and stayed attack-free over six months of follow-up. The authors discuss how these amino acids might stir brain signaling and urge formal study of the connection.
pmc-13548651:
Zhengxi Zhang and colleagues test whether thinning in one retinal layer can separate two forms of frontotemporal dementia, in a 2026 imaging study. Frontotemporal lobar degeneration comes in a tau form and a TDP-43 form that look alike in clinic yet differ in brain chemistry. Eighty-six participants, sorted by brain scans and clinical criteria into the two probable subtypes or healthy controls, received detailed retinal imaging segmented by a custom deep learning program.

The outer nuclear layer of the retina thinned widely in the tau group compared with both controls and the TDP group, whose layer stayed intact. A model mixing three retinal measures separated the subtypes with strong exploratory accuracy, clearly beating models built on inner layers alone. Thickness in that layer also tracked thinking scores in tau patients. The authors call the retina a promising window, pending confirmation.
pmc-13549951:
Liankun Song and colleagues created mice carrying the human SKP2 gene switched on only in the prostate, to watch how prostate cancer begins. SKP2 is a protein that drives cell division, and blocking it can prevent tumours in other models. Their 2026 study uses CRISPR to insert the human gene under a prostate-specific promoter.

Extra human SKP2 produced precancerous prostate lesions and low-grade carcinoma in the mice. Gene expression analysis showed changes in cell-shape transition, tissue scaffolding, and interferon signalling pathways. The tumour surroundings also shifted, with more fibroblasts and fewer CD8 T cells and B cells. Human prostate tissue likewise showed raised SKP2 in benign enlargement, precancerous lesions, and cancer. Two known SKP2-blocking compounds reversed the shape-change programme and selectively killed organoids, lab-grown tissue models, from the humanised mice but not from normal mice.
pmc-13551751:
Huan Wang, Ran Zhang, Xiaonan Liu, and Zhen Yang published a 2026 study of clot prevention by nurses in brain surgery. Clots in veins are a key risk during such surgery. Nurses play a central role in prevention. Yet skill in practice lags stated support for the work. The team interviewed twenty nurses at two large hospitals in China in mid to late 2025.

Four themes came out of the talks. Nurses backed prevention in principle. Their grasp of the topic stayed limited, though. Hands-on skill fell short as well. System hurdles blocked good practice. The team calls for structured training and clearer duty lines. They also want a risk tool built for the operating room and stronger teamwork.
pmc-13554051:
Cheng Wang leads a nine-author team tracing how a sticking protein helps gut fistula tracts heal in a 2026 study. Fistula tracts after surgery heal poorly, and the steps behind their closure are little known. The team built the injury in rabbits and watched tissue over twenty-eight days. They also grew gut lining cells in dishes, turning the protein up or down to see effects.

Activity of the protein rose as tracts matured, side by side with scar collagen. Turning it up sped cell growth and travel, and shifted cells toward a mobile form. Turning it down in living rabbits slowed healing and cut scar tissue. A partner pathway inside the cells proved needful for the effect, making the pair a target for future drugs.
pmc-13554151:
Linan Sun leads a seven-author team grading how well counties develop in Henan, a big farming province of China, in a 2026 study. Most past work skipped the county level or gave every place the same scoring weights. Their system uses nineteen measures for 102 counties across 2010 to 2021. A new weighting method lets each county's own pattern set its weights, and links between counties count as well.

Quality rose broadly over the decade, yet strong counties clustered ever tighter near big cities. Weaker counties sat mostly at the province's edges. What drove scores differed sharply by place, from farm and factory roots to land shape. Single factors explained less than pairs acting together. The authors propose tailored paths for each county type.
pmc-13554751:
Kaida Ren leads a large Chinese team setting out a trial of clip-based repair for a leaking tricuspid heart valve in a 2026 protocol. Severe leakage burdens the heart, and drugs ease symptoms without fixing the valve, while open surgery carries high risk. The trial will enrol 236 patients across thirty-five centres. Half receive a catheter clip device, and half receive drug care alone.

Patients must stay symptomatic despite at least a month of drug care and face middling or higher surgical risk. Follow-up runs to five years, with checks at one month, six months, and yearly. The main yardstick at one year blends deaths, valve procedures, hospital stays for heart failure, and health status scores. Results should guide future care for severe leakage.
pmc-13555951:
Faizal Maulana leads a nine-author team charting family ties and chemistry across ten umbrella-plant species from Java and Sumatra in a 2026 study. The genus Heptapleurum holds medicinal promise, yet its family tree stays tangled. The team assembled ten fresh chloroplast genomes plus ribosomal DNA sequences. Chemical profiling named 152 compounds, mostly phenolics and terpenoids.

Two species branched away from the main family group in both gene and chemical trees. Four other species shared nearly identical genomes yet brewed clearly distinct chemistries. Overall, chemical family trees did not match genetic ones. The authors argue genes must rule naming decisions, while chemistry maps useful diversity for conservation and drug hunting in this Sundaland group.
pmc-13558051:
Luigia Trabace and eleven colleagues ran a pilot trial in 2026 of a nutraceutical blend called GeNeurofil in people with mild cognitive impairment. This early stage of decline raises dementia risk and still lacks approved treatments. Earlier animal work suggested the blend protects neurons against amyloid toxicity. The team therefore tested it in 54 patients with mild to moderate impairment. The trial ran six months with a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design.

Patients kept their usual medicines and took the blend or an identical placebo three times a day. After six months, the treated group improved on global dementia rating, mental state testing, and a depression scale relative to placebo. Blood levels of two damage markers, neurofilament light and phosphorylated tau, also fell. The authors present the results as pilot evidence that justifies a larger, longer trial.
pmc-13558651:
Hao Liu and four colleagues mined the UK Biobank in 2026 for links between psychological distress and disorders of the urinary and genital systems. Earlier work treated distress as one blob and rarely followed people forward in time. With half a million participants, the team scored six validated distress instruments covering mood, anxiety, neuroticism, and bodily symptoms, then related them to eight non-infectious urogenital conditions, both at enrolment and prospectively.

Higher scores on every scale came with more urogenital disease. Bodily symptom scores showed the strongest links, roughly raising the hazard of urgency incontinence, bladder pain syndrome, and pelvic pain by about half. Age, sex, and menopause status modified several associations, with bladder conditions tying closer to distress in women and pelvic floor dysfunction in men. Chronic prostate inflammation showed little prospective link. Mental health screening, the authors suggest, belongs in urology clinics.
pmc-13563951:
Natsumi Toyoda and colleagues report, in a 2026 case study, a 59-year-old Japanese man whose anaplastic meningioma, a high-grade tumor of the membranes around the brain, spread widely outside the skull. He first had numbness on the right side of his face and double vision, and scans showed a mass reaching toward the sinuses and the eye canal.

Microscope work found two cell patterns side by side, one resembling typical meningioma and one poorly formed with sarcoma-like features. Spread through that second element reached twelve organs outside the skull, including lung, bone, and liver, confirmed at autopsy. Such extensive spread is rare, and the report helps pathologists recognize the aggressive form.
pmc-13571351:
Yurie Yoshikado and co-authors report a single difficult heart case from 2026: severe mitral regurgitation, a badly leaking mitral valve, in a patient who could not safely receive heparin. The 59-year-old man developed cardiogenic shock and needed an intra-aortic balloon pump, a device that helps the heart pump blood.

While awaiting surgery, his platelet count fell sharply and antibody testing supported suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, a dangerous immune reaction to heparin. Because bypass surgery requires full heparin treatment, the team instead performed catheter-based edge-to-edge valve repair while giving argatroban, an alternative blood thinner. Two implants reduced the leak from severe to trivial, with no clotting or bleeding problems. The patient recovered quickly, the pump was removed at once, and he was taken off the ventilator early.
pmc-13572351:
Haiyan Dong and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, small engineered binding proteins aimed at E6. This viral protein destroys the guardian protein p53 in cervical cancers driven by human papillomavirus type 18. Candidates were fished from a phage display library and fitted with a tag that carries them inside cells.

The best candidate bound E6 specifically in cancer cells, gathered quickly in mouse tumors, and stayed there for hours. Inside cells it stabilized p53 and switched on death-promoting and braking genes. Pairing it with a sibling molecule against the partner viral protein E7 killed more cancer cells than either alone. The pair strategy offers a targeted route against HPV-driven cervical cancer.
pmc-13572451:
Noemí Tomsen, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of a cooling-flavoured drink that aids swallowing after stroke. Many stroke survivors swallow poorly, which raises the risk of food or fluid entering the airway. The drink holds compounds that trigger a cold sensor in the mouth and throat, which may sharpen the swallow reflex.

Fifty patients with chronic swallowing trouble took part in a crossover trial, so each person tried both the active drink and a plain control in random order. Swallow tests and counts of spontaneous swallows gauged the effect. The active drink raised spontaneous swallow rate by 51.6 percent and cut unsafe swallows by 22 percent. Saliva levels of substance P, a signal tied to swallowing, rose by 15 percent. The plain drink changed none of these measures.
pmc-13572551:
Nuha Desi Anggraeni, with two colleagues, reports on a 2026 study of see-through solar panels on the tropical coast of Indonesia. Panels that pass some light can serve as windows or shades, but heat and damp air test their output. The team asked which weather factors drive their performance and how steady it stays over years.

Ten years of daily weather data, from 2012 to 2022, fed regression models of the performance ratio and energy yield. Three model shapes were compared, from a full set of weather inputs down to a fixed benchmark. Sunlight on the tilted panel and air temperature drove most of the change in output. A lean model with just those two inputs matched the full model closely. Performance ratio estimates sat between 0.78 and 0.80, in line with past tropical values.
pmc-13574151:
Weitong Su and a large team report a 2026 study of a fat that weakens immune guard cells inside belly fat during obesity. Those guard cells, regulatory T cells, keep metabolism calm in lean tissue. In obesity they falter, and the team asked which food fat flips the switch.

Palmitic acid, a saturated fat, but not its cousin oleic acid, switched on a factor called Crebzf in the guard cells of obese mice. Animals lacking that factor in these cells resisted diet-driven obesity and inflammation, since their guard cells suppressed immune attack better. Moving such cells into mice with no lymphocytes calmed disease more than normal cells did. The factor teams with a partner to blunt Foxp3, the master guard gene. In human fat, the factor ran high where Foxp3 ran low.
pmc-13587551:
Ningning Xia and colleagues map how symptoms cluster in the first week after pancreatic cancer surgery. The operation is among the hardest in cancer care, and patients wake to a crowd of complaints at once. Their 2026 study asked 213 patients on day seven to rate 22 symptoms on a standard inventory. The team then drew a network showing which symptoms travel together and which sit at the web's center.

Seventeen symptoms touched more than three in ten patients. Lost appetite, broken sleep, distress, pain, and fatigue were the most common, and lost appetite, vomiting, and fatigue cut deepest. In the network, vomiting sat at the very center, with distress and sweating close behind, while swelling, fatigue, and irritability bridged between clusters. The authors suggest that easing a central symptom like vomiting might calm several neighbors at once.
pmc-13590251:
Shunsuke Shiota and four colleagues tackle a planning problem for studies that test how well a test finds disease. Such studies must fix their size in advance: too few people gives shaky results, while too many wastes money and burdens patients. Older methods treat key rates, such as how often a test catches disease, as fixed known values. Their method instead uses Bayesian tools, which fold prior belief and doubt into the plan.

Two kinds of prior are used, one for the study design and one for the final read of results. The team works out how often a future study of each size would meet a preset success mark. In their tests, less doubt in the design priors shrank the size needed. A more hopeful read prior did the same, which planners should note with care.
pmc-13593651:
Ana Freifrau von Rotenhan and colleagues tested whether a therapy dog in the dental chair can calm anxious children, measuring heart rate before, during, and after treatment. Sixty children aged five to twelve took part in their 2026 study, half treated with a dog present and half receiving standard care.

Heart rate in the dog group fell by about five beats per minute across the visit. It rose slightly in the control group. The gap between groups was clearest after treatment ended. Blood oxygen stayed steady throughout. Parents often said they felt calmer themselves and saw their children cooperate better with the dog nearby. The authors are careful about one gap: anxiety questionnaires were collected only in the dog group, so claims about felt anxiety rest on weaker ground than the heart rate findings.
pmc-13596751:
Marina Abdelshahid leads an eleven-author study of blood-based inflammation scores in 130 adults who had knee ligament reconstruction, asking whether metabolic syndrome leaves a measurable immune signature after surgery. Six composite indices were computed from routine blood counts taken at least ninety days after the operation, and patients were grouped by whether they met the syndrome's criteria.

Overall, the inflammation indices did not separate the metabolic syndrome group from the rest. The picture changed by sex: women with the syndrome ran significantly higher on four indices than men with it. Higher body mass and blood sugar tracked with one index, while low protective cholesterol tracked with several. Postoperative complications also came with elevated scores. The authors suggest that sex and individual metabolic traits shape post-surgical inflammation more than the syndrome label alone.
pmc-13607251:
Mehmet Melih Yılmaz leads an eleven-author team testing two vitamin supplements as protectors for frozen ram semen. Freezing damages ram sperm badly, and oxidative stress is a chief culprit. Pooled semen was split into four extender groups: plain control, nicotinic acid alone, and two nicotinic-folic acid combinations. After thawing, the team measured motility, membrane and DNA integrity, oxidative markers, and two genes' activity and methylation.

The middle combination, 10 millimolar nicotinic acid with 50 nanomolar folic acid, gave the highest motility numerically at 53.34 percent against the control's 43.44 percent, though that gap missed significance. Its clear wins were the lowest acrosome damage, 36.50 percent against 48.00 percent in controls, and better mitochondrial membrane potential. That combination also changed OGG1 gene expression alongside matching DNA methylation shifts. The authors suggest these supplements, especially paired, improve post-thaw ram semen quality.
pmc-13615051:
Marie Line Chedid and colleagues review in 2026 the non-surgical causes of nasal necrosis. This is the death of skin or soft tissue on the nose. They gather case reports and case series from three databases up to December 2025. Causes span severe infection, immune attacks on small blood vessels, drug harm, cancer, and pressure from medical devices. Surgery is often the first thought, yet some patients are treated without it and guidance for them is thin.

Thirty-nine publications met the team's rules. They pulled out each case's cause, signs, tests, treatment, and outcome, and rated the quality of each report with a standard tool. The result is a map of how this rare, alarming problem shows up when an operation is not the driver, giving clinicians a clearer path for diagnosis and drug-based care.
pmc-13616251:
Jinjin Tong and colleagues build a smart nanoparticle that delivers silymarin, a milk thistle extract that protects the liver, to patients recovering from liver surgery. Plain silymarin absorbs poorly. Their particles are built from a modified chitosan shell and measure 250 to 300 nanometres. They release cargo faster in acid and amid reactive oxygen. Those are exactly the conditions at a healing wound site.

Against standard tests the particles beat free silymarin at mopping up harmful radicals, scoring 92.31 percent on one measure, and they mildly curbed two common bacteria. Blood and cell tests showed good safety. Given by mouth to dogs after liver surgery, the particles shifted gut microbes and their chemical output in directions tied to liver health, underlining the gut-liver partnership in recovery.
pmc-13616751:
Faruk Gazi Ceranoğlu, Mehmet Tuğrul Yılmaz, Duygu Akın Saygın, and Cengiz Kadıyoran report 2026 reference values for six angles of the heel bone. Their group held 540 healthy adults aged 20 to 65. They also test how well those angles guess a person's sex. The heel bone carries walking and balance and is often rebuilt after fractures, so normal angle ranges guide surgery. Measurements came from X-rays of both feet.

Some angles differed between right and left sides, and the compression angle differed between men and women. The standard accuracy test for sex prediction gave a weak separation of the sexes. The verdict follows from that result. These angles make useful clinical references for this population, but poor tools for sexing a skeleton. Local reference data matter, since angles measured elsewhere may not fit Turkish patients.
pmc-13617151:
Rohan A. Phadke and seven colleagues compare the long-term value of two operations for lumbar spinal stenosis, the narrowing of the spinal canal that is the most common reason older adults have spine surgery. One option is minimally invasive tubular decompression through a small tube; the other is traditional open laminectomy. Their computer model followed a simulated group of ten thousand sixty-five-year-olds for ten years from a United States payer viewpoint.

In the base case the minimally invasive route cost over four thousand dollars less per patient while giving slightly more quality-adjusted life years, a rare win on both cost and health. It stayed cost-effective in most simulations at common funding thresholds, helped by fewer complications and a cheaper initial operation. The authors say the result should inform coverage policy rather than dictate it, since some inputs remain uncertain.
pmc-13617351:
Iman Nazari and three colleagues present an automated workflow that computes GenePy scores, a gene-level burden measure for rare disease genomes. Single-variant reading of a genome can miss the combined weight of several mild variants in one gene. GenePy instead folds variant consequence, allele frequency, and zygosity into one score per gene per person. The workflow runs inside the Genomics England research environment.

Built on the Nextflow system and deployed through the Lifebit CloudOS platform, the pipeline is fully containerized, meaning each step carries its own software environment for reproducibility. It harmonizes variant annotation, quality control, and chunked aggregation so burden scores can be computed securely across population-scale cohorts under strict governance rules. The authors say auditable gene-level scoring sharpens the search for diagnosis in unresolved single-gene disorders and feeds statistical prioritization and phenotype matching downstream.
pmc-13618951:
Ioannis Kyvernitakis and seven colleagues track cervical stiffness in pregnant women fitted with a cervical pessary, a silicone ring meant to support a shortening cervix and prevent preterm birth. Eighty-nine women were measured with the Pregnolia system early in the second half of pregnancy and again four weeks later. Thirty had received a pessary for a cervix of twenty-five millimeters or less, and fifty-nine healthy women served as controls.

In controls, median stiffness drifted downward over the four weeks, a change that was nominally significant but faded after statistical correction. In the pessary group, stiffness stayed flat, while cervical length and the uterocervical angle did not change in either group, and birth weights were similar. The authors read this as a potential stabilizing association worth confirming. They stress that studies including untreated women with short cervixes are needed to separate the device's effect from natural variation.
pmc-13619051:
Nyissa A. Walsh and five colleagues review what is known about sex differences in sleep waves, in a 2026 synthesis spanning adults with and without insomnia. Sleep spindles and slow-wave activity shape sleep quality, and insomnia is more prevalent in women. Yet sex effects on these oscillations are poorly mapped. The team searched four databases, appraised bias with two scales, and pooled results where possible.

Forty-three studies qualified, but thirteen, covering six hundred sixty-eight normal sleepers, reported enough for meta-analysis. There, women showed higher spindle density and stronger sigma and delta power than men. Most remaining studies recruited people with insomnia. Their statistics were too incompletely reported to pool, and interactions between sex and diagnosis were sparse. The authors conclude that the female advantage in these sleep rhythms is real among healthy sleepers, while the insomnia side urgently needs better-designed and better-reported studies.
pmc-13619751:
C Van der Meer and three colleagues audited a fracture liaison service at a Johannesburg hospital, a program meant to prevent second fractures in people with fragile bones. They reviewed 247 patients admitted to the orthopedic ward and enrolled between October 2022 and June 2024. Records covered risk factors, test results, treatments given, and how long patients stayed.

Most patients were women between sixty and eighty-nine, and hip fractures dominated the caseload. Calcium and vitamin D reached most patients, yet only about a quarter received the bone-strengthening infusion drug while in hospital. Drug shortages explained most missed doses, and kidney disease ruled out others. Vitamin D insufficiency was common, men smoked and drank far more than women, and many patients had fallen before or showed poor thinking scores. The authors say the service helps but cannot reach full effect while drug supply stays unreliable.
pmc-13620851:
Hamid Valizadeh, Mehdi Taghinejad-Roudbaneh, and Ruhollah Kianfar worked out how much lysine young Japanese quail chicks actually need, and how that need shifts with the protein level of the feed. The first two weeks after hatching set up a quail's lifetime productivity, yet requirement tables for modern fast-growing strains are thin. Nine hundred chicks were raised on fifteen diets mixing three protein levels with five lysine levels.

Growth, feed use, and carcass traits all responded to both factors, and the two interacted for several measures. A mid-range lysine level gave the best weight and protein efficiency before gains leveled off. Requirement estimates from a linear broken-line model, which finds the point where gains plateau, rose with protein level and fit the data better than a curved model. The authors advise setting lysine as a share that climbs with dietary protein.
pmc-13621351:
Anjusha Prakash and four colleagues tested simple, flexible molecular sensors that grab phosphate-type anions out of water. Phosphates run everything from cell energy to fertilizer, yet their strong love of water makes them hard to catch and measure. Ring-shaped receptors bind well but are painful to make, so the team tried straight-chain sensors armed with charged hydrogen-bond donors of three kinds.

Fluorescence titrations showed the chains bound dihydrogen phosphate most tightly, with a clear pecking order across related anions, including the cell energy carriers ATP and ADP. The sensors also caught glyphosate, the widely used herbicide flagged as a possible carcinogen, at weaker strength. Because each sensor answers slightly differently, arrays of them plus machine learning sorted and measured mixtures with perfect classification in the reported tests. Detection limits reached about one micromole per liter for phosphate.
pmc-13623451:
Patrick Steven Tajanlangit and Sean Michael Tajanlangit published a 2026 review of shared epigenetic mechanisms linking eczema and food allergy. Epigenetics covers chemical marks that switch genes up or down without changing the DNA code. The two conditions often appear together in the atopic march, the childhood drift from eczema toward hay fever and asthma, and genetics explains only part of the risk.

The review pulls together studies of DNA methylation, histone changes, and small regulatory RNAs across skin and gut tissue. Recurring marks sit on the genes for two immune signals, IL-4 and IL-13, and on FOXP3, a gene that keeps immune tolerance in place. Silencing of barrier genes in skin and gut lining appears in both diseases. The authors argue that this layer of control lets early skin damage prime the gut to react to foods, and they point to allergy biomarkers and treatments as the payoff.
pmc-13624051:
Iasmin Góes Frossard leads a study of how worker body size shapes the skin, or cuticle, of two leaf-cutting ant species. Colonies of these ants split work among small, medium, and large workers, and small bodies lose water faster through their surface. The cuticle's thickness and its fatty outer layer are its main defence against drying out.

Workers of both species were sorted by head width into the three size classes, and cuticle traits were measured on each. Small workers carried thicker cuticles and a stronger lipid signal than medium and large workers, in both species. The lipid response did not separate the species, but cuticle thickness did: one species ran thicker-skinned at every size. The authors argue that size sets the pattern, while each species' work roles tune it, since small workers tend the fungus gardens indoors and large ones forage and defend outside.
pmc-13625251:
Walid Shaalan and a large team audit how far genetic counseling reaches women treated for ovarian cancer at one center.
